Tutorial

# Chapter 1 - Jump Start

`Goal`: Observe how Daana generates an integrated, time-aware data warehouse from four different source-data shapes, using only YAML declarations and three CLI commands.

`What you'll see`: Customer data merged from three independent source systems and full change history tracked automatically, all available for query immediately.

`Time`: typically 10-15 minutes

``Before starting`: Complete the Quickstart Tutorial to set up your project and databases.

## The Source Data

The Book Retailer's customer data resides in four independent source tables. The columns differ between tables, and the `shape` of each table differs as well. Daana represents each shape with one value of a single mapping field, `ingestion_strategy`. The four shapes used in this tutorial are described below.

``stage.customers`` (shape: change log). One row is written each time CRM data changes, timestamped with `updated_at`. Customer 1 appears twice because their status changed:

` customer_id | first_name | last_name | account_status | updated_at
-------------+------------+-----------+----------------+---------------------
 1 | John | Smith | Active | 2024-11-09 17:44:59
 2 | Emily | Johnson | Active | 2024-11-04 18:24:50
 3 | Michael | Brown | Active | 2024-10-16 10:37:12
 ...
 1 | John | Smith | Inactive | 2024-11-25 14:30:22 <- status changed
 3 | Michael | Brown | Suspended | 2024-11-27 16:45:18 <- status changed
`

``stage.customer_addresses`` (shape: daily snapshot). The source writes one row per customer per night, regardless of whether the address changed. Most rows are duplicates of the previous day's row (275 in total, one per customer per day):

` customer_id | city | state | snapshot_date
-------------+--------------+-------+---------------
 2 | Boston | MA | 2024-11-05
 2 | Boston | MA | 2024-11-28
 2 | Philadelphia | PA | 2024-11-29 <- address changed
 ...
`

``stage.loyalty_memberships`` (shape: current-state lookup). One row per active member, updated in place when the tier changes. The source system stores no history of its own; only the current state is available:

` customer_id | tier_level | join_date
-------------+------------+------------
 1 | Gold | 2023-01-10
 2 | Silver | 2023-02-14
 4 | Gold | 2023-04-20
 6 | Platinum | 2023-06-10
 ...
`

When a tier value changes between runs, Daana writes a new version instead of overwriting; chapter 4 covers how.

``stage.sales_orders`` (shape: transactional). Immutable order events. Each row is written once when the order is placed and never updated, and the row carries both a monetary amount and its currency code:

` order_id | customer_id | order_status | total_amount | currency | order_date
----------+-------------+--------------+--------------+----------+---------------------
 1 | 1 | Delivered | 60.33 | USD | 2024-11-01 10:30:00
 2 | 2 | Delivered | 24.49 | USD | 2024-11-02 14:15:00
 6 | 6 | Delivered | 92.38 | USD | 2024-11-06 13:20:00
`

### Why this is hard without Daana

Producing a single unified, time-aware customer view from these four shapes the traditional way requires four different ingestion patterns inside one pipeline:

- `CDC merge` for the change log, picking the latest version per `updated_at`.

- `Snapshot deduplication` for the daily address dumps, reducing 275 rows to one row per actual address change.

- `SCD2 reconstruction` for loyalty memberships, because the source overwrites in place and history has to be derived downstream.

- `Append-only inserts with deduplication` for the orders, plus a separate decision about how to keep `total_amount` and `currency` aligned if either ever changes.

Then a `FULL OUTER JOIN` across the four streams, key reconciliation, and `valid_from`/`valid_to` columns so analysts can answer "what did this customer look like on 27 November?". The result is a custom ETL implementation that has to be re-checked whenever the source schema drifts.

In Daana, each shape maps to one `ingestion_strategy`. This chapter uses three: `FULL_LOG` for both the change log and the daily snapshot, `FULL` for the loyalty lookup, and `TRANSACTIONAL` for the orders. This configuration is enough for Daana to generate the merging, attribute-level history, and snapshot deduplication automatically. Chapter 4 walks through each strategy in detail.

## Author Your Model and Mappings

You've already run `daana-cli init my-tutorial --example quickstart`, which set up the data, Docker, and a workflow scaffold. Two pieces remain for you to author by hand:

- `model.yaml` at the project root, which declares the business entities, attributes, and relationships. The file ships with a placeholder so this chapter can replace it directly.

- Two mapping files in `mappings/`, which connect each entity to its source tables. The directory ships empty; you generate the skeletons with `daana-cli generate mapping` and complete them.

This is the same authoring loop used on real projects. The remainder of this chapter walks through each file.

### Author the Model

Start with the model file. Open `model.yaml` in your editor and replace its contents with the following:

`model:
 id: BOOK_RETAILER_MODEL
 name: BookRetailerModel
 definition: Unified customer and order data from multiple sources
 description: Merges customer data with address snapshots for time-travel analytics

 entities:
 - id: CUSTOMER
 name: CUSTOMER
 definition: Customer who places orders
 description: Unified customer data from customers table and address snapshots
 attributes:
 - id: customer_id
 name: customer_id
 definition: Unique customer identifier
 type: STRING

 - id: customer_name
 name: customer_name
 definition: Full name of the customer
 type: STRING
 effective_timestamp: true

 - id: customer_status
 name: customer_status
 definition: Account status (Active, Inactive, Suspended)
 type: STRING
 effective_timestamp: true

 - id: customer_city
 name: customer_city
 definition: City where customer is located
 type: STRING
 effective_timestamp: true

 - id: customer_state
 name: customer_state
 definition: State where customer is located
 type: STRING
 effective_timestamp: true

 - id: customer_loyalty_tier
 name: customer_loyalty_tier
 definition: Loyalty program tier level (Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum)
 type: STRING
 effective_timestamp: true

 - id: ORDER
 name: ORDER
 definition: Purchase order
 description: Orders placed by customers
 attributes:
 - id: order_id
 name: order_id
 definition: Unique order identifier
 type: STRING

 - id: order_status
 name: order_status
 definition: Current order status
 type: STRING
 effective_timestamp: true

 - id: order_purchase_ts
 name: order_purchase_ts
 definition: When order was placed
 type: START_TIMESTAMP

 - id: order_value
 name: order_value
 definition: Total monetary value of the order
 description: Amount and currency bundled as an atomic concept
 effective_timestamp: true
 group:
 - id: order_value_amount
 name: order_value_amount
 definition: Monetary amount
 type: NUMBER
 - id: order_value_currency
 name: order_value_currency
 definition: Currency code (ISO 4217, e.g. USD, EUR)
 type: UNIT

 relationships:
 - name: IS_PLACED_BY
 definition: Order is placed by a customer
 source_entity_id: ORDER
 target_entity_id: CUSTOMER
`

Validate the file:

`daana-cli check model
`

The model declares two entities (CUSTOMER and ORDER) and the `IS_PLACED_BY` relationship between them. Most attributes carry `effective_timestamp: true` so Daana tracks their change history independently. Chapter 2 walks through that and the other field types in detail. One type is worth flagging now because it explains an asymmetry between the two mappings you are about to write:

- ``type: START_TIMESTAMP`` marks `order_purchase_ts` as the event timestamp that places the order on the timeline. Daana uses it as the entity's effective timestamp for the order, so the order mapping does not need to set `entity_effective_timestamp_expression` for this attribute. See START_TIMESTAMP.

### Generate Mapping Skeletons

Bootstrap one mapping file per entity:

`daana-cli generate mapping
`

Output:

`Generating mapping templates...

Model: model.yaml
Output: mappings/

Generated 2 mapping template(s)
 Generated CUSTOMER: customer-mapping.yaml
 Generated ORDER: order-mapping.yaml
`

This writes `mappings/customer-mapping.yaml` and `mappings/order-mapping.yaml`. Each skeleton lists every entity attribute once with a placeholder `transformation_expression`, sets `primary_keys` to the natural-key attribute id (`customer_id`, `order_id`), defaults `ingestion_strategy` to `FULL_LOG`, and pre-fills `connection`, `table`, and (where applicable) `entity_effective_timestamp_expression` with placeholder values you replace. The order skeleton also lists each model relationship once with the correct `id` and a placeholder `target_transformation_expression`. None of the placeholders are validated against the source schema; the next two sections replace them with the real expressions.

Each skeleton starts with a single source table block. CUSTOMER is sourced from three systems in this tutorial, so the next section adds two more table blocks under `tables:`; ORDER is sourced from a single table and stays one block.

### Complete the Customer Mapping

Open `mappings/customer-mapping.yaml` and replace its contents with the following:

`entity_id: CUSTOMER

mapping_groups:
 - name: default_mapping_group
 tables:
 # Source 1: CRM data, core customer records with full status change history
 - connection: dev
 table: stage.customers
 primary_keys:
 - customer_id
 ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG
 entity_effective_timestamp_expression: updated_at
 attributes:
 - id: customer_id
 transformation_expression: customer_id
 - id: customer_name
 transformation_expression: CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)
 - id: customer_status
 transformation_expression: account_status

 # Source 2: Address snapshots, merged automatically with Source 1
 - connection: dev
 table: stage.customer_addresses
 primary_keys:
 - customer_id
 ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG
 entity_effective_timestamp_expression: snapshot_date
 attributes:
 - id: customer_city
 transformation_expression: city
 - id: customer_state
 transformation_expression: state

 # Source 3: Loyalty tier, merged automatically with Sources 1 and 2
 - connection: dev
 table: stage.loyalty_memberships
 primary_keys:
 - customer_id
 ingestion_strategy: FULL
 entity_effective_timestamp_expression: join_date
 attributes:
 - id: customer_loyalty_tier
 transformation_expression: tier_level
`

The mapping assembles CUSTOMER from three source tables in a single mapping group: the CRM change log (`stage.customers`, `FULL_LOG`), the daily address snapshots (`stage.customer_addresses`, `FULL_LOG`), and the current-state loyalty roster (`stage.loyalty_memberships`, `FULL`). Each table block specifies the connection, the source table, the primary key column, the ingestion strategy, the column that supplies the effective timestamp, and the transformation expression for each attribute. Merging across tables is generated by Daana when the entity is materialized.

`connection: dev` resolves against the `dev` profile in `connections.yaml`, which `--example quickstart` set to point at the local PostgreSQL container. See Connection Profiles for the full reference.

The `mapping_groups` list has a single entry in this chapter; Chapter 2 covers when an entity needs more than one.

### Complete the Order Mapping

Open `mappings/order-mapping.yaml` and replace its contents with the following:

`entity_id: ORDER

mapping_groups:
 - name: default_mapping_group
 tables:
 - connection: dev
 table: stage.sales_orders
 primary_keys:
 - order_id
 ingestion_strategy: TRANSACTIONAL
 batch_expression: ingested_at
 entity_effective_timestamp_expression: order_date
 attributes:
 - id: order_id
 transformation_expression: order_id
 - id: order_status
 transformation_expression: order_status
 - id: order_purchase_ts
 transformation_expression: order_date
 - id: order_value_amount # child attribute of the order_value group
 transformation_expression: total_amount
 - id: order_value_currency # child attribute of the order_value group
 transformation_expression: currency

 relationships:
 - id: ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER
 source_table: stage.sales_orders
 target_transformation_expression: customer_id
`

The order is sourced from a single table (`stage.sales_orders`, `TRANSACTIONAL`). The two child attributes of the `order_value` group are mapped individually (`order_value_amount` and `order_value_currency`), and the `relationships` block resolves `IS_PLACED_BY` by pointing at the `customer_id` column on the source table. `daana-cli generate mapping` pre-filled the relationship `id`. Chapter 2 walks through the naming rule.

### Validate

`daana-cli check workflow
`

A successful check confirms the model and both mappings parse, the entity and attribute references resolve, and the mappings cover every attribute declared on the model. `deploy` and `execute` invoke `check` internally, so this step is optional, but running it once after authoring catches typos before any database changes happen.

The check also surfaces three warnings about the `dev` connection profile: the `password` and `user` fields are hardcoded rather than read from environment variables, and `sslmode` is `disable`. These are intentional for the local sandbox so the tutorial runs without extra setup. Chapter 6 covers the production hardening (secrets, TLS, separate profiles).

## Deploy and Execute

You already ran `daana-cli install` during the tutorial setup. Install is environment-level and runs once per database. From here, deploy the workflow and execute it:

`daana-cli deploy

daana-cli execute
`

## Explore What Daana Built

For each entity in your model, Daana generates three types of views in the `daana_dw` schema:

ViewContents

 | `view_<entity>` | Current state, one row per entity

 | `view_<entity>_hist` | Full change history, one row per tracked version

 | `view_<entity>_with_rel` | Current state with all related entities joined

Daana also generates per-relationship junction views (such as `view_order_is_placed_by_customer`) and internal `v_<entity>_desc` views (here `v_customer_desc` and `v_order_desc`) over the raw EAV-style storage (Entity-Attribute-Value: each attribute lives in its own row keyed by entity id and attribute name, instead of as a wide table column); Chapter 2 lists the full set and explains the underlying tables.

These views form a complete, historized business layer. They can be queried directly or used as building blocks for a traditional dimensional mart (dimensions and fact tables). Chapter 7 walks through that process. Future versions of Daana will generate dimensional marts automatically.

`customer_key` is each customer's surrogate key (always typed `character varying`); the `::integer` cast in `ORDER BY` clauses sorts numerically. Chapter 2 explains how Daana derives it.

Open a `psql` shell against the local container so you can run the upcoming SQL queries:

`docker exec -it daana-customerdb psql -U dev -d customerdb
`

### Query 1: Three sources, one unified view

All three source systems are merged into a single row per customer:

`SELECT
 customer_key,
 customer_name,
 customer_status,
 customer_city,
 customer_state,
 customer_loyalty_tier
FROM daana_dw.view_customer
ORDER BY customer_key::integer;
`

Result:

` customer_key | customer_name | customer_status | customer_city | customer_state | customer_loyalty_tier
--------------+---------------------+-----------------+---------------+----------------+-----------------------
 1 | John Smith | Inactive | New York | NY | Gold
 2 | Emily Johnson | Active | Philadelphia | PA | Silver
 3 | Michael Brown | Suspended | Brooklyn | NY | Bronze
 4 | Sarah Davis | Active | Cambridge | MA | Gold
 5 | David Wilson | Active | Queens | NY | Silver
 6 | Jennifer Martinez | Active | New York | NY | Platinum
 7 | Robert Anderson | Active | San Francisco | CA |
 8 | Lisa Taylor | Active | San Francisco | CA | Bronze
 9 | James Thomas | Active | Los Angeles | CA | Silver
 10 | Maria Garcia | Active | Boston | MA | Bronze
(10 rows)
`

One row per customer, assembled from three independent source tables. Robert Anderson (customer 7) has no loyalty membership record; his `customer_loyalty_tier` is empty. Daana handles missing data across sources without additional configuration.

The 12 rows in `stage.customers` reduce to 10 here because customers 1 and 3 each carry an additional status-change row (`Active` -> `Inactive`, `Active` -> `Suspended`); `FULL_LOG` ingestion preserves those as historical versions rather than duplicate customers, and the current-state view shows only the latest version per entity.

### Query 2: The full change history for one customer

Emily (customer 2) has dozens of rows in `stage.customer_addresses` and two rows in `stage.customers`. Daana deduplicates the snapshots, detects only actual changes, and stores one row per distinct version:

`SELECT
 customer_name,
 customer_city,
 customer_state,
 customer_status,
 customer_loyalty_tier,
 eff_tmstp
FROM daana_dw.view_customer_hist
WHERE customer_key = '2'
ORDER BY eff_tmstp;
`

Result:

---------------+---------------+----------------+-----------------+-----------------------+---------------------

- Two mapping files in `mappings/`, which connect each entity to its source tables. The directory ships empty; you generate the skeletons with `daana-cli generate mapping` and complete them.

This is the same authoring loop used on real projects. The remainder of this chapter walks through each file.

### Author the Model

Start with the model file. Open `model.yaml` in your editor and replace its contents with the following:

`model:
 id: BOOK_RETAILER_MODEL
 name: BookRetailerModel
 definition: Unified customer and order data from multiple sources
 description: Merges customer data with address snapshots for time-travel analytics

 entities:
 - id: CUSTOMER
 name: CUSTOMER
 definition: Customer who places orders
 description: Unified customer data from customers table and address snapshots
 attributes:
 - id: customer_id
 name: customer_id
 definition: Unique customer identifier
 type: STRING

 - id: customer_name
 name: customer_name
 definition: Full name of the customer
 type: STRING
 effective_timestamp: true

 - id: customer_status
 name: customer_status
 definition: Account status (Active, Inactive, Suspended)
 type: STRING
 effective_timestamp: true

 - id: customer_city
 name: customer_city
 definition: City where customer is located
 type: STRING
 effective_timestamp: true

 - id: customer_state
 name: customer_state
 definition: State where customer is located
 type: STRING
 effective_timestamp: true

 - id: customer_loyalty_tier
 name: customer_loyalty_tier
 definition: Loyalty program tier level (Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum)
 type: STRING
 effective_timestamp: true

 - id: ORDER
 name: ORDER
 definition: Purchase order
 description: Orders placed by customers
 attributes:
 - id: order_id
 name: order_id
 definition: Unique order identifier
 type: STRING

 - id: order_status
 name: order_status
 definition: Current order status
 type: STRING
 effective_timestamp: true

 - id: order_purchase_ts
 name: order_purchase_ts
 definition: When order was placed
 type: START_TIMESTAMP

 - id: order_value
 name: order_value
 definition: Total monetary value of the order
 description: Amount and currency bundled as an atomic concept
 effective_timestamp: true
 group:
 - id: order_value_amount
 name: order_value_amount
 definition: Monetary amount
 type: NUMBER
 - id: order_value_currency
 name: order_value_currency
 definition: Currency code (ISO 4217, e.g. USD, EUR)
 type: UNIT

 relationships:
 - name: IS_PLACED_BY
 definition: Order is placed by a customer
 source_entity_id: ORDER
 target_entity_id: CUSTOMER
`

Validate the file:

`daana-cli check model
`

The model declares two entities (CUSTOMER and ORDER) and the `IS_PLACED_BY` relationship between them. Most attributes carry `effective_timestamp: true` so Daana tracks their change history independently. Chapter 2 walks through that and the other field types in detail. One type is worth flagging now because it explains an asymmetry between the two mappings you are about to write:

- ``type: START_TIMESTAMP`` marks `order_purchase_ts` as the event timestamp that places the order on the timeline. Daana uses it as the entity's effective timestamp for the order, so the order mapping does not need to set `entity_effective_timestamp_expression` for this attribute. See START_TIMESTAMP.

### Generate Mapping Skeletons

Bootstrap one mapping file per entity:

`daana-cli generate mapping
`

Output:

`Generating mapping templates...

Model: model.yaml
Output: mappings/

Generated 2 mapping template(s)
 Generated CUSTOMER: customer-mapping.yaml
 Generated ORDER: order-mapping.yaml
`

This writes `mappings/customer-mapping.yaml` and `mappings/order-mapping.yaml`. Each skeleton lists every entity attribute once with a placeholder `transformation_expression`, sets `primary_keys` to the natural-key attribute id (`customer_id`, `order_id`), defaults `ingestion_strategy` to `FULL_LOG`, and pre-fills `connection`, `table`, and (where applicable) `entity_effective_timestamp_expression` with placeholder values you replace. The order skeleton also lists each model relationship once with the correct `id` and a placeholder `target_transformation_expression`. None of the placeholders are validated against the source schema; the next two sections replace them with the real expressions.

Each skeleton starts with a single source table block. CUSTOMER is sourced from three systems in this tutorial, so the next section adds two more table blocks under `tables:`; ORDER is sourced from a single table and stays one block.

### Complete the Customer Mapping

Open `mappings/customer-mapping.yaml` and replace its contents with the following:

`entity_id: CUSTOMER

mapping_groups:
 - name: default_mapping_group
 tables:
 # Source 1: CRM data, core customer records with full status change history
 - connection: dev
 table: stage.customers
 primary_keys:
 - customer_id
 ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG
 entity_effective_timestamp_expression: updated_at
 attributes:
 - id: customer_id
 transformation_expression: customer_id
 - id: customer_name
 transformation_expression: CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)
 - id: customer_status
 transformation_expression: account_status

 # Source 2: Address snapshots, merged automatically with Source 1
 - connection: dev
 table: stage.customer_addresses
 primary_keys:
 - customer_id
 ingestion_strategy: FULL_LOG
 entity_effective_timestamp_expression: snapshot_date
 attributes:
 - id: customer_city
 transformation_expression: city
 - id: customer_state
 transformation_expression: state

 # Source 3: Loyalty tier, merged automatically with Sources 1 and 2
 - connection: dev
 table: stage.loyalty_memberships
 primary_keys:
 - customer_id
 ingestion_strategy: FULL
 entity_effective_timestamp_expression: join_date
 attributes:
 - id: customer_loyalty_tier
 transformation_expression: tier_level
`

The mapping assembles CUSTOMER from three source tables in a single mapping group: the CRM change log (`stage.customers`, `FULL_LOG`), the daily address snapshots (`stage.customer_addresses`, `FULL_LOG`), and the current-state loyalty roster (`stage.loyalty_memberships`, `FULL`). Each table block specifies the connection, the source table, the primary key column, the ingestion strategy, the column that supplies the effective timestamp, and the transformation expression for each attribute. Merging across tables is generated by Daana when the entity is materialized.

`connection: dev` resolves against the `dev` profile in `connections.yaml`, which `--example quickstart` set to point at the local PostgreSQL container. See Connection Profiles for the full reference.

The `mapping_groups` list has a single entry in this chapter; Chapter 2 covers when an entity needs more than one.

### Complete the Order Mapping

Open `mappings/order-mapping.yaml` and replace its contents with the following:

`entity_id: ORDER

mapping_groups:
 - name: default_mapping_group
 tables:
 - connection: dev
 table: stage.sales_orders
 primary_keys:
 - order_id
 ingestion_strategy: TRANSACTIONAL
 batch_expression: ingested_at
 entity_effective_timestamp_expression: order_date
 attributes:
 - id: order_id
 transformation_expression: order_id
 - id: order_status
 transformation_expression: order_status
 - id: order_purchase_ts
 transformation_expression: order_date
 - id: order_value_amount # child attribute of the order_value group
 transformation_expression: total_amount
 - id: order_value_currency # child attribute of the order_value group
 transformation_expression: currency

 relationships:
 - id: ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER
 source_table: stage.sales_orders
 target_transformation_expression: customer_id
`

The order is sourced from a single table (`stage.sales_orders`, `TRANSACTIONAL`). The two child attributes of the `order_value` group are mapped individually (`order_value_amount` and `order_value_currency`), and the `relationships` block resolves `IS_PLACED_BY` by pointing at the `customer_id` column on the source table. `daana-cli generate mapping` pre-filled the relationship `id`. Chapter 2 walks through the naming rule.

### Validate

`daana-cli check workflow
`

A successful check confirms the model and both mappings parse, the entity and attribute references resolve, and the mappings cover every attribute declared on the model. `deploy` and `execute` invoke `check` internally, so this step is optional, but running it once after authoring catches typos before any database changes happen.

The check also surfaces three warnings about the `dev` connection profile: the `password` and `user` fields are hardcoded rather than read from environment variables, and `sslmode` is `disable`. These are intentional for the local sandbox so the tutorial runs without extra setup. Chapter 6 covers the production hardening (secrets, TLS, separate profiles).

## Deploy and Execute

You already ran `daana-cli install` during the tutorial setup. Install is environment-level and runs once per database. From here, deploy the workflow and execute it:

`daana-cli deploy

daana-cli execute
`

## Explore What Daana Built

For each entity in your model, Daana generates three types of views in the `daana_dw` schema:

ViewContents

 | `view_<entity>` | Current state, one row per entity

 | `view_<entity>_hist` | Full change history, one row per tracked version

 | `view_<entity>_with_rel` | Current state with all related entities joined

Daana also generates per-relationship junction views (such as `view_order_is_placed_by_customer`) and internal `v_<entity>_desc` views (here `v_customer_desc` and `v_order_desc`) over the raw EAV-style storage (Entity-Attribute-Value: each attribute lives in its own row keyed by entity id and attribute name, instead of as a wide table column); Chapter 2 lists the full set and explains the underlying tables.

These views form a complete, historized business layer. They can be queried directly or used as building blocks for a traditional dimensional mart (dimensions and fact tables). Chapter 7 walks through that process. Future versions of Daana will generate dimensional marts automatically.

`customer_key` is each customer's surrogate key (always typed `character varying`); the `::integer` cast in `ORDER BY` clauses sorts numerically. Chapter 2 explains how Daana derives it.

Open a `psql` shell against the local container so you can run the upcoming SQL queries:

`docker exec -it daana-customerdb psql -U dev -d customerdb
`

### Query 1: Three sources, one unified view

All three source systems are merged into a single row per customer:

`SELECT
 customer_key,
 customer_name,
 customer_status,
 customer_city,
 customer_state,
 customer_loyalty_tier
FROM daana_dw.view_customer
ORDER BY customer_key::integer;
`

Result:

` customer_key | customer_name | customer_status | customer_city | customer_state | customer_loyalty_tier
--------------+---------------------+-----------------+---------------+----------------+-----------------------
 1 | John Smith | Inactive | New York | NY | Gold
 2 | Emily Johnson | Active | Philadelphia | PA | Silver
 3 | Michael Brown | Suspended | Brooklyn | NY | Bronze
 4 | Sarah Davis | Active | Cambridge | MA | Gold
 5 | David Wilson | Active | Queens | NY | Silver
 6 | Jennifer Martinez | Active | New York | NY | Platinum
 7 | Robert Anderson | Active | San Francisco | CA |
 8 | Lisa Taylor | Active | San Francisco | CA | Bronze
 9 | James Thomas | Active | Los Angeles | CA | Silver
 10 | Maria Garcia | Active | Boston | MA | Bronze
(10 rows)
`

One row per customer, assembled from three independent source tables. Robert Anderson (customer 7) has no loyalty membership record; his `customer_loyalty_tier` is empty. Daana handles missing data across sources without additional configuration.

The 12 rows in `stage.customers` reduce to 10 here because customers 1 and 3 each carry an additional status-change row (`Active` -> `Inactive`, `Active` -> `Suspended`); `FULL_LOG` ingestion preserves those as historical versions rather than duplicate customers, and the current-state view shows only the latest version per entity.

### Query 2: The full change history for one customer

Emily (customer 2) has dozens of rows in `stage.customer_addresses` and two rows in `stage.customers`. Daana deduplicates the snapshots, detects only actual changes, and stores one row per distinct version:

`SELECT
 customer_name,
 customer_city,
 customer_state,
 customer_status,
 customer_loyalty_tier,
 eff_tmstp
FROM daana_dw.view_customer_hist
WHERE customer_key = '2'
ORDER BY eff_tmstp;
`

Result:

` customer_name | customer_city | customer_state | customer_status | customer_loyalty_tier | eff_tmstp
---------------+---------------+----------------+-----------------+-----------------------+---------------------

[Resource from github at repo://mattiasthalen/adss-fable-poc/sha/49b3551a382451b8cf87bb343d606c8385b37f59/contents/README.md] # adss-fable-poc

An **Analytical Data Storage System** (ADSS) built end to end on one DuckDB file, one thin
slice at a time. Three layers, one direction of flow, no shortcuts between them:

| layer | schema(s) | what it does | engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DAS** | `das__meta`, `das__raw`, `das__staged` | captures the source, persists it append-only, unpacks it strictly per contract | [dlt](https://dlthub.com) |
| **DAB** | `dab`, `dab__stage`, `dab__meta` | the integrated business model — the only place the data is explained | `daana-cli` focal model |
| **DAR** | `dar__uss` | a **generated** Unified Star Schema (one event bridge + peripherals) | the ADSS USS generator |

Destinations (a marimo notebook) read `dar__uss` and nothing else.

## Status

Slice 1 of 6, commit 1: the repository scaffold. The layers, the business questions that
accept them, and the documentation arrive in the commits that follow.

## Getting started

```bash
uv sync --all-groups
uv run adss --version
uv run pytest
uv run pre-commit run --all-files
```

## Slices

Each slice answers one business question, opens red and closes green.

| # | question | status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many orders were placed per order month and ship country? | in progress |

The full build (`uv run adss build --offline`) lands recorded fixtures, so everything in
this repository runs without network access.

[Resource from github at repo://mattiasthalen/adss-fable-poc/sha/49b3551a382451b8cf87bb343d606c8385b37f59/contents/docs/deviations.md] # Deviations register

Every knowing departure from a principle in [blueprint.md](blueprint.md) or a hard rule in
[conventions.md](conventions.md) is recorded here, together with the ADR that decided it.

The register exists because an unregistered exception is indistinguishable from a mistake. Once
one exists, the next person reads it as precedent and copies it, and a year later the rule is
folklore. Writing the cost down keeps the trade visible, and writing an exit condition down keeps
it from becoming permanent by default.

A deviation is legitimate only when all four fields are answerable. If the cost cannot be named,
the deviation has not been understood; if the exit condition cannot be named, it is not a
deviation but a change of rule, and the rule should be superseded instead.

## Entries

| # | Rule deviated from | Why | Cost | Exit condition | ADR | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D-0001 | [blueprint.md](blueprint.md), DAR: *No cross-dependency* — "a data product owns its structures and does not consume another product's. Duplication between products is accepted deliberately" — and *Reuse the definition, never the instance* | Six personas share one `dab/model.yaml`, so they share one meaning of every measure. The structure being shared is the generated Unified Star Schema, which is additive by construction: keys inherit, measures stay on their own stage, and the sliceability contract says which breakdowns are legitimate before a query is written. The fan trap the principle protects against cannot occur in it | A change made for one persona is visible to all of them the moment it is generated; there is no per-group access control, so "this group may not see freight" cannot be expressed; two personas cannot hold different definitions of the same measure. The first thing to break will be a slice that needs a measure defined one way for one persona and another way for another, and it will have to be modelled as two measures | A second consumer needs isolation — a different shape of the same structure, or a group that must not see part of it. Then the generator gains per-group projections over the same bridge (`adss dar project --group <name>`) and this entry is resolved | [0017](adr/0017-one-shared-dar-uss-deviation.md) | open |

## Entry format

Entries are appended in the order they are decided and never removed — a deviation that has been
resolved is marked resolved, with the date and the commit or ADR that resolved it, because the
history of why something looked necessary is worth as much as the fact that it no longer is.

| # | Rule deviated from | Why | Cost | Exit condition | ADR | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D-NNNN | *(the principle or hard rule, quoted or linked)* | *(what made the conforming option unworkable here — a constraint, not a preference)* | *(what this costs, concretely: what breaks first, who pays, what it makes harder later)* | *(the observable condition under which the deviation is removed)* | *(link)* | open / resolved |

Field by field:

* **Rule deviated from** — quote or link the exact rule. "The spirit of layering" is not a rule;
  a row in a blueprint table is.
* **Why** — the constraint that made the conforming option unworkable *here*. Convenience, time
  pressure and unfamiliarity are not constraints; they are reasons to do it properly.
* **Cost** — what this buys the system in trouble. Name the first thing that will break, who
  pays for it, and which future change it makes more expensive. A deviation with no cost is
  evidence the rule is wrong, so supersede the rule instead of deviating from it.
* **Exit condition** — the observable thing that has to become true for the deviation to be
  removed. "When we have time" is not observable. "When a second data product needs a different
  shape of the same structure" is.
* **ADR** — the decision record that argued it. Every deviation has one; the register is the
  index, the ADR is the argument.
* **Status** — `open` while it stands, `resolved` once it is gone, with the date and what
  removed it appended to the row.

## Review

The register is read at the start of every slice, and each open entry is checked against its exit
condition. An entry whose exit condition has been met and which is still open is a defect in the
same way a failing test is: the system is no longer doing what its own documentation says.

It names no technologies, files, commands, schemas or column conventions — so it constrains what DAS/DAB/DAR may contain and how data may move between them, not how to implement them.

entries.name: TaskList
entries.description:
Use this tool to list all tasks in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

- To see what tasks are available to work on (status: 'pending', no owner, not blocked)
- To check overall progress on the project
- To find tasks that are blocked and need dependencies resolved
- After completing a task, to check for newly unblocked work or claim the next available task
- **Prefer working on tasks in ID order** (lowest ID first) when multiple tasks are available, as earlier tasks often set up context for later ones

## Output

Returns a summary of each task:
- **id**: Task identifier (use with TaskGet, TaskUpdate)
- **subject**: Brief description of the task
- **status**: 'pending', 'in_progress', or 'completed'
- **owner**: Agent ID if assigned, empty if available
- **blockedBy**: List of open task IDs that must be resolved first (tasks with blockedBy cannot be claimed until dependencies resolve)

Use TaskGet with a specific task ID to view full details including description and comments.

- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task
- Returns the task output along with status information
- Use block=true (default) to wait for task completion
- Use block=false for non-blocking check of current status
- Task IDs can be found using the /tasks command
- Works with all task types: background shells, async agents, and remote sessions

# DAR is a generated Unified Star Schema: an event bridge, peripheral tables, one calendar, and a fixed column contract

## Context and Problem Statement

DAR is the layer a person reads. The blueprint says it may be volatile and must be generated,
and the Unified Star Schema is the shape chosen for it: one *bridge* holding a row per
measurement event, one *peripheral* table per entity holding its current state, and one
calendar every process is dated against. The question this record answers is what exactly the
generator emits, because everything downstream — the questions, the notebook, any future
consumer — is written against those column names and will not survive them changing.

Three things about the source made the shape less obvious than the post makes it sound.

*Fan-out.* The Unified Star Schema post says keys and measures "propagate downward" along
many-to-one relationships. Keys can. Measures cannot: if a parent's measure were copied onto
every child row that points at it, summing that measure would multiply it by the number of
children. That is the classic fan trap, and it is exactly what a bridge exists to avoid.

*History.* daana keeps a version of every entity row and of every relationship pair. A
question about something that happened reads the current view; a question about a state as it
was observed reads the history view. The two need different stages, not different tables.

*The relationship view lies to us.* daana publishes `view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` for each
relationship, and it ranks pairs by the effective timestamp and then keeps the open rows. Our
effective timestamp is the moment DAS observed the row, while the row that *closes* a pair is
stamped with the engine's wall clock. Verified in this session: change one foreign key,
re-execute, and the source key disappears from the relationship view altogether. Reading that
view would silently drop rows from the bridge — the worst kind of wrong, because the query
still runs and the total is merely smaller.

## Decision Drivers

* a sum over the bridge is right without anybody having to know how the model is shaped
* one calendar, so two processes can be compared
* a stable, published column contract that consumers can be written against
* deterministic output: the same model file always produces the same SQL
* nothing silently missing

## Considered Options

* an event bridge with one stage per (entity, event), keys for every entity, measures on
  their own stage only, and peripherals as tables
* one bridge row per entity instance, with measures joined on
* hand-written star schemas per question
* reading daana's relationship views for the inherited keys

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: **an event bridge with one stage per (entity, event)**, with this column
contract:

| column | type | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `_stage` | VARCHAR | the entity the row is about |
| `_event` | VARCHAR | `<entity>_<event>`, the one thing that happened |
| `_event_date` | DATE | the day it happened, or the day the state was observed |
| `_is_current` | BOOLEAN | true for a transaction; for a snapshot, the latest row per key |
| `<entity>_key` | VARCHAR | one per entity in the model, in model order |
| `_measure__<entity>__<measure>` | DECIMAL(28, 8) | one per measure, in model order |

*Keys inherit, measures do not.* The blog's "measures propagate downward along n:1" is
realised here as **own-stage-only measures plus inherited keys**: a stage carries the key of
every entity it reaches along many-to-one relationships, and a measure is non-NULL only on the
stage of the (entity, event) that owns it. Copying a measure down would multiply it — that is
the fan-out proof, and it is a test, not a hope: three children, two parents, and
`sum(_measure__parent__…)` is still two.

Transaction stages read `dab.view_<E>` and keep only rows whose date is not null, so "an
unshipped order has no shipment event" is true by construction rather than by a filter
somebody has to remember. Snapshot stages read `dab.view_<E>_hist`, are dated by `eff_tmstp`,
and mark the latest row per key as current.

Peripherals are `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dar__uss.<entity>` (quoted when the name is a word
DuckDB has other plans for, hence `dar__uss."order"`), one row per instance, key first and
attributes in declaration order. They are tables and not views, so what DAR served is exactly
what the build log describes.

`_calendar` is day-grained and padded to whole years around the events, with column names
chosen to avoid SQL keywords (`year_number`, `year_month_key`, …), and every stage joins it by
`_event_date = date_key`.

**Relationship pairs are read from the pair table, not from the relationship view.** Each
relationship the plan walks becomes one common table expression over `dab."<SRC>_<TGT>_x"`
that keeps the latest version of each pair and then keeps it only if that version is open:

```sql
QUALIFY
    row_number() OVER (
        PARTITION BY x."CHILD_key", x."PARENT_key" ORDER BY x.ver_tmstp DESC
    ) = 1 AND x.row_st = 'Y'
```

`adss dar build` therefore asserts that the pair *tables* exist, not the views.

Emitter rules, all of them found by running sqlfluff and DuckDB against the real thing: every
branch of the union aliases every column of one column list, in one order; every measure is
`cast(… AS DECIMAL(28, 8))`; a column a stage cannot fill is a typed NULL; functions are lower
case; DAB identifiers are quoted because they are mixed case on purpose; DAR identifiers are
bare unless they are DuckDB keywords; a join condition names the earlier table first.

### Consequences

* Good, because a sum over the bridge is additive whatever the shape of the model, and the
  proof is a test rather than a convention
* Good, because every process lands on one calendar, so two of them can be compared
* Good, because a consumer writes against a published contract that a model change extends
  rather than rearranges — new entities and measures are appended
* Good, because a changed foreign key keeps its row, which reading the relationship view
  would not have done
* Bad, because the bridge is sparse: most cells of most rows are NULL. At this scale that
  costs nothing, and it is the price of one table instead of one per process
* Bad, because ratios and snapshot states need care at query time (a ratio is `sum(a)/sum(b)`,
  a state needs `_is_current`). Both are written down in the sliceability contract and in the
  `dar` skill
* Bad, because an attribute whose lower-cased id is a keyword in the *linter's* dialect but
  not in DuckDB's would fail the lint. The fix is to name the attribute better, which is the
  same decision that was already made for the calendar's columns

### Confirmation

`tests/dar/test_plan.py` asserts the column order, the padding, the event filter, the
inheritance and the refusals; `tests/dar/test_sql.py` asserts that every branch aliases every
column exactly once and every measure is cast, then runs the whole generated set against an
in-memory database with DAB's shapes faked into it — including a pair table with a changed
foreign key, where it checks both that the bridge keeps the row and that daana's own view
would have dropped it; `tests/dar/test_build.py` asserts `DESCRIBE dar__uss._bridge` equals
the plan on the real warehouse.

# `dab/model.yaml` is the only place the data is explained, and DAR's declarations live in it as `x_uss` keys

## Context and Problem Statement

Exactly one artefact may say what the data means. Contracts say what a source field *is*;
questions point at meanings; the generated layer serves them; none of them may restate one,
because a restatement is a second explanation and two explanations drift.

That leaves a problem for DAR. The generator needs to know things the business model does not
otherwise say: which of an entity's dates makes it a measurement event, which numbers are
measures of that event, whether a measure may be summed, and what each of those declarations
means in words. Those facts are business facts — "an order is placed on a day, and counting
orders means counting orders and not the lines on them" — so they belong beside the concepts they
describe, not in a second file that has to be kept in step with the first.

daana's validator accepts unknown keys on entities and attributes (it refuses them on
relationships), and strips them from the compiled `model.json`.

## Decision Drivers

* one file explains the data, and one file only
* a DAR declaration sits next to the concept it is about
* no second model to keep in step
* the glossary DAR serves must be able to copy text, never compose it

## Considered Options

* `x_uss` extension keys inside `dab/model.yaml`
* a sidecar `dar/uss/declarations.yaml` keyed by entity and attribute id
* encoding events and measures as naming conventions on attributes
* teaching the generator to infer events from types

## Decision Outcome

Chosen option: **`x_uss` keys inside `model.yaml`.**

At entity level: `name` (the DAR spelling, defaulting to the lower-cased id), `role`
(`entity` or `junction`), `events`, and `derived_measures`. An event carries a `name`, a
**required** `definition`, a `kind` (`transaction` or `snapshot`), a `date` for a transaction
event — its own attribute, or `ENTITY.ATTRIBUTE` of an entity it reaches — and an optional
`count_measure`, which is itself an object of `name` and `definition`. At attribute level:
`x_uss.measure` with a name, the event it measures, and its additivity.

Every definition is required because of what the glossary is. `dar__uss._glossary` copies these
strings verbatim; it never writes prose of its own. A generator that composed a definition would
be a third place the data is explained, and the worst kind — one nobody wrote and nobody reviews.
So a declaration without a definition is refused when the model is read, not filled in later.

The generator reads `model.yaml` and never `model.json`, because `model.json` is exactly the file
these keys have been stripped from.

Contracts stay in the source's words; questions carry `{{ENTITY.ATTRIBUTE}}` tokens that resolve
against this file; DAR carries the definitions forward as data. If a future engine rejects the
extension keys, the same types read a sidecar `dab/uss.yaml` instead — the grammar does not
change, only where it is written.

### Consequences

* Good, because every fact DAR needs is declared once, beside the business definition it belongs to
* Good, because there is no second model file and therefore no way for two models to disagree
* Good, because a missing definition is a load-time error with a name in it, rather than a blank
  row in a glossary somebody notices in a screenshot
* Bad, because it leans on an engine tolerating keys it does not know. That tolerance is asserted
  on every CI run: the wrapper test deploys a model with `x_uss` in it and then reads the compiled
  output to confirm the keys were dropped

### Confirmation

`tests/domain/test_model.py` pins the grammar against a generic PARENT/CHILD model, including the
refusals: an event without a date, a snapshot with one, an event without a definition, a count
measure without one, a measure on something that is not a number, a derived expression reaching
into another entity. `tests/dab/test_model_reader.py` asserts that this repository's own model
explains every entity, attribute, event and measure, and that no source property name appears
anywhere in it — the forbidden words being read from the contracts rather than kept in a list.
`tests/questions/test_questions_static.py::test_definitions_resolve` asserts every `{{token}}` in
every question resolves to a definition somebody wrote.
`tests/dab/test_daana_wrapper.py::test_the_uss_declarations_survive_deploy_and_are_stripped_from_the_compiled_model`
is the tolerance check.

id: q01
slice: 1
status: green
persona: Sales director
question: How many orders were placed per order month and ship country?
aggregation: count
measure: order.placed_orders_count
dimensions: [_calendar.year_month_key, order.ship_country]
time_grain: month
requires: [[order, order], [order, _calendar]]
definitions: [ORDER, ORDER.PLACED_ON, ORDER.SHIP_COUNTRY, ORDER.events.placed, ORDER.measures.placed_orders_count]
decimals: 0
order_by: [order_month, ship_country]
---

## Story

As the **sales director**, I want to see how many orders were placed per order month and
ship country, so that I can staff sales where demand moves.

## Definitions

- {{ORDER}}
- {{ORDER.PLACED_ON}}
- {{ORDER.SHIP_COUNTRY}}
- {{ORDER.events.placed}}
- {{ORDER.measures.placed_orders_count}}

## W's

- **Why**: demand shifts between countries and seasons, and staffing follows demand.
- **What**: the count of orders placed.
- **Who**: customers place the orders; the sales director tracks them.
- **How**: one `order_placed` event per order, counted per month and per country.
- **Where**: the country the order ships to; a missing country is kept as its own group.
- **When**: all history, at the calendar month of the day the order was placed
  (`_calendar.year_month_key`, `YYYY-MM`).

[Resource from github at repo://mattiasthalen/adss-fable-poc/sha/49b3551a382451b8cf87bb343d606c8385b37f59/contents/docs/conventions.md] # Conventions

This is the **one** convention document for this repository: naming, SQL style, YAML style,
Python style, commit format. There is deliberately no second, machine-readable copy of these
rules — no custom linter, no regex list that has to be kept in step with this page. Where an
off-the-shelf tool can already check a rule (ruff, sqlfluff, yamllint) the tool's configuration
*is* the rule and this page only records the reason; everything else is checked by whoever — or
whatever — reviews the change, reading this page.

The reason for that arrangement is drift. A convention that exists both as prose and as a linter
config exists twice, the two copies disagree within a quarter, and the disagreement is discovered
by an argument in a pull request. Keeping one artefact means a clarification takes effect the
moment it is written here.

Principles live in [blueprint.md](blueprint.md); decisions in [adr/](adr/README.md); registered
departures in [deviations.md](deviations.md).

## How to read a rule

Every rule below carries a **why**, and a severity. The why is not decoration: it is what lets a
reviewer tell a genuine violation from a case the rule was never aimed at, and it is what gets
quoted back when a change is asked for.

| Severity | Meaning | On a pull request |
|---|---|---|
| **Hard rule** | Breaking it breaks a contract something else depends on. | Blocks. Fix it, or register a deviation with an ADR. |
| **Guideline** | Judgement, taste, and the shape of things that are merely easier to read. | A comment, not a block. A reasoned "no thanks" ends the discussion. |

Grading matters. A convention system that blocks on everything trains people to resent it, and a
resented system is routed around.

When something is flagged that should not have been, the fix is to clarify **this page**, not to
argue the case a second time on the next pull request.

## 1. Naming by layer

Names are the interface between the layers, so each layer names things in its own vocabulary and
never in its neighbour's.

### 1.1 DAS — the source-vocabulary exemption

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| DAS object and column names mirror the source. The source's own words are **required** here, even when they are words the other layers forbid. | DAS exists to say what the source said. Renaming a source field to a business term buries an interpretation in the one layer that is supposed to make none, and disguises the next source change as a business change. | Hard rule |
| The mechanical translation is allowed and expected: a source property becomes `snake_case`, a source object becomes a `snake_case` plural table named after the source's own name for it. | A consistent spelling of the source's word is still the source's word; it is not a reinterpretation. | Hard rule |
| A contract file's stem is the landed table name, and both are the name used in every schema of this layer. | One name for one thing, so that a grep for a table finds its contract. | Hard rule |
| A source name that would be a violation anywhere else — `total_orders`, `nbr_of_subs`, `ShipVia` — is **not** a violation here. | It is a column in a table nobody on this side controls. A rule that cannot distinguish that case from a name we chose is a rule that produces false accusations. | Hard rule |
| Field descriptions in a contract stay in system vocabulary: the source's type, its nullability, what the source calls it. Not what it means to the business. | Business meaning has exactly one home (§1.2). Two homes means two definitions, and eventually two numbers. | Hard rule |

### 1.2 DAB — the business vocabulary

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| Entity, attribute and relationship identifiers are `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`. | It is the modelling language's own convention, and the visual break from every other layer's lower case makes a leak obvious on sight. | Hard rule |
| Entity and attribute names are **singular**: `ORDER`, `ORDER_LINE`, `SHIP_COUNTRY`. | An entity names a kind of thing, not a pile of them. The pile is what a query produces. | Hard rule |
| No source name appears anywhere in the business model — not in an id, not in a definition, not in a description. | This is the layer whose whole purpose is being source-agnostic; a source name in it means the dependency was moved rather than broken. | Hard rule |
| Every entity, attribute and relationship has a `definition` written in business language, and that definition is the **only** place the data is explained. | Definitions that exist in several places drift apart, and the drift surfaces as two dashboards that disagree. Everything else — contracts, questions, the generated layer, notebooks — references these. | Hard rule |
| A relationship's name is a verb phrase, so that `<SOURCE>_<NAME>_<TARGET>` reads as a sentence: `ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER`. | The direction of a relationship is the thing people get wrong; a sentence cannot be read backwards by accident. | Hard rule |
| Names say what a thing *is* to the business, not how it is stored or derived. `PLACED_ON`, not `ORDER_DATE_TS`. | The physical shape changes; the concept does not. | Guideline |
| Prefer the word the business already uses over a more precise one it does not. | A model nobody recognises is a model nobody checks. | Guideline |

### 1.3 DAB — mapping conventions (M1–M7)

A mapping says how one entity is loaded from DAS. These seven rules exist because daana accepts
several kinds of wrong mapping without complaint; `adss dab check` refuses them and names the rule.
The reasoning is in [ADR-0012](adr/0012-mapping-conventions-keys-full-loaded-at.md).

| # | Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | `connection: adss`, and `table: das__staged.<contract table>` — never a subquery, never a join. | DAB reads the latest view of a contract and nothing else; a join here would be business logic in the wrong layer, and a raw read would skip the contract's casts. | Hard rule |
| M2 | Exactly **one** `primary_keys` entry, whose VARCHAR result *is* the entity key: `CAST(col AS VARCHAR)`, a bare string column, or `CONCAT(CAST(a AS VARCHAR), '-', CAST(b AS VARCHAR))`. | Two entries are two *alternate identifiers*, not a composite key, and that mode cannot be undone once loaded. | Hard rule |
| M3 | `ingestion_strategy: FULL`, everywhere, always. Never switch a deployed table. | FULL keeps a changed value's history, which is what the state questions need; a switch on a live table writes closed-row duplicates of everything already there. | Hard rule |
| M4 | `entity_effective_timestamp_expression: _loaded_at`. | The effective timestamp of a fact is when DAS observed it. Anything else — a wall clock, a source column — dates the fact by something that is not about the fact. | Hard rule |
| M5 | An attribute expression reads its own row: a column, a cast, or a CASE. Dates become `CAST(x AS TIMESTAMP)`; flags become `CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END`. | An expression that reaches beyond the row is a join, and every join must come from a declared relationship. | Hard rule |
| M6 | A relationship's `id` is `<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`; its `source_table` is byte-identical to the group's `table`; its target expression mirrors the target entity's own key expression. | A mismatched `source_table` is skipped silently, and a differently spelled key produces pairs that join to nothing. Neither says anything at load time. | Hard rule |
| M7 | Every mapped table carries at least one attribute — a junction's may be a literal. | daana refuses to deploy an entity with none, and the failure arrives at deploy rather than at review. | Hard rule |

Start from `uv run adss dab generate-mapping ENTITY`, and replace **every** placeholder it writes:
they are all wrong on purpose, and all of them compile.

### 1.4 DAR — the generated layer

Names here are emitted by the generator, so these rules are what the generator implements; they
appear on this page because they are the contract every consumer reads against.

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| Object names are `snake_case` **singular**, derived from the entity: `order`, `order_line`. | Same reason as §1.2, in the other layer's spelling. A reserved word is quoted, never abbreviated around. | Hard rule |
| A key column is `<object>_key`. | One predictable spelling means a join can be written without looking anything up. | Hard rule |
| Attribute columns are the lower-cased attribute identifier, unchanged. | The mapping back to the definition must be mechanical, so a consumer can find the meaning of any column in one step. | Hard rule |
| Structural columns carry a leading underscore: `_bridge`, `_event_date`, `_is_current`, `_measure__…`. | The underscore says "the generator owns this"; anything without one came from the business model. | Hard rule |
| Nothing in this layer is hand-edited. A wrong name is fixed in the business model and regenerated. | An edit to generated output is lost on the next generation, and until then the code and the model quietly disagree. | Hard rule |

## 2. Measure naming

The single most consequential convention in the repository, and the one to get right first.

**Pattern: `<descriptor>_<entities>_<unit>`.**

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| A measure name has three parts in that order: what distinguishes it, the entity it counts or sums over, the unit it is in. | Three fixed slots make names comparable at a glance and searchable by any of the three parts. | Hard rule |
| The entity part is **plural**: `orders`, `order_lines`, `products`. | A measure is always about a set. The singular is reserved for the entity itself, which keeps the two readable side by side. | Hard rule |
| Scope and aggregation words never appear: no `total_`, `sum_`, `avg_`, `count_of_`, `num_`, `nbr_`, `_ytd`, `_by_month`. | Aggregation and scope are chosen by the query — the filter, the grain, the grouping — not baked into the name. `total_orders` is a lie the moment somebody filters it, and `orders_ytd` is a second measure that has to be maintained in step with the first. | Hard rule |
| The unit is a real unit: `count`, `amount`, `days`, `units`. | It is what tells a reader whether two measures can be added, and it is the first thing anybody wants to know. | Hard rule |
| A name must be self-explanatory without a documentation lookup, and must describe the business concept rather than the implementation. | If understanding a measure requires opening the glossary, the name has failed at the only job a name has. | Guideline |
| No abbreviations, and no unusual word order. `paid_subscriptions_count`, not `nbr_of_paid_subs`. | Abbreviations are unsearchable, and searchability is most of a name's value in a system with hundreds of them. | Guideline |

Worked examples:

| Instead of | Write | Because |
|---|---|---|
| `total_orders` | `placed_orders_count` | The scope word goes; the descriptor says *which* orders; the unit says what the number is. |
| `sum_revenue` | `revenue_order_lines_amount` | `sum` is the query's job; the entity says at what grain revenue is measured. |
| `avg_days_to_ship` | `ship_lag_orders_days` | The average is `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)` at query time, from two additive measures. |
| `nbr_of_products_below_reorder` | `below_reorder_products_count` | Abbreviation removed, slots put in order. |

Ratios are not stored. Store the numerator and the denominator as additive measures and divide at
query time — an average of averages is wrong at every grain but the one it was computed at.

## 3. SQL style

Every rule in this section that a tool can check is checked by `sqlfluff` with the repository's
`.sqlfluff`; this page records why the settings are what they are. All of them are hard rules,
because generated SQL and hand-written SQL have to be indistinguishable to a reviewer.

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| Keywords upper case (`SELECT`, `LEFT JOIN`); functions lower case (`cast(`, `sum(`); identifiers lower case. | Three visual classes, so structure, computation and data are separable at a glance in a long generated statement. |
| Four-space indentation; one selected expression per line; every expression aliased with `AS`. | Diffs of generated SQL are read constantly. One expression per line makes a one-column change a one-line diff. |
| Every table reference has an explicit alias, and a join condition lists the earlier table first: `ON e."ORDER_key" = r_customer."ORDER_key"`. | Reading order matches join order, so a wrong join key is visible without tracing back up the statement. |
| Identifiers whose case matters — anything crossing over from the business layer — are double-quoted; everything this repository creates is lower case and unquoted, except reserved words. | The two conventions must be visually distinct, because a mixed-case identifier that loses its quotes fails only at run time. |
| A reserved word is quoted, not renamed. Calendar columns avoid reserved words entirely (`year_number`, `year_month_key`). | Renaming to dodge a keyword breaks the mechanical link between a column and the attribute it came from. |
| No `SELECT *` in anything a consumer reads, except composing a union of stages whose column list is fixed by the generator. | A star is a schema change waiting to be silent. |
| Line length 140. | Long enough for a `cast(… AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS …` alias on one line, short enough to review side by side. |
| SQL that lives in a Python string is dumped to a file so that the same linter sees it. | A rule that applies only to the SQL somebody remembered to put in a `.sql` file is not a rule. |

## 4. YAML style

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| Two-space indentation, no tabs; lines ≤ 160 characters; checked by `yamllint`. | The configuration files are read far more often than they are written. | Hard rule |
| Flow mappings (`{a: 1, b: 2}`) are allowed for short, homogeneous rows — a contract column, a mapping attribute — but never column-aligned with padding spaces. | Alignment looks tidy and re-aligns the whole block the day one value grows, turning a one-line change into a twenty-line diff. It also trips the linter. | Hard rule |
| Anything with an interpolation, a multi-line value, or more than about four keys is written in block style. | Flow style stops being readable exactly where the value stops being simple, and in some contexts (workflow expressions) it is not even parseable. | Hard rule |
| Booleans are `true`/`false`. | One spelling; `yes`/`on` are the same value wearing a disguise. | Hard rule |

## 5. Python style

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| `ruff` (lint and format) with the repository configuration is the style. Double quotes, 100 columns, import sorting. | No style discussions, ever. | Hard rule |
| **No data vocabulary anywhere under `src/`, or in test code.** No entity, attribute or business term from the model appears in the machinery or in the code of a test. | The machinery is supposed to work for any source and any business model; a data name in it is proof that it does not. Test fixtures use neutral models (`PARENT`, `CHILD`) held as data files, so the tests prove the machinery is generic instead of asserting it. | Hard rule |
| Data vocabulary belongs in the YAML, SQL and Markdown artefacts — contracts, the business model, generated SQL, questions, this repository's documentation. | Those artefacts *are* the description of this particular business. That is the whole point of keeping them out of the code. | Hard rule |
| Names describe the machinery's concepts: `contract`, `pipeline`, `plan`, `stage`, `peripheral`, `question`. | The machinery has its own domain, and it deserves its own vocabulary. | Guideline |
| Every module and every test starts with a one-line docstring saying what it is for. | The first line of a file is the cheapest documentation there is. | Guideline |

## 6. Tests

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| Tests are written inside the commit that implements the change, and they fail before the implementation lands. | A test written afterwards is a test that has only ever been seen to pass. | Hard rule |
| No `pytest.skip`, no imperative `pytest.xfail()` in a test body, no collection hooks inside a test module. | A skip is a test that silently does not exist. An imperative `xfail` can never report an unexpected pass, so it cannot tell you the day the bug is fixed. | Hard rule |
| A test that is expected to fail is marked declaratively and strictly, via the parameter that produces it. | Strictness is what makes an accidental pass a loud failure rather than a quiet green. | Hard rule |
| A failing check is fixed by fixing the code or by making the configuration honest — never by weakening the test. | A weakened test is worse than no test: it costs the same to run and reports the opposite of the truth. | Hard rule |

## 7. Commits, branches and pull requests

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| Conventional commits: `<type>(<scope>): <imperative>`. Types `feat`, `fix`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`, `refactor`, `ci`. Scopes: `repo`, `domain`, `das`, `dab`, `dar`, `questions`, `destination`, `ci`, `docs`, `skills`. | The scope names the layer, so the history reads as a map of the architecture and a reviewer knows which rules apply before opening the diff. | Hard rule |
| The subject is imperative, lower case, no trailing period, and fits in about 72 characters. | It is a heading, and it is read in lists a hundred times more often than the body. | Guideline |
| Every commit passes lint and the whole test suite on its own. | Bisect is only worth anything if every point in history is a working system. | Hard rule |
| One business question per slice; one branch per slice, named `slice/NN-<slug>`, branched off the previous slice. | The unit of delivery is an answered question, not a file. | Hard rule |
| Stacked branches are **rebased**, never merged; pull requests are rebase-merged, never squashed. | Squashing destroys the red-to-green trail, which is the evidence that the question drove the change rather than the other way round. Merge commits make a stack unreadable. | Hard rule |
| The commit that makes a red question pass flips it to green in that same commit. | Otherwise the strict expected-failure marker turns the good news into a build failure — which is the mechanism working, but the fix belongs in the commit that caused it. | Hard rule |

## 8. Documentation

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| A decision goes in an ADR under `docs/adr/`, numbered, in MADR format, and is superseded by a new file rather than edited. | The value of a decision record is the record of what was true when it was made. | Hard rule |
| A departure from a rule in [blueprint.md](blueprint.md) or a hard rule here needs an entry in [deviations.md](deviations.md) and an ADR. | An unregistered exception is indistinguishable from a mistake, and the next person copies it. | Hard rule |
| Markdown lines stay reasonable — roughly 100 characters, breaking at a sentence or clause — except table rows, which stay on one line. | Prose diffs stay legible; a re-wrapped paragraph should not look like a rewrite. | Guideline |
| Prefer a table when there are three or more parallel things to say. | Parallel structure is easier to check for gaps than parallel prose. | Guideline |

## 9. When a rule does not fit

Rules here are aimed at cases; a case the rule was not aimed at is not a violation. The order of
recourse, cheapest first:

1. **Clarify this page.** If the rule was ambiguous, say what it means and add the case. The
   clarification is in force immediately, for everyone.
2. **Register a deviation.** If the rule is right and this one place genuinely cannot follow it,
   add an entry to [deviations.md](deviations.md) — rule, reason, cost, exit condition — and an
   ADR explaining the decision.
3. **Change the rule.** If it is wrong, supersede the ADR that established it and edit this page.
   A rule nobody follows should be deleted rather than left as a reason to distrust the rest.

What is not on the list: a quiet exception. That is how a system of conventions turns into a set
of stories about why each file is the way it is.
