content.text: {"number":1,"title":"Slice 1 — How many orders were placed per order month and destination country?","body":"One business question, answered end to end through all three layers, and presented. *Pinned to the commit, not the branch: a record of what was delivered should not move when the branch does.* ## The question > How many orders were placed per order month and destination country? > — asked by the sales director **830 orders**, across 23 months and 21 destination countries, 1996-07 to 1998-05. ## The two answers, which must agree Straight from the source, bypassing both layers: ```sql SELECT strftime(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS order_month, o.ship_country AS destination_country, count(*) AS placed_orders_count FROM das__staged.orders__current AS o WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL GROUP BY strftime(o.order_date, '%Y-%m'), o.ship_country ORDER BY order_month, destination_country ``` From the generated star schema: ```sql SELECT cal.month_label AS order_month, o.destination_country AS destination_country, cast(sum(b._measure__order__placed_orders_count) AS BIGINT) AS placed_orders_count FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key INNER JOIN dar__uss."order" AS o ON b.order_key = o.order_key WHERE b._event = 'placed' GROUP BY cal.month_label, o.destination_country ORDER BY order_month, destination_country ``` 322 rows each, identical. That catches the failure this architecture is most exposed to and least able to see — that routing a number through integration and generation changed it. It would **not** catch a wrong definition; both queries would be written to it and both would be wrong together. ## What is here | | | |---|---| | **DAS** | one contract, 830 records recorded verbatim over nine pages, landed whole as JSON into hive-partitioned parquet, unpacked strictly into a change log plus a current view | | **DAB** | `ORDER` in business language — `PLACED_ON`, `DESTINATION_COUNTRY`, no source word anywhere — historized by when the system observed it | | **DAR** | a generated bridge, peripheral and calendar, with a published column contract | | **Destination** | a marimo page reading `dar__uss` and nothing else, running the question's own query | | **Decisions** | five ADRs, written before the code they decide | | **Skills** | one per layer, one for the destination, one for the whole | ```bash uv run adss build # the whole system from the recording, offline, ~11s uv run adss check # eight checks, all green ``` ## Verification Four independent lenses, then a code review, then CI. Each found something the ones before it could not. The recomputation lens rebuilt the answer from the raw recorded payloads in plain Python — 830 orders, 322 rows, byte-identical to what the star schema returns — and accepted it. The rest found real work, all fixed in the last four commits: - **A bug that only bites elsewhere.** `extracted_at` carries a time zone, so casting it to a date resolved in the reader's session zone while the partition key is the loader's UTC date. On UTC it passed; on `Asia/Tokyo` it reported 830 disagreements for a warehouse that was perfectly correct. - **A mutation that stayed green.** The bridge test counted column aliases per branch. A union takes its column names from its first branch, so a branch emitting the right columns in a *different order* puts one measure's values into another measure's column — and `DESCRIBE` still matches. It now asserts the sequence. - **The check machinery named a source.** `das__staged.orders` was hardcoded in a SQL string, so the check covered exactly one contract; a second would have been silently unchecked while `adss check` still printed PASS. Contracts now generate their own checks into files. - **Two tests could only pass on the machine that wrote them**, so "every commit passes the gate" was not true from a fresh checkout. - **Four ADRs described confirmations nobody had written.** Most now exist. The fan-out test is not among them and cannot be — it needs two grains and this slice has one entity — so ADR 0002 says that rather than claiming it. - **CI found the one the others structurally could not.** The oldest test in the repo asserted `"Usage: adss"` in help output. Rich styles that per phrase, so with colour enabled the bytes are `Usage: ␛adss` and the substring does not exist. CI turns colour on; the container does not. It had only ever been seen to pass under the one condition that hid it. A security review has since run over this diff as well — three lenses (injection and code execution, supply chain and CI, and data flow), each adversarially filtered. **No findings survived.** It did catch one documentation defect out of its own scope: ADR 0004's confirmation section named a test that does not exist. The control it described is real and stronger than the one claimed — the engine binary is hashed against its committed checksum before *every* invocation, and again in CI — so the correction was to the record, in slice 2. ## Known and deliberate - **D-0001 stands, and is carried on assertion.** One shared `dar__uss` departs from the DAR no-cross-dependency principle. Its argument rests on a walk over many-to-one relationships, which a single-entity slice has none of. Slice 4, the first with a second grain, is where the fan-out proof becomes possible. - **The branch slug says "ship country".** The question became *destination country* when the no-source-names rule was applied to the model, after the branch was cut. The conventions now say the slug is the question's slug. - **The control query has a shelf life.** It stays writable only while a question needs no integration. Slice 6, where one entity is assembled from two systems, is where that bill arrives. ## Next Slice 2 adds a second contract, a second entity and the first relationship — *what freight did we pay per customer country and order quarter?* — the first question whose answer needs a key to inherit. The full prioritised list is in [`docs/questions/`](https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/blob/28a6065823f4e5dac12b35b6ad752314af7fbb8d/docs/questions/README.md). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_019rspwWhmXfxoTvKg5jmNWh","state":"open","draft":false,"merged":false,"mergeable_state":"clean","html_url":"https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/pull/1","user":{"login":"mattiasthalen","id":2592140,"profile_url":"https://github.com/mattiasthalen","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/2592140?v=4"},"head":{"ref":"claude/adss-slice-01-orders-per-month-and-ship-country","sha":"28a6065823f4e5dac12b35b6ad752314af7fbb8d","repo":{"full_name":"mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07"}},"base":{"ref":"claude/adss-blog-implementation-vy62ci","sha":"eaea5fdb61528f266a432bbf19fd1fc3e1f354f3","repo":{"full_name":"mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07"}},"additions":5444,"deletions":25,"changed_files":105,"commits":15,"created_at":"2026-09-07T22:13:22Z","updated_at":"2026-09-07T23:08:12Z"}

That catches the failure this architecture is most exposed to and least able to see — that routing a number through integration and generation changed it. It would **not** catch a wrong definition; both queries would be written to it and both would be wrong together. ## What is here | | | |---|---| | **DAS** | one contract, 830 records recorded verbatim over nine pages, landed whole as JSON into hive-partitioned parquet, unpacked strictly into a change log plus a current view | | **DAB** | `ORDER` in business language — `PLACED_ON`, `DESTINATION_COUNTRY`, no source word anywhere — historized by when the system observed it | | **DAR** | a generated bridge, peripheral and calendar, with a published column contract | | **Destination** | a marimo page reading `dar__uss` and nothing else, running the question's own query | | **Decisions** | five ADRs, written before the code they decide | | **Skills** | one per layer, one for the destination, one for the whole | ```bash uv run adss build # the whole system from the recording, offline, ~11s uv run adss check # eight checks, all green ``` ## Verification Four independent lenses, then a code review, then CI. Each found something the ones before it could not. The recomputation lens rebuilt the answer from the raw recorded payloads in plain Python — 830 orders, 322 rows, byte-identical to what the star schema returns — and accepted it. The rest found real work, all fixed in the last four commits: - **A bug that only bites elsewhere.** `extracted_at` carries a time zone, so casting it to a date resolved in the reader's session zone while the partition key is the loader's UTC date. On UTC it passed; on `Asia/Tokyo` it reported 830 disagreements for a warehouse that was perfectly correct. - **A mutation that stayed green.** The bridge test counted column aliases per branch. A union takes its column names from its first branch, so a branch emitting the right columns in a *different order* puts one measure's values into another measure's column — and `DESCRIBE` still matches. It now asserts the sequence. - **The check machinery named a source.** `das__staged.orders` was hardcoded in a SQL string, so the check covered exactly one contract; a second would have been silently unchecked while `adss check` still printed PASS. Contracts now generate their own checks into files. - **Two tests could only pass on the machine that wrote them**, so "every commit passes the gate" was not true from a fresh checkout. - **Four ADRs described confirmations nobody had written.** Most now exist. The fan-out test is not among them and cannot be — it needs two grains and this slice has one entity — so ADR 0002 says that rather than claiming it. - **CI found the one the others structurally could not.** The oldest test in the repo asserted `"Usage: adss"` in help output. Rich styles that per phrase, so with colour enabled the bytes are `Usage: ␛adss` and the substring does not exist. CI turns colour on; the container does not. It had only ever been seen to pass under the one condition that hid it. A security review has since run over this diff as well — three lenses (injection and code execution, supply chain and CI, and data flow), each adversarially filtered. **No findings survived.** It did catch one documentation defect out of its own scope: ADR 0004's confirmation section named a test that does not exist. The control it described is real and stronger than the one claimed — the engine binary is hashed against its committed checksum before *every* invocation, and again in CI — so the correction was to the record, in slice 2. ## Known and deliberate - **D-0001 stands, and is carried on assertion.** One shared `dar__uss` departs from the DAR no-cross-dependency principle. Its argument rests on a walk over many-to-one relationships, which a single-entity slice has none of. Slice 4, the first with a second grain, is where the fan-out proof becomes possible. - **The branch slug says "ship country".** The question became *destination country* when the no-source-names rule was applied to the model, after the branch was cut. The conventions now say the slug is the question's slug. - **The control query has a shelf life.** It stays writable only while a question needs no integration. Slice 6, where one entity is assembled from two systems, is where that bill arrives. ## Next Slice 2 adds a second contract, a second entity and the first relationship — *what freight did we pay per customer country and order quarter?* — the first question whose answer needs a key to inherit. content.content:
========================================================================================
LENS Layering — does anything read across a boundary it should not (F1: analytical usage reads only DAR; F2: DAR reads only DAB; F3: DAB reads only DAS) -> accept-with-fixes
Every actual read in this slice stays inside its layer: DAR names only objects in the `dab` schema, the mappings name only `das__staged.orders`/`das__staged.customers`, the destination executes nothing but each question's `uss.sql`, and `das/sql/customers.sql` is pure extraction with no interpretation. On the sharp question — `dar/uss/_bridge.sql` reading `dab."v_ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER"`, which INNER JOINs `dab__meta.atom_contx_desc` — I do not believe this breaks F2. Against: F2 is worded "DAR reads only DAB", and if `dab__meta` is a fourth thing rather than part of DAB, DAR now reaches it. For: every artefact in the repository that enumerates DAB's schemas includes `dab__meta` (README.md:9, .claude/skills/adss/SKILL.md:14, src/adss/names.py:26 where `Schema.layer` maps it to `Layer.DAB`); the harm F2 names is "reaches past the business layer to a source", and `atom_contx_desc` is not a source but the business model's own name registry — I read it and `val_str` holds `ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER`, `ORDER_FREIGHT_CHARGE`, i.e. the identifiers straight out of `dab/model.yaml`, so the read is what makes `rel_name = 'ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER'` possible instead of `type_key = 1`; and a transitive-closure reading of F2 would already have condemned slice 1, since `dab.view_ORDER_hist` composes from `dab.ORDER_desc`, which is populated from `dab__stage`, which is populated from `das__staged`. DAR names one object, it is in `dab`, and what it joins to internally is DAB's own composition. The three findings are about what is written down and what is pinned, not about a misplaced read.

  [worth fixing] docs/conventions.md:169-190 (§6 Tests); checks/order_is_placed_by_customer__loaded.sql:6; checks/order_is_placed_by_customer__one_target.sql:7
  The checks suite now spans all three layers and nothing in the repository states that a conformance check may sit outside F1. F1 has exactly one written exemption — conventions §10 requires the control query to read `das__staged.<table>__current` — and no rule generalises it. This slice adds the first committed check files that read `dab.*` directly, so the unwritten exemption became visible in reviewable artefacts for the first time.

  [note] src/adss/names.py:1,11-31 (and src/adss/question.py:100-123)
  Nothing mechanically enforces F2 over the generated DAR SQL. `names.py` exists, by its own docstring, to give a flow check something to check against, but `Layer` and `Schema.layer` have no call sites anywhere. The only flow enforcement in the repository is `check_question`, which covers the two question SQL bodies. Pre-existing, but the exposure grew here: DAR's DAB read set went from one object family (`dab."view_<E>_hist"`) to two, adding `dab."v_<edge>"`.

  [note] src/adss/checks.py:69-117; checks/order_is_placed_by_customer__one_target.sql
  ADR 0006 rests DAR's safety on pinning, but the one property that makes `v_<edge>` the right object to read — that it is the raw, unranked, unfiltered pairs — is the one engine behaviour not pinned. If a vendor release added ranking inside that view, the as-of rule ADR 0006 spends generated SQL to own would silently revert to the vendor's "as of now", and every check and both questions would still pass.
========================================================================================
LENS conventions — does the slice obey the rules this repository set itself? -> accept-with-fixes
The built artefacts of this slice conform closely: no source name leaks into dab/model.yaml, no data vocabulary reaches src/ or tests/ (checked mechanically, atom by atom, against every id in the model and every column in both contracts), FREIGHT_ORDERS_AMOUNT satisfies every clause of §2, the generated DAR SQL obeys §1.3 and §3, and ruff, sqlfluff, yamllint --strict, 112 pytest tests, 18 data checks and `adss dar generate --check` are all clean. Everything I found is prose that the code has moved past: README.md still says question 2 is "not started", ADR 0004 still repeats the `_with_rel` claim the probe disproved, and conventions §1.4 M6 still states a rule ("exactly", "its group's table") that src/adss/mapping.py deliberately does not enforce. None of it is a data or correctness defect, so none of it blocks; all of it is a page that now disagrees with the system it governs.

  [worth fixing] README.md:19 and README.md:43
  The repository's front page is stale about the slice it just delivered. Line 19 still says "Slice 1 is green: one business question answered end to end", and the Slices table at line 43 still says question 2 is "not started". Both are contradicted by artefacts committed in this same slice.

  [worth fixing] docs/adr/0004-daana-cli-is-the-dab-engine.md:36
  ADR 0004 still states as observed fact the claim this slice's probe disproved: "`view_<entity>_with_rel` carries no relationship keys despite its name." ADR 0006 corrects that claim where ADR 0002 makes it, and commit 3650b66 corrects it in both skills, but the copy in ADR 0004 was missed — in the very file this slice edited (015f9c5) for a different stale claim, and in the record that says of itself it is "where someone will look for it".

  [worth fixing] docs/conventions.md:93 vs src/adss/mapping.py:176-194,255-262 and tests/test_relationship_rules.py:73-80
  M6's stated rule and its enforced rule differ, and the page was not clarified. conventions.md M6 says a relationship's "target expression mirrors the target entity's own key expression exactly", with the why "a differently spelled key produces pairs that join to nothing". The implementation deliberately compares shape with the names stripped out, and a test asserts that a differently spelled key is accepted. The code's reasoning is better than the page's — a foreign key is routinely named differently from the primary key it points at, and it is the casting that decides the VARCHAR — but conventions.md §11 says the recourse is to clarify that page, "in force immediately, for everyone", and conventions.md is untouched in this slice.

  [worth fixing] docs/adr/0004-daana-cli-is-the-dab-engine.md (edited by 015f9c5) vs docs/conventions.md:207-208 and docs/adr/README.md:9-12
  A slice-1 ADR was edited in slice 2, and the rule permitting it was written six minutes later, on a different page from the one that carries the rule it amends. conventions.md §8 is a hard rule — an ADR "is superseded by a new file rather than edited", with exactly one exception, "within the slice that wrote it, before any code depends on it". ADR 0004 is a slice-1 record with code depending on it, so the edit is outside that exception as conventions.md states it. The new carve-out for Confirmation sections lives only in docs/adr/README.md, so the exception set for §8 now exists in two documents that do not agree.

  [note] src/adss/mapping.py:241-248
  The source_table check is one scope wider than M6 describes. M6 says source_table is "byte-identical to its group's `table`", and the error message says "not byte-identical to any table in its group" — but the set compared against is every table in the whole mapping, because read_mapping flattens tables across all mapping_groups (mapping.py:96-111). A relationship declared in one group that names a table belonging to another group passes the check and would still be the silent skip M6 exists to catch. Nothing in the repository exercises it today: every mapping has exactly one group.

  [note] docs/deviations.md:46
  D-0001's review paragraph still frames the assertion gap in slice-1 terms, in the slice that added the first edge. The register says it is read at the start of every slice and each open entry checked "against whether its argument is still being carried on assertion"; a reader arriving in slice 3 is told the walk is unexercised because slice 1 had one entity, which no longer describes the state of the argument. ADR 0006 is honest that the property is still asserted and first provable in slice 4 — that is what the register should now say.

  [note] docs/conventions.md:53 vs dab/model.yaml:104-111 and src/adss/model.py:89-92
  §1.2's first hard rule cannot be satisfied by a relationship, which only becomes visible now that the first one exists. It says identifiers are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE "with `id` and `name` holding the identical string", but a relationship in dab/model.yaml carries only `name: IS_PLACED_BY`; its id, ORDER_IS_PLACED_BY_CUSTOMER, is composed from source, name and target, and the engine's relationship grammar has no `id` field at all. So id and name are necessarily different strings for every relationship. M6 (line 93) already describes relationship ids correctly; line 53 does not.
========================================================================================
LENS Independent recomputation — is the number right? -> accept
I recomputed the answer from scratch in plain Python (json + Decimal, no adss import, no repository SQL) directly off /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/das/fixtures/orders/page-*.json and /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/das/fixtures/customers/page-*.json, joining Orders.CustomerId to Customers.CustomerId myself, and got 153 rows across 8 quarters and 21 customer countries totalling exactly 64942.6900. Running docs/questions/02-.../uss.sql against warehouse.duckdb read-only returns the identical 153 rows with zero key differences and zero value differences, and so does staged.sql; I also verified all 830 bridge rows individually against their source records (customer, event date, freight, count=1 — zero mismatches). The question's load-bearing honesty claim — that the customer's Country and the order's ShipCountry are equal on every one of the 830 orders — is TRUE: I compared all 830 and got 830 equal, 0 unequal, 0 skipped. I have no findings.
========================================================================================
LENS The inheritance mechanism — does the generated SQL do what ADR 0006 says it does? -> accept-with-fixes
I checked every claim ADR 0006 makes against the emitted `dar/uss/_bridge.sql`, the generator that writes it, and the real warehouse, and then replayed the emitted SQL verbatim against scratch DuckDB databases holding the shapes this recording does not contain. Seven of the eight mechanical claims hold and I proved each one by making the opposite case: the pair source, the LEFT join, `row_number()` over a deterministic tiebreak, the as-of predicate on the observation time (not on now, not on the event date), the `row_st` filter, and matching by `rel_name` are all correct and all load-bearing. All three generated relationship checks pass on the real build and all three can be made to fail. One thing is not as the ADR describes: the as-of resolution is partitioned by the source key rather than by the bridge row, so the property the ADR spends its whole decision buying — that the rule survives a stage keeping more than the latest version — does not hold in the emitted SQL. It is latent today and does not affect this slice's answer.

  [worth fixing] src/adss/uss.py:215-221 and :248-251 (emitted as dar/uss/_bridge.sql:29-30 and :47-48)
  The inherited key is resolved per source KEY, not per bridge ROW. `_inherit_cte` ranks with `PARTITION BY revision.{source.key_column}` and `_stage_cte` joins the result back on `{entity.key_column}` alone, so the CTE collapses to one parent per order regardless of how many versions of that order the stage retains, and every retained version then receives that single parent. ADR 0006's stated reason for choosing `_observed_at` over `now` is exactly this case: "it is what keeps the rule stated at the level of a bridge row rather than at the level of a table, so it survives a stage that keeps more than the latest version, which is what a snapshot event and a `_is_current = FALSE` row will both need." It does not survive it. This is latent, not live: `_version_cte` (uss.py:184-187) always QUALIFYs to one version per key and `read_uss` refuses `kind: snapshot` (uss.py:140-146), so no bridge today has two rows for one key. Nothing in the suite would catch it when that changes — `test_an_inherited_key_is_the_one_in_force_when_the_row_was_observed` (tests/test_uss.py:200-207) is a regex over the predicate's text, and the predicate text stays correct while the partition is wrong.

  [note] src/adss/uss.py:304-308 (`bridge_columns`), with src/adss/checks.py:52-60
  `bridge_columns`'s docstring says "A model change appends; it never rearranges." It does rearrange. Key columns are emitted in `dab/model.yaml` entity order (`entity_ids`, uss.py:291), so an additive model change — a new entity plus a new edge, blueprint B7's canonical safe change — that is not written at the end of `model.yaml` shifts every existing key column right. Nothing guards it: the "bridge matches its published column contract" check derives `expected` from the same `bridge_columns()` call that generated the built table, so both sides move together and it still passes, and `test_the_key_columns_follow_the_model_order_not_the_declaration_order` (tests/test_uss.py:159-167) reverses the *events*, never the model's entities. The `entity_keys` docstring is candid that the check cannot catch a rearrangement; `bridge_columns`'s is not. Practical impact today is small — the question SQL and the destination read by name, and conventions §3 forbids `SELECT *` — so this is the docstring promising an invariant the code does not hold, not a live defect.
========================================================================================
LENS Test quality — would these tests fail if the code were wrong? -> do-not-accept
I read every file in tests/, then copied the repo to /tmp (no .venv, no warehouse.duckdb, no das/lake) and ran 16 one-at-a-time mutations against the 112-test suite with /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/.venv/bin/python -m pytest. Nine went red, seven went green. The red ones are the prescribed list and they are genuinely good tests. The green ones are the problem: the slice's central new behaviours — that the inherited key can never fan out, and that the generated relationship checks assert anything at all — have no test that can fail, and for the fan-out case nothing downstream can catch it either, because the built warehouse contains zero pair ties (verified read-only: 0 children with more than one target at one eff_tmstp, 0 null customer_key, 830 pairs for 830 bridge rows). The machinery tests are the only line of defence for exactly the shapes the data does not yet have, and for those they assert substrings over one blob of SQL rather than the window's PARTITION BY, its ORDER BY term order, or the join conditions.

  [blocking] src/adss/checks.py:153 relationship_checks() — no test anywhere in tests/
  The three generated data checks this slice introduces (__one_target, __loaded, __resolves) come from a pure function over a data file — machinery by conventions §6's own definition — and it has zero tests. Nothing else can catch a weakened check either: `adss dar generate --check` compares the committed .sql to the same generator, so it agrees with a weakened generator; and a weakened check passes trivially at `adss check`. ADR 0006 rests its cardinality argument on this check ("the check is not optional decoration on top of the inference — it is the half of the argument the inference cannot make"), so this is the half of the argument with nothing behind it. It is also the only SQL emitter in the repo absent from tests/test_generated_sql_lints.py's `emitters()` dict (raw, staged, current, clock_check, key_check, bridge, peripheral, calendar are all there).

  [blocking] tests/test_uss.py:218 test_the_pairs_are_ranked_deterministically_and_can_never_fan_out vs src/adss/uss.py:216
  The test named for the no-fan-out property never asserts the window's PARTITION BY. Adding the target key to the partition makes row_number() return 1 for each distinct parent, so a child with two parents yields two inherit-CTE rows, two bridge rows, and doubled measures — the exact failure ADR 0006 says the bridge exists to prevent. The suite stays green, and no data check can catch it either: __one_target is a statement about the data, and today's warehouse has no tie, so the fan-out never materialises. The repo already knows how to pin this: tests/test_das_sql.py:72-73 asserts `PARTITION BY staged.parent_id` and `ORDER BY staged.extracted_at DESC` for the DAS dedup window.

  [worth fixing] tests/test_uss.py:224 (`assert "ver_tmstp DESC" in sql`) vs src/adss/uss.py:218-219
  ADR 0006 states the ranking is "row_number() over eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC". The test only asserts the substring "ver_tmstp DESC" appears somewhere in the SQL, so the two ORDER BY terms can be swapped — ranking by version timestamp before effective timestamp, which picks a different (wrong) parent whenever the two orderings disagree — and the suite is green. Today's data cannot catch it either, since every order has exactly one open pair row.

  [worth fixing] tests/test_uss.py:223
  The guard against a ranking function that ties is `re.search(r"(?<!row_number\(\) OVER \()\brank\s*\(", sql)`. The `\b` before `rank` does not match inside `dense_rank`, so `dense_rank()` — which ties exactly as `rank()` does — slips through, and the companion assertion `"row_number() OVER (" in sql` is still satisfied by the version CTE and the peripheral. The test that exists specifically to refuse a tying window function does not refuse one.

  [worth fixing] tests/test_uss.py:186 test_a_stage_carries_the_key_of_everything_it_inherits_from (assertion at :193)
  The test that names the slice's headline behaviour cannot tell a carried key from a typed NULL in a column of the same name. `assert "AS parent_key" in occurred` is satisfied by `cast(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS parent_key`. Two independent mutations that destroy the inheritance — emitting NULL for every inherited key, and emitting the child's own key as the parent's — both leave the suite green. ADR 0006 says all three M6 failures present as "an inherited key that is simply null everywhere, which looks like data rather than like a defect"; this is the machinery test that ought to distinguish the two, and it does not. (Both mutations are caught downstream at `adss check` — by question disagreement and by __resolves respectively — which is why this is not blocking.)

  [worth fixing] src/adss/uss.py:250 (the stage CTE's ON clause) — no test in tests/ references it
  The join that attaches the inherit CTE back to the version CTE is new in this slice and its condition is asserted nowhere. Replacing it with a cross join — the most extreme fan-out available, 830 orders × 830 inherited keys, every measure multiplied 830× — leaves the machinery suite entirely green.

  [worth fixing] tests/test_uss.py:214-215 test_a_row_that_inherits_nothing_keeps_its_row
  The guard is two substring tests over the whole bridge SQL: `"LEFT JOIN" in sql` and `"INNER JOIN" not in sql`. A bare `JOIN` is an inner join in SQL and matches neither, and the second LEFT JOIN (uss.py:249) satisfies the positive assertion on its own — so either of the two joins can quietly become inner and the suite stays green. Today the redundancy between uss.py:210 and :249 means one inner join alone loses no rows, but the test proves a whole-file property that either join satisfies, not the property of the join it is written about. Nothing in the built warehouse would notice either: there are no childless rows (null customer_key = 0).

  [note] src/adss/mapping.py:258 and tests/fixtures/mappings/bad_relationship_table.yaml
  The M6 message and docstring claim source_table must be "byte-identical", and the parametrised test matches on the word "byte-identical" in the message — but the only fixture differs by spelling (`das__staged.children` vs `das__staged.child`), so the byte-identity property itself is not exercised. A case- or whitespace-insensitive comparison passes the suite while contradicting the stated rule.
========================================================================================
LENS Ordinary code review and security -> accept-with-fixes

"""The checks that carry half of ADR 0006's argument, run against the shapes they exist to catch.

The cardinality of an edge cannot be read off the model -- the language has nowhere to state
it -- and it cannot be read off the data, which is allowed to be many-to-many. So it is
inferred from the mapping and pinned by these checks, and the check is not decoration on top
of the inference: it is the half the inference cannot make.

Nothing else can catch a weakened one. `adss dar generate --check` compares the committed SQL
to the same generator, so it agrees with a weakened generator; and a weakened check passes
trivially at `adss check`. So each one is run here against a warehouse built to fail it, and
against one built to pass it. A check that cannot fail is not a check.
"""

from pathlib import Path

import duckdb
import pytest

from adss.checks import relationship_checks
from adss.model import read_model

NEUTRAL = Path(__file__).parent / "fixtures" / "dab" / "model.yaml"

EDGE = "child_points_at_parent"
NAME = "CHILD_POINTS_AT_PARENT"


def checks() -> dict[str, str]:
    return relationship_checks(read_model(NEUTRAL))


def warehouse(connection: duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection) -> None:
    """The objects a relationship check reads, empty. Shaped as the engine shapes them."""
    connection.execute("CREATE SCHEMA dab")
    connection.execute("CREATE SCHEMA dar__uss")
    for edge, source, target in (
        (NAME, "CHILD", "PARENT"),
        ("CHILD_SITS_BESIDE_NEIGHBOUR", "CHILD", "NEIGHBOUR"),
    ):
        connection.execute(
            f'CREATE TABLE dab."v_{edge}" ('
            f'  "{source}_key" VARCHAR, "{target}_key" VARCHAR, rel_name VARCHAR,'
            f"  eff_tmstp TIMESTAMP, ver_tmstp TIMESTAMP, row_st VARCHAR)"
        )
    connection.execute(
        "CREATE TABLE dar__uss._bridge ("
        "  _stage VARCHAR, child_key VARCHAR, parent_key VARCHAR, neighbour_key VARCHAR)"
    )
    for peripheral in ("parent", "neighbour", "child"):
        connection.execute(f"CREATE TABLE dar__uss.{peripheral} ({peripheral}_key VARCHAR)")


def answer(connection: duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection, check: str) -> int:
    body = "\n".join(
        line for line in checks()[check].splitlines() if not line.lstrip().startswith("--")
    )
    found = connection.execute(body).fetchone()
    assert found is not None
    return int(found[0])


@pytest.fixture
def scratch(tmp_path: Path):
    connection = duckdb.connect(str(tmp_path / "scratch.duckdb"))
    warehouse(connection)
    yield connection
    connection.close()


def pair(connection, child: str, parent: str, at: str, wrote: str = "2026-01-01", st: str = "Y"):
    connection.execute(
        f'INSERT INTO dab."v_{NAME}" VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)',
        [child, parent, NAME, at, wrote, st],
    )


def test_there_is_one_set_of_checks_per_declared_edge():
    written = checks()
    model = read_model(NEUTRAL)
    for edge in model.relationships:
        for suffix in ("one_target", "loaded", "resolves"):
            assert f"{edge.id.lower()}__{suffix}" in written
    assert len(written) == len(model.relationships) * 3, "no edge is checked twice or not at all"


def test_every_check_reads_only_open_pairs_of_its_own_relationship():
    for name, sql in checks().items():
        if name.endswith("__resolves"):
            continue
        assert "rel_name = '" in sql, f"{name} must name the relationship, never a type key"
        assert "row_st = 'Y'" in sql, f"{name} must ignore a retracted pair"
        assert "type_key" not in sql


def test_one_target_fails_when_a_source_has_two_targets_at_one_instant(scratch):
    """The tie the engine's own rank() would return twice, doubling a measure."""
    pair(scratch, "CH1", "P1", "2026-01-01")
    pair(scratch, "CH2", "P2", "2026-01-01")
    assert answer(scratch, f"{EDGE}__one_target") == 0, "one target each is not an ambiguity"

    pair(scratch, "CH1", "P9", "2026-01-01")
    assert answer(scratch, f"{EDGE}__one_target") == 1


def test_one_target_accepts_a_source_whose_target_changed_over_time(scratch):
    """Two parents at DIFFERENT instants is history, not ambiguity, and must not be refused."""
    pair(scratch, "CH1", "P1", "2026-01-01")
    pair(scratch, "CH1", "P2", "2026-02-01")
    assert answer(scratch, f"{EDGE}__one_target") == 0


def test_one_target_ignores_a_retracted_pair(scratch):
    pair(scratch, "CH1", "P1", "2026-01-01")
    pair(scratch, "CH1", "P9", "2026-01-01", st="N")
    assert answer(scratch, f"{EDGE}__one_target") == 0


def test_one_target_ignores_another_relationships_pairs(scratch):
    pair(scratch, "CH1", "P1", "2026-01-01")
    scratch.execute(
        f'INSERT INTO dab."v_{NAME}" VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)',
        ["CH1", "P9", "SOMETHING_ELSE", "2026-01-01", "2026-01-01", "Y"],
    )
    assert answer(scratch, f"{EDGE}__one_target") == 0


def test_loaded_fails_when_a_declared_edge_produced_no_pair_at_all(scratch):
    """What a source_table the engine could not match looks like: nothing, in silence."""
    assert answer(scratch, f"{EDGE}__loaded") == 1

    pair(scratch, "CH1", "P1", "2026-01-01")
    assert answer(scratch, f"{EDGE}__loaded") == 0


def test_loaded_is_not_satisfied_by_a_retracted_pair(scratch):
    pair(scratch, "CH1", "P1", "2026-01-01", st="N")
    assert answer(scratch, f"{EDGE}__loaded") == 1


def test_resolves_fails_when_an_inherited_key_names_no_row_in_the_peripheral(scratch):
    """What a target expression of the wrong shape looks like: pairs that join to nothing."""
    scratch.execute("INSERT INTO dar__uss.parent VALUES ('P1')")
    scratch.execute("INSERT INTO dar__uss._bridge VALUES ('child', 'CH1', 'P1', NULL)")
    assert answer(scratch, f"{EDGE}__resolves") == 0

    scratch.execute("INSERT INTO dar__uss._bridge VALUES ('child', 'CH2', 'P404', NULL)")
    assert answer(scratch, f"{EDGE}__resolves") == 1


def test_resolves_accepts_a_row_that_inherited_nothing(scratch):
    """A child with no parent keeps its bridge row and a null key. That is not a dangling key."""
    scratch.execute("INSERT INTO dar__uss._bridge VALUES ('child', 'CH6', NULL, NULL)")
    assert answer(scratch, f"{EDGE}__resolves") == 0


def test_resolves_looks_only_at_the_stage_that_inherits(scratch):
    """Every other stage emits a typed NULL for this key, and a null is not a dangling key."""
    scratch.execute("INSERT INTO dar__uss._bridge VALUES ('parent', NULL, NULL, NULL)")
    assert answer(scratch, f"{EDGE}__resolves") == 0

## 8. Documentation

| Rule | Why | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| A decision goes in an ADR under [`adr/`](adr/README.md), numbered, in MADR format, and is superseded by a new file rather than edited. | The value of a decision record is the record of what was true when it was made. | Hard rule |
| The one exception: a record may be corrected **within the slice that wrote it**, before any code depends on it, when an observation it rests on turns out to be false. Say so in the commit. | Superseding a record that was wrong before it was ever built on preserves nothing but the mistake, and leaves a reader two documents to reconcile where there was never a real decision to reverse. After that slice, supersede. | Hard rule |

| Generated artefacts are **committed**, and a `--check` regeneration in the gate fails on any diff. The drift check is what stops the committed copy becoming a second truth nothing compares against the model. Any formatting the generator's output needs must happen *inside* the generator, or every regeneration produces a spurious diff. | Hard rule |

--- deviations 44-48 ---
## Review

The register is read at the start of every slice. Each open entry is checked against its exit
condition **and against whether its argument is still being carried on assertion** — D-0001's
justification rests on a walk over many-to-one edges, which slice 1's single entity does not
exercise at all. An entry should also be re-read the moment a second consumer appears, not only
when isolation is demanded, because by then the shared structure will already have shaped both
readers. An entry whose exit condition has been met and which is still open is a defect in the
same way a failing test is: the system is no longer doing what its own documentation says.

8	# An inherited key is resolved from the raw pairs, as of the observation time of the row that inherits it
9	
10	## Context and Problem Statement
11	
12	Slice 1 built a bridge with one entity and no relationships. ADR 0002 asserted that one shared
13	bridge is safe because keys inherit along many-to-one edges while measures do not, and said in as
14	many words that the walk had zero edges and the property was asserted rather than exercised. This
15	slice is the first with an edge: an order is placed by a customer, and the question groups the
16	freight of an order by the *customer's* country, which exists nowhere on the order.
17	
18	So the generator has to get `customer_key` onto an order row. The engine offers four places to get
19	it from, they do not agree with each other, and the names do not say which is which. A probe built
20	a two-entity model with one relationship, changed a foreign key, and read every object the engine
21	produced. It overturned two things ADR 0002 states as fact.
22	
23	**The relationship view is a *current* view, not a historical one.** ADR 0002 says reading it would
24	lose a row whose foreign key changed. That is not what happens. The macro behind
25	`dab.view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` is:
26	
27	```sql
28	rank() OVER (PARTITION BY <SRC>_key, type_key ORDER BY eff_tmstp DESC, ver_tmstp DESC) AS nbr
29	... WHERE nbr = 1 AND row_st = 'Y'
30	```
31	
32	Partitioned by the child, so the child never drops out — it is re-pointed. After the probe moved
33	CH1 from P1 to P2, the pair table held both rows with `row_st = 'Y'` and the view held `CH1|P2`
34	alone. Nothing is lost; the *old* pair is what is lost, for every row of that child, retroactively.
35	The reason to read the raw pairs is therefore history, not disappearance, and ADR 0002 got the
36	right answer from the wrong mechanism.
37	
38	**`view_<entity>_with_rel` does carry relationship keys — on the target side, and it fans out.**
39	ADR 0002 says its column list is byte-identical to `view_<entity>`. That is true only for the
40	relationship's *source* entity. Once an entity is a relationship *target*, its `_with_rel` view
41	becomes a double left join through the pair macro and gains the source entity's key **and every one
42	of its attributes**, one row per child. The probe measured the consequence:
43	`sum(CHILD_AMOUNT)` over `view_PARENT_with_rel` returned 200.75 against a true 150.75. That is a
44	live fan trap in a view whose name invites exactly the join that springs it.
45	
46	**`rank()` is not `row_number()`, so a tie returns both rows.** The probe's CH5 had two parent codes
47	in one load, so two pair rows shared an `eff_tmstp`, and the relationship view returned CH5 twice.
48	A child appearing twice in the bridge multiplies its measures — the precise failure the bridge
49	exists to prevent, arriving from the engine's own view rather than from anything we wrote.
50	
51	**The model cannot say that an edge is many-to-one.** This is the finding that decides how the rule
52	is enforced, and it is settled by the engine's own error rather than inferred: adding
53	`cardinality:` to a relationship is rejected with *"Valid fields are: name, definition, description,
54	source, target, source_entity_id, target_entity_id, type"*, and that list is the whole grammar. The
55	one candidate, `type`, is not a cardinality slot — it accepts any string without validation
56	(`1:N`, `MANY_TO_ONE`, `BOGUS_VALUE` all pass `check model`) and is **dropped on compile**: it does
57	not appear in the compiled `model.json` and never reaches the engine. Nor is the engine merely
58	silent about cardinality. It is agnostic by design: it treats a child's parents as a *set*,
59	aggregating all target keys per `(source key, eff_tmstp)` into a fingerprint and writing a row when
60	that set changes. Many-to-many is a supported case, not a defect.
61	
62	So the generator cannot learn "many-to-one" from the model, and it cannot learn it from the data,
63	because the data is legitimately allowed to be many-to-many. Something else has to say it.
64	
65	## Decision Drivers
66	
67	* a measure summed over the bridge is additive at every grain, whatever the model's shape
68	* a bridge row is true as of one instant, and every column on it is true as of that same instant
69	* the generator reads objects whose behaviour has been observed, never ones whose names suggest it
70	* a case the design cannot handle fails the build loudly rather than answering a question wrongly
71	* the walk works for zero edges, one edge and, later, a chain — without a special case per depth
72	
73	## Considered Options
74	
75	* `dab.view_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` — the engine's ranked relationship view
76	* `dab.v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>` — the raw pairs plus a relationship name, ranked here
77	* `dab.<SRC>_<TGT>_x` — the pair table directly, with `dab__meta` for the type key
78	* `dab.view_<TGT>_with_rel` — the view named as though it were for this
79	
80	## Decision Outcome
81	
82	Chosen option: **`dab.v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`, ranked in the generated SQL as of the child row's own
83	`_observed_at`, one parent per child, with the tie refused by a data check.**
84

fix(repo): act on the verification, which refused the slice on its test quality

Six lenses ran. The recomputation accepted it -- 153 rows and 64,942.69 rebuilt from the raw
payloads in plain Python, identical, and the question's load-bearing claim independently
confirmed: customer country and ship country are equal on all 830 orders, 0 unequal. The
test-quality lens refused the slice, and it was right.

Two blocking findings, both of the same shape: the slice's central new behaviours had tests
that could not fail.

The test named for the no-fan-out property never looked at the window's PARTITION BY. Adding
the target key to it makes row_number() return 1 for EACH parent, so a child with two parents
yields two bridge rows and a doubled measure -- the exact failure the bridge exists to
prevent -- and the suite stayed green. Nor could any data check catch it, because a check is a
statement about data and this warehouse has no tie. The tests now assert the window whole: the
function, the partition terms, and the ORDER BY as a sequence. Nine mutations that were green
before are red now, including a bare JOIN where a LEFT was meant, dense_rank slipping past a
word boundary, and the two ranking terms swapped.

The three generated relationship checks -- the half of ADR 0006's cardinality argument that
the inference cannot make -- had no tests at all, and nothing else could catch a weakened one:
`dar generate --check` compares the committed SQL to the same generator, so it agrees with a
weakened generator, and a weakened check passes trivially. Each is now run against a scratch
warehouse built to fail it and one built to pass it. Six weakenings are caught, including
raising the threshold, counting rows instead of distinct targets, and inverting the NOT
EXISTS. They are also linted now, which every other emitter already was.

Then the latent defects, none of which bite today and all of which would have bitten later.

The inherited key was resolved per source KEY rather than per bridge ROW, which is exactly
the property ADR 0006 spends its whole decision buying: the ranking now partitions by the key
and its observation time, so a stage that keeps more than the latest version does not hand
every one of them the same parent. Two edges from one entity to the same target -- or an edge
to the entity itself -- would have emitted one key column twice under one name, and DuckDB
resolves that silently rather than raising, so one inherited key would have vanished. Both
shapes are refused, and ADR 0006's claim that rel_name prevented it is corrected: it separates
the pair objects, not the bridge's columns.

M6's checker validated only the last mapping declaring a given edge, so an entity loaded from
a second source -- which the blueprint exists to make possible -- could carry the silent skip
the check was installed to catch. And the key-shape comparison anonymised function names along
with column names, so lpad(x, 5, '0') and a bare x compared as the same shape; a function
decides the value as surely as a cast does.

`dar generate` had become a second writer into checks/ and swept nothing, so renaming a
relationship left a check that aborts the whole run before a finding is printed -- the hazard
the other sweep was installed for. It sweeps now, and the DAS command asks for names rather
than building SQL it throws away, which also stops a DAS command failing on an unreadable DAB
model.

A question id names a file and an environment variable and was validated nowhere. The empty
one is the dangerous case, not the obviously broken one: the page reads an empty selection as
"show everything", so that question's committed answer.png -- the record of what was
delivered -- would have been a picture of every question with nothing looking wrong. The page
also rendered drafts that `adss check` deliberately skips, and indexed positionally, so one
new draft directory sorting first would have broken every page at once.

The rest was prose the code had moved past: the README still called slice 2 not started, M6
described a rule stricter than the one enforced (the code's reasoning is the better one, so
the page moved), section 1.2 required an `id` field that a relationship's grammar does not
have, the deviations register still explained the assertion gap in slice-1 terms, and the two
documents carrying the exceptions to "never edit a record" did not agree with each other.

def test_an_entity_appended_to_the_model_appends_its_key_and_moves_nothing():

    An entity inserted in the middle of the model moves every key column after it, and nothing
    can catch that: the check derives what it expects from the same function that built the
    table, so both sides move together. So the property is pinned here, on the one shape that

content.text: The test surfaced something sharper: a new key column shifts every *measure* right, because keys are grouped before measures. Stating what's actually true:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("src/adss/uss.py")
t = p.read_text()
old = '''    An entity APPENDED to `dab/model.yaml` appends its key column; one inserted in the middle
    moves every key column after it. So the model file's own order is part of this contract,
    which is worth stating rather than claiming the contract only ever grows: nothing here can
    tell the two apart, and the check that compares the built bridge to this contract derives
    what it expects from this same function, so both sides move together and it still passes.
    New entities go at the end. Blueprint B7.
    """'''
new = '''    Grouped: the structural columns, then one key per entity in model order, then one column
    per measure in declaration order.

    That grouping means the contract does NOT only ever grow at the end, and saying otherwise
    would be the more comfortable lie. A new entity appends a key, and because keys precede
    measures, every measure column moves right. An entity inserted in the middle of the model
    moves the keys after it as well. So the model file's own order is part of this contract,
    and nothing here can catch a rearrangement: the check that compares the built bridge to
    this contract derives what it expects from this same function, so both sides move together
    and it passes either way.

    What makes that tolerable rather than a defect is that nothing reads this table by
    position. Conventions section 3 forbids `SELECT *`, the questions name their columns and
    so does the destination. A consumer that did read positionally would be reading a contract
    this docstring does not offer it. New entities still go at the end, because moving a key
    column is a bigger change than moving a measure. Blueprint B7.
    """'''
assert old in t
p.write_text(t.replace(old, new))
PY
python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("tests/test_uss.py")
t = p.read_text()
old = '''    after = bridge_columns(later, read_uss(FIXTURES / "uss.yaml", later))
    assert after[: len(before)] == before, "an appended entity may not move a published column"
    assert "latecomer_key" in after'''
new = '''    after = bridge_columns(later, read_uss(FIXTURES / "uss.yaml", later))
    keys = [c for c in before if c.endswith("_key")]
    assert [c for c in after if c.endswith("_key")] == [*keys, "latecomer_key"], (
        "the new key goes last among the keys; no existing key moves"
    )
    measures = [c for c in before if c.startswith("_measure__")]
    assert [c for c in after if c.startswith("_measure__")] == measures, (
        "and no measure is added, reordered or renamed by adding an entity"
    )
    # But the measures DO all move right, because keys precede them. That is the property the
    # docstring used to deny, and it is why nothing may read this table by position.
    assert after.index(measures[0]) == before.index(measures[0]) + 1'''
assert old in t
p.write_text(t.replace(old, new))
PY

from pathlib import Path

old = '''    # The description table is where an ingestion-strategy defect would be visible, and the
    # only place: every presentation view hides it.'''
new = '''    # The one engine behaviour the whole as-of rule rests on, and the only one not pinned
    # until now: that `v_<edge>` hands over the RAW pairs. If a release added ranking inside
    # it, the rule ADR 0006 spends generated SQL to own would silently revert to the vendor's
    # "as of now", and every check and both questions would still pass. Pinned two ways: it
    # still exposes the columns only an unranked read has, and it still returns every row the
    # pair table holds for that relationship.
    for edge in model.relationships:
        exposed = _columns(connection, f"v_{edge.id}")
        findings.append(
            Finding(
                f"dab.v_{edge.id} still hands over the raw pairs",
                {"row_st", "ver_tmstp", "rel_name"} <= set(exposed),
                f"{exposed} -- the ranked view drops row_st and ver_tmstp, so losing them "
                f"here means this object has become a ranked one and the as-of rule is the "
                f"vendor's again",
            )
        )
        counted = connection.execute(
            f'SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM dab."v_{edge.id}" WHERE rel_name = ?), '
            f'(SELECT count(*) FROM dab."{edge.source_entity_id}_{edge.target_entity_id}_x")',
            [edge.id],
        ).fetchone()
        through, raw = counted if counted else (None, None)
        findings.append(
            Finding(
                f"dab.v_{edge.id} filters nothing out of the pair table",
                through == raw,
                f"{through} through the view, {raw} in the pair table -- a gap means the view "
                f"has started ranking or filtering, and the generator ranks it a second time",
            )
        )

    # The description table is where an ingestion-strategy defect would be visible, and the
    # only place: every presentation view hides it.'''
assert old in t
p.write_text(t.replace(old, new))

fix(dar): pin the one engine behaviour the as-of rule rests on, and stop the contract lying

Two things the adversarial filter kept after trying to kill them.

`v_<edge>` hands over the raw pairs, and nothing said so. It is the single object the
generated inherited-key SQL reads, and the whole reason for reading it rather than the engine's
own ranked view is that it does no ranking. If a release started ranking inside it, the as-of
rule ADR 0006 spends generated SQL to own would silently revert to the vendor's "as of now" --
and every check and both questions would still pass, because today no order has ever changed
customer. It is pinned two ways now: the view still exposes the columns only an unranked read
has, and it still returns every row the pair table holds for that relationship.

And the bridge's column contract claimed "a model change appends; it never rearranges", which
is not true and is the more comfortable thing to say. Writing the test to pin it is what showed
why: the columns are grouped, keys before measures, so appending an entity appends a key and
moves every measure column right. An entity inserted mid-model moves the keys after it too, and
nothing can catch either -- the check that compares the built bridge to the contract derives
what it expects from the same function, so both sides move together and it passes.

What makes that tolerable is not the docstring's promise but a different fact: nothing reads
this table by position. Section 3 forbids SELECT *, and the questions and the page name their
columns. The docstring now says that, and the test pins the property that actually holds --
appending adds a key at the end of the keys, adds no measure, reorders none, and moves the
measures right by exactly one.

input.head: claude/adss-slice-02-freight-per-customer-country-and-quarter
input.body: The first question whose answer needs a key to inherit. Stacked on slice 1. ## The question > What freight did we pay per customer country and order quarter? > — asked by the logistics manager **64,942.69** across 8 quarters and 21 customer countries. The customer's own country, which is not where the goods went. ## What it widens A second contract and entity, the **first relationship**, the first key a stage inherits, and the first sum measure. `CUSTOMER` has no event of its own — it exists in the bridge only because an order reaches it. ## The decision this slice forced, and how it changed A probe built a two-entity model, moved a foreign key, and read every object the engine produced. It overturned **two facts ADR 0002 rested on**: - **The relationship view is a *current* view.** ADR 0002 said reading it would lose a row whose foreign key changed. It does not. It partitions by the child, so the child never drops out — it is re-pointed, and the *old* pair is erased for that child's whole history, retroactively and invisibly. The reason to read the raw pairs is history, not disappearance. - **`view__with_rel` does carry relationship keys** — on a target side, along with every attribute of the source entity, fanned out. The probe measured `sum(CHILD_AMOUNT)` at **200.75 against a true 150.75**. A live fan trap in the view whose name most invites the join. And a third nobody had looked for: the engine ranks with `rank()`, not `row_number()`, so a child whose source named two parents at one instant comes back **twice** — doubling its measures, from the vendor's own view. A fourth finding decided how the rule is *enforced*: **the model cannot say an edge is many-to-one.** `cardinality:` is rejected outright; `type:` takes any string without validation and is dropped on compile, never reaching the engine. The engine is agnostic by design — it treats a child's parents as a set. So cardinality is inferred from the mapping (M5 already forbids the reaches that would make a target expression multi-valued) and pinned by a data check, because the inference cannot cover one key appearing on several staged rows of a single load. Three generated checks assert the mechanism: no source has two targets at one instant, every declared edge loaded at least one pair, and every inherited key names a row in its peripheral. Each is the signature of one of M6's three silent failures. ## The two answers, which must agree ```sql -- straight from the source, bypassing both layers SELECT strftime(o.order_date, '%Y') || '-Q' || cast(quarter(o.order_date) AS VARCHAR) AS order_quarter, c.country AS customer_country, cast(sum(o.freight) AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS freight_orders_amount FROM das__staged.orders__current AS o LEFT JOIN das__staged.customers__current AS c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY order_quarter, customer_country ``` ```sql -- from the generated star schema SELECT cal.quarter_label AS order_quarter, cu.based_in_country AS customer_country, cast(sum(b._measure__order__freight_orders_amount) AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS freight_orders_amount FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key LEFT JOIN dar__uss.customer AS cu ON b.customer_key = cu.customer_key WHERE b._event = 'placed' GROUP BY cal.quarter_label, cu.based_in_country ORDER BY order_quarter, customer_country ``` 153 rows each, identical, totalling all the freight the business paid. ## ⚠️ What agreeing proves here, and what it does not **This is the thing to read before accepting the slice.** The dimension is the customer's country. The obvious wrong implementation is the order's destination country — the value already on the same row, one join cheaper. **In this recording those two columns are equal on every one of the 830 orders.** So an implementation that inherited nothing and read `DESTINATION_COUNTRY` would produce this same answer and the agreement check would pass it. That claim is not mine: an independent lens recomputed it from the raw payloads and got 830 equal, 0 unequal. So the number is checked by the two queries, and the **mechanism** is checked by the three data checks, which hold regardless of whether the two columns coincide. Neither would have been enough alone. It took looking at the data to find that out, and the prioritised list — which asserted "customer country is not destination country" as though it were a fact about the data — has been corrected to say it is a fact about the model. ## Verification Six independent lenses, then every finding attacked by an agent trying to kill it. Fourteen survived at confidence ≥ 7; three were killed. **The test-quality lens refused the slice**, and it was right. Two blocking findings, both the same shape — the slice's central behaviours had tests that could not fail: - **The test named for the no-fan-out property never looked at the window's `PARTITION BY`.** Adding the target key to it makes `row_number()` return 1 for *each* parent, so a child with two parents yields two bridge rows and a doubled measure — the exact failure the bridge exists to prevent — and the suite stayed green. No data check could catch it either: a check is a statement about data, and this warehouse has no tie. Nine previously-green mutations are now red, including a bare `JOIN` where a `LEFT` was meant, `dense_rank` slipping past a word boundary, and the two ranking terms swapped. - **The three generated checks had no tests at all** — the half of ADR 0006's argument the inference cannot make. Nothing else could catch a weakened one: `dar generate --check` compares the committed SQL to the same generator, so it agrees with a weakened generator. Each now runs against a scratch warehouse built to fail it and one built to pass it. Latent defects, none of which bite today: - The inherited key was resolved per source **key** rather than per bridge **row** — exactly the property ADR 0006 spends its decision buying. A reviewer reproduced it by retaining two versions of one order. - Two edges from one entity to the same target, or a self-edge, would emit one key column **twice under one name**, and DuckDB resolves that silently. Both shapes are now refused, and ADR 0006's claim that `rel_name` prevented it is corrected — it separates the pair objects, not the bridge's columns. - M6's checker validated only the **last** mapping declaring a given edge, so an entity loaded from a second source could carry the silent skip the check exists to catch. - The key-shape comparison anonymised **function names** along with column names, so `lpad(x, 5, '0')` and a bare `x` compared as the same shape. - `dar generate` had become a second writer into `checks/` and swept nothing, so renaming a relationship left a check that aborts the whole run before a finding is printed. - A question id names a file and an environment variable and was validated nowhere. The **empty** one is the dangerous case: the page reads an empty selection as "show everything", so that question's committed `answer.png` would have been a picture of every question with nothing looking wrong. - The bridge's column contract claimed "a model change appends; it never rearranges". It does rearrange — keys precede measures, so a new entity moves every measure right. The docstring now says what is true, and why it is tolerable: nothing reads this table by position. Also pinned: that `v_` hands over the **raw** pairs. It is the one object the generated SQL reads and the only engine behaviour the as-of rule rests on that nothing checked. If a release started ranking inside it, the rule would silently revert to the vendor's "as of now" and every check would still pass. ## What this slice still does not prove Both entities on this edge are at the **same grain** — one order has one customer — so no measure *can* multiply across it however the join is written. **D-0001 is still carried on assertion.** The first measure at a finer grain arrives in slice 4, and that is where the fan-out proof becomes possible. ADR 0006 and the deviations register both say so rather than claiming otherwise. ```bash uv run adss build # the whole system from the recording, offline uv run adss check # 20 checks, all green ``` ## Next Slice 3: *how many orders shipped per shipping month, and how many days did they take?* — two events on one entity, a second bridge stage, and a ratio computed at query time from two additive measures. 21 orders in the recording have never shipped, so "an event that did not happen has no row" stops being theoretical. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_019rspwWhmXfxoTvKg5jmNWh

{"number":2,"title":"Slice 2 — What freight did we pay per customer country and order quarter?","body":"The first question whose answer needs a key to inherit. Stacked on slice 1. ## The question > What freight did we pay per customer country and order quarter? > — asked by the logistics manager **64,942.69** across 8 quarters and 21 customer countries. The customer's own country, which is not where the goods went. ## What it widens A second contract and entity, the **first relationship**, the first key a stage inherits, and the first sum measure. `CUSTOMER` has no event of its own — it exists in the bridge only because an order reaches it. ## The decision this slice forced, and how it changed A probe built a two-entity model, moved a foreign key, and read every object the engine produced. It overturned **two facts ADR 0002 rested on**: - **The relationship view is a *current* view.** ADR 0002 said reading it would lose a row whose foreign key changed. It does not. It partitions by the child, so the child never drops out — it is re-pointed, and the *old* pair is erased for that child's whole history, retroactively and invisibly. The reason to read the raw pairs is history, not disappearance. - **`view__with_rel` does carry relationship keys** — on a target side, along with every attribute of the source entity, fanned out. The probe measured `sum(CHILD_AMOUNT)` at **200.75 against a true 150.75**. A live fan trap in the view whose name most invites the join. And a third nobody had looked for: the engine ranks with `rank()`, not `row_number()`, so a child whose source named two parents at one instant comes back **twice** — doubling its measures, from the vendor's own view. A fourth finding decided how the rule is *enforced*: **the model cannot say an edge is many-to-one.** `cardinality:` is rejected outright; `type:` takes any string without validation and is dropped on compile, never reaching the engine. The engine is agnostic by design — it treats a child's parents as a set. So cardinality is inferred from the mapping (M5 already forbids the reaches that would make a target expression multi-valued) and pinned by a data check, because the inference cannot cover one key appearing on several staged rows of a single load. [ADR 0006](https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/blob/9b34378/docs/adr/0006-an-inherited-key-is-resolved-as-of-the-row-that-inherits-it.md) records all of it, and corrects ADR 0002 and ADR 0004 rather than editing them. ## What the generator does now Reads `v___` — the raw pairs — matched on `rel_name` (never `type_key`, which is not stable across models), open pairs only, joined **LEFT** because a childless row has no pair row at all and absence is the only evidence there is, ranked with `row_number()` over `eff_tmstp, ver_tmstp, target key`, **as of the observation time of the row that inherits**, partitioned by that row rather than by its key. Three generated checks assert the mechanism: no source has two targets at one instant, every declared edge loaded at least one pair, and every inherited key names a row in its peripheral. Each is the signature of one of M6's three silent failures. ## The two answers, which must agree ```sql -- straight from the source, bypassing both layers SELECT strftime(o.order_date, '%Y') || '-Q' || cast(quarter(o.order_date) AS VARCHAR) AS order_quarter, c.country AS customer_country, cast(sum(o.freight) AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS freight_orders_amount FROM das__staged.orders__current AS o LEFT JOIN das__staged.customers__current AS c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY order_quarter, customer_country ``` ```sql -- from the generated star schema SELECT cal.quarter_label AS order_quarter, cu.based_in_country AS customer_country, cast(sum(b._measure__order__freight_orders_amount) AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS freight_orders_amount FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key LEFT JOIN dar__uss.customer AS cu ON b.customer_key = cu.customer_key WHERE b._event = 'placed' GROUP BY cal.quarter_label, cu.based_in_country ORDER BY order_quarter, customer_country ``` 153 rows each, identical, totalling all the freight the business paid. ## ⚠️ What agreeing proves here, and what it does not **This is the thing to read before accepting the slice.** The dimension is the customer's country. The obvious wrong implementation is the order's destination country — the value already on the same row, one join cheaper. **In this recording those two columns are equal on every one of the 830 orders.** So an implementation that inherited nothing and read `DESTINATION_COUNTRY` would produce this same answer and the agreement check would pass it. That claim is not mine: an independent lens recomputed it from the raw payloads and got 830 equal, 0 unequal. So the number is checked by the two queries, and the **mechanism** is checked by the three data checks, which hold regardless of whether the two columns coincide. Neither would have been enough alone. It took looking at the data to find that out, and the prioritised list — which asserted "customer country is not destination country" as though it were a fact about the data — has been corrected to say it is a fact about the model. ## Verification Six independent lenses, then every finding attacked by an agent trying to kill it. Fourteen survived at confidence ≥ 7; three were killed. **The test-quality lens refused the slice**, and it was right. Two blocking findings, both the same shape — the slice's central behaviours had tests that could not fail: - **The test named for the no-fan-out property never looked at the window's `PARTITION BY`.** Adding the target key to it makes `row_number()` return 1 for *each* parent, so a child with two parents yields two bridge rows and a doubled measure — the exact failure the bridge exists to prevent — and the suite stayed green. No data check could catch it either: a check is a statement about data, and this warehouse has no tie. Nine previously-green mutations are now red, including a bare `JOIN` where a `LEFT` was meant, `dense_rank` slipping past a word boundary, and the two ranking terms swapped. - **The three generated checks had no tests at all** — the half of ADR 0006's argument the inference cannot make. Nothing else could catch a weakened one: `dar generate --check` compares the committed SQL to the same generator, so it agrees with a weakened generator. Each now runs against a scratch warehouse built to fail it and one built to pass it. Latent defects, none of which bite today: - The inherited key was resolved per source **key** rather than per bridge **row** — exactly the property ADR 0006 spends its decision buying. A reviewer reproduced it by retaining two versions of one order. - Two edges from one entity to the same target, or a self-edge, would emit one key column **twice under one name**, and DuckDB resolves that silently. Both shapes are now refused, and ADR 0006's claim that `rel_name` prevented it is corrected — it separates the pair objects, not the bridge's columns. - M6's checker validated only the **last** mapping declaring a given edge, so an entity loaded from a second source could carry the silent skip the check exists to catch. - The key-shape comparison anonymised **function names** along with column names, so `lpad(x, 5, '0')` and a bare `x` compared as the same shape. - `dar generate` had become a second writer into `checks/` and swept nothing, so renaming a relationship left a check that aborts the whole run before a finding is printed. - A question id names a file and an environment variable and was validated nowhere. The **empty** one is the dangerous case: the page reads an empty selection as "show everything", so that question's committed `answer.png` would have been a picture of every question with nothing looking wrong. - The bridge's column contract claimed "a model change appends; it never rearranges". It does rearrange — keys precede measures, so a new entity moves every measure right. The docstring now says what is true, and why it is tolerable: nothing reads this table by position. Also pinned: that `v_` hands over the **raw** pairs. It is the one object the generated SQL reads and the only engine behaviour the as-of rule rests on that nothing checked. If a release started ranking inside it, the rule would silently revert to the vendor's "as of now" and every check would still pass. ## What this slice still does not prove Both entities on this edge are at the **same grain** — one order has one customer — so no measure *can* multiply across it however the join is written. **D-0001 is still carried on assertion.** The first measure at a finer grain arrives in slice 4, and that is where the fan-out proof becomes possible. ADR 0006 and the deviations register both say so rather than claiming otherwise. ```bash uv run adss build # the whole system from the recording, offline uv run adss check # 20 checks, all green ``` ## Next Slice 3: *how many orders shipped per shipping month, and how many days did they take?* — two events on one entity, a second bridge stage, and a ratio computed at query time from two additive measures. 21 orders in the recording have never shipped, so "an event that did not happen has no row" stops being theoretical. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_019rspwWhmXfxoTvKg5jmNWh --- _Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code/session_019rspwWhmXfxoTvKg5jmNWh)_","state":"open","draft":false,"merged":false,"mergeable_state":"unstable","html_url":"https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/pull/2","user":{"login":"mattiasthalen","id":2592140,"profile_url":"https://github.com/mattiasthalen","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/2592140?v=4"},"head":{"ref":"claude/adss-slice-02-freight-per-customer-country-and-quarter","sha":"9b34378238d212b545e7498ea3883d1e01822e32","repo":{"full_name":"mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07"}},"base":{"ref":"claude/adss-slice-01-orders-per-month-and-ship-country","sha":"28a6065823f4e5dac12b35b6ad752314af7fbb8d","repo":{"full_name":"mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07"}},"additions":2294,"deletions":119,"changed_files":53,"commits":11,"created_at":"2026-09-08T00:32:01Z","updated_at":"2026-09-08T00:32:01Z"}
