A fourth finding decided how the rule is *enforced*: **the model cannot say an edge is many-to-one.** `cardinality:` is rejected outright; `type:` takes any string without validation and is dropped on compile, never reaching the engine. The engine is agnostic by design — it treats a child's parents as a set. So cardinality is inferred from the mapping (M5 already forbids the reaches that would make a target expression multi-valued) and pinned by a data check, because the inference cannot cover one key appearing on several staged rows of a single load. [ADR 0006](https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/blob/9b34378/docs/adr/0006-an-inherited-key-is-resolved-as-of-the-row-that-inherits-it.md) records all of it, and corrects ADR 0002 and ADR 0004 rather than editing them. ## What the generator does now Reads `v___` — the raw pairs — matched on `rel_name` (never `type_key`, which is not stable across models), open pairs only, joined **LEFT** because a childless row has no pair row at all and absence is the only evidence there is, ranked with `row_number()` over `eff_tmstp, ver_tmstp, target key`, **as of the observation time of the row that inherits**, partitioned by that row rather than by its key. Three generated checks assert the mechanism: no source has two targets at one instant, every declared edge loaded at least one pair, and every inherited key names a row in its peripheral. Each is the signature of one of M6's three silent failures. ## The two answers, which must agree ```sql -- straight from the source, bypassing both layers SELECT strftime(o.order_date, '%Y') || '-Q' || cast(quarter(o.order_date) AS VARCHAR) AS order_quarter, c.country AS customer_country, cast(sum(o.freight) AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS freight_orders_amount FROM das__staged.orders__current AS o LEFT JOIN das__staged.customers__current AS c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY order_quarter, customer_country ``` ```sql -- from the generated star schema SELECT cal.quarter_label AS order_quarter, cu.based_in_country AS customer_country, cast(sum(b._measure__order__freight_orders_amount) AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS freight_orders_amount FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key LEFT JOIN dar__uss.customer AS cu ON b.customer_key = cu.customer_key WHERE b._event = 'placed' GROUP BY cal.quarter_label, cu.based_in_country ORDER BY order_quarter, customer_country ``` 153 rows each, identical, totalling all the freight the business paid. ## ⚠️ What agreeing proves here, and what it does not **This is the thing to read before accepting the slice.** The dimension is the customer's country. The obvious wrong implementation is the order's destination country — the value already on the same row, one join cheaper. **In this recording those two columns are equal on every one of the 830 orders.** So an implementation that inherited nothing and read `DESTINATION_COUNTRY` would produce this same answer and the agreement check would pass it. That claim is not mine: an independent lens recomputed it from the raw payloads and got 830 equal, 0 unequal. So the number is checked by the two queries, and the **mechanism** is checked by the three data checks, which hold regardless of whether the two columns coincide. Neither would have been enough alone. It took looking at the data to find that out, and the prioritised list — which asserted "customer country is not destination country" as though it were a fact about the data — has been corrected to say it is a fact about the model. ## Verification Six independent lenses, then every finding attacked by an agent trying to kill it. Fourteen survived at confidence ≥ 7; three were killed. **The test-quality lens refused the slice**, and it was right. Two blocking findings, both the same shape — the slice's central behaviours had tests that could not fail: - **The test named for the no-fan-out property never looked at the window's `PARTITION BY`.** Adding the target key to it makes `row_number()` return 1 for *each* parent, so a child with two parents yields two bridge rows and a doubled measure — the exact failure the bridge exists to prevent — and the suite stayed green. No data check could catch it either: a check is a statement about data, and this warehouse has no tie. Nine previously-green mutations are now red, including a bare `JOIN` where a `LEFT` was meant, `dense_rank` slipping past a word boundary, and the two ranking terms swapped. - **The three generated checks had no tests at all** — the half of ADR 0006's argument the inference cannot make. Nothing else could catch a weakened one: `dar generate --check` compares the committed SQL to the same generator, so it agrees with a weakened generator. Each now runs against a scratch warehouse built to fail it and one built to pass it. Latent defects, none of which bite today: - The inherited key was resolved per source **key** rather than per bridge **row** — exactly the property ADR 0006 spends its decision buying. A reviewer reproduced it by retaining two versions of one order. - Two edges from one entity to the same target, or a self-edge, would emit one key column **twice under one name**, and DuckDB resolves that silently. Both shapes are now refused, and ADR 0006's claim that `rel_name` prevented it is corrected — it separates the pair objects, not the bridge's columns. - M6's checker validated only the **last** mapping declaring a given edge, so an entity loaded from a second source could carry the silent skip the check exists to catch. - The key-shape comparison anonymised **function names** along with column names, so `lpad(x, 5, '0')` and a bare `x` compared as the same shape. - `dar generate` had become a second writer into `checks/` and swept nothing, so renaming a relationship left a check that aborts the whole run before a finding is printed. - A question id names a file and an environment variable and was validated nowhere. The **empty** one is the dangerous case: the page reads an empty selection as "show everything", so that question's committed `answer.png` would have been a picture of every question with nothing looking wrong. - The bridge's column contract claimed "a model change appends; it never rearranges". It does rearrange — keys precede measures, so a new entity moves every measure right. The docstring now says what is true, and why it is tolerable: nothing reads this table by position. Also pinned: that `v_` hands over the **raw** pairs. It is the one object the generated SQL reads and the only engine behaviour the as-of rule rests on that nothing checked. If a release started ranking inside it, the rule would silently revert to the vendor's "as of now" and every check would still pass. ## What this slice still does not prove Both entities on this edge are at the **same grain** — one order has one customer — so no measure *can* multiply across it however the join is written. **D-0001 is still carried on assertion.** The first measure at a finer grain arrives in slice 4, and that is where the fan-out proof becomes possible. ADR 0006 and the deviations register both say so rather than claiming otherwise. ```bash uv run adss build # the whole system from the recording, offline uv run adss check # 20 checks, all green ``` ## Next Slice 3: *how many orders shipped per shipping month, and how many days did they take?* — two events on one entity, a second bridge stage, and a ratio computed at query time from two additive measures. 21 orders in the recording have never shipped, so "an event that did not happen has no row" stops being theoretical. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_019rspwWhmXfxoTvKg5jmNWh --- _Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code/session_019rspwWhmXfxoTvKg5jmNWh)_","state":"open","draft":false,"merged":false,"mergeable_state":"unstable","html_url":"https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/pull/2","user":{"login":"mattiasthalen","id":2592140,"profile_url":"https://github.com/mattiasthalen","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/2592140?v=4"},"head":{"ref":"claude/adss-slice-02-freight-per-customer-country-and-quarter","sha":"9b34378238d212b545e7498ea3883d1e01822e32","repo":{"full_name":"mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07"}},"base":{"ref":"claude/adss-slice-01-orders-per-month-and-ship-country","sha":"28a6065823f4e5dac12b35b6ad752314af7fbb8d","repo":{"full_name":"mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07"}},"additions":2294,"deletions":119,"changed_files":53,"commits":11,"created_at":"2026-09-08T00:32:01Z","updated_at":"2026-09-08T00:32:01Z"}

content.text: That's the real hazard, and it's concrete: DuckDB's float `sum` is order-dependent (`[0.1,0.2,0.3]` → 0.6000000000000001, reversed → 0.6). The acceptance check compares row by row, so any float-valued measure makes it order-dependent. Recording it for the ADR:

input.command:
S=/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-adss-2026-09-07/45a0041f-5559-570b-bd39-1d1517807233/scratchpad
cat > $S/slice-03-float-finding.md <<'MD'
# Measured before the slice-3 ADR: the acceptance check and floating point

`run_checks` compares a question's two answers **row by row as Python values**. That is exact
only while every value is exact.

Measured in this DuckDB (2026-09-08):

| expression | type |
|---|---|
| `datediff('day', a, b)` | BIGINT |
| `sum(datediff(...))` | HUGEINT |
| `HUGEINT / BIGINT` | **DOUBLE** |
| `DECIMAL(28,8) / BIGINT` | **DOUBLE** |

So a ratio is a DOUBLE whichever way it is reached, and the two queries agree today across all
23 shipping months — because both reduce to one IEEE division of two *exact integer* sums, and
IEEE division of identical operands is deterministic.

**The hazard is not the division. It is the sum.** Float addition is not associative, and
DuckDB's `sum` does not impose an order:

    SELECT sum(v) FROM (SELECT unnest([0.1, 0.2, 0.3]::DOUBLE[]) AS v)  -> 0.6000000000000001
    SELECT sum(v) FROM (SELECT unnest([0.3, 0.2, 0.1]::DOUBLE[]) AS v)  -> 0.6

So the moment any measure is a float, the two queries can sum it in different orders and the
check reports a disagreement that is not one — on some machines, some of the time.

Today this cannot happen: every measure is a count (BIGINT) or a sum cast to DECIMAL(28,8),
both exact. That is a property worth *pinning* rather than assuming, and it is an argument for
returning the two additive measures from the question and letting the page divide — then both
answers hold only exact values and the comparison is exact by construction.
MD

Slice 3 is framed and under way. Where things stand:

**PR #2 (slice 2)** — all four checks green, no comments, watched. **PR #1 (slice 1)** — green, clean, watched. Both waiting on you.

**Slice 3** is on `claude/adss-slice-03-shipped-orders-and-days-to-ship`. The data is a good shape for what it's meant to widen: 21 of 830 orders never shipped, so "an event that did not happen has no row" stops being theoretical; lags run 1–37 days with no negatives; 23 shipping months.

The frame workflow is out on the one decision this slice forces — **where a measure derived from two attributes of one row gets computed**. Every measure so far has been a count or a sum of one existing attribute; "days to ship" is the first derived one, and there are three defensible homes for it (a NUMBER attribute in DAB computed in the mapping, an expression in `dab/uss.yaml` that the generator emits, or arithmetic in the question's SQL). Each sets a precedent slice 4 will inherit, since revenue is quantity × price × discount.

While it runs I measured something the ADR will need. The acceptance check compares two answers row by row as Python values, which is exact only while every value is exact. A ratio comes back as a `DOUBLE` whichever path you reach it by — but that isn't the hazard. The hazard is that **float `sum` is not associative and DuckDB imposes no order**: `[0.1, 0.2, 0.3]` sums to 0.6000000000000001, reversed to 0.6. So the first float-valued measure would let the two queries disagree by a bit, on some machines, some of the time. It can't happen today — every measure is a BIGINT count or an exact DECIMAL sum — and that's a property worth pinning rather than assuming. It also argues for returning the two additive measures and letting the page divide, which is what conventions §2 asks for anyway.

<result>{"options":"## What the repository already settles, before the decision is even framed

Three things are not open, and an ADR that re-argues them will look like it did not read the standard.

**The measure's name is already written down.** `docs/conventions.md:119` is a worked example in the §2 table:

> | `avg_days_to_ship` | `ship_lag_orders_days` | The average is `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)` at query time, from two additive measures. |

So conventions §2 already names both measures this slice needs, already says the ratio is computed from two *additive measures*, and already implies `ship_lag_orders_days` is a **stored measure** — a name in the `_measure__<entity>__<measure>` column contract of `docs/conventions.md:76`. That sentence is the single most load-bearing quotation for this decision, and it points away from option (c).

**The event that did not happen is already decided.** ADR 0002:70-71 — "A transaction stage reads `dab.view_<E>_hist`, keeps the latest version in which the event's date is set, and dates the row by that attribute. An unshipped order therefore has no shipment event *by construction* rather than by a filter somebody has to remember." `src/adss/uss.py:217` emits `WHERE {held}.{date} IS NOT NULL`, and `tests/test_uss.py:100-104` pins it. The 21 orders are not a new problem; they are the case that design was written for. The slice should say so and move on.

**Two events on one entity already work.** `tests/fixtures/dab/uss.yaml:3-24` declares `HAPPENED` and `FINISHED` both on `PARENT`, and `tests/test_uss.py:158` asserts "three declared events are three branches". I generated the slice-3 bridge from a scratch copy of the model and sidecar (in `/tmp`, nothing written to the repository) and it emits cleanly with **zero generator changes**: `shipped__version`, `shipped__order_is_placed_by_customer`, `shipped`, and a second union branch. `ADR 0002:95` even names the value in advance — "`_event` | VARCHAR | no | the event, lower-cased: `placed`, `shipped`, `observed`".

What is genuinely new is only this: `_measure__order__ship_lag_orders_days` has no attribute to point at.

---

## The decision, stated in the repository's terms

`src/adss/uss.py:104-108` refuses a sum with nothing to sum:

```python
if aggregate is Aggregate.SUM and not attribute_id:
    raise UssError(
        f"{path}: measure {raw['id']} declares aggregate: sum and names nothing "
        f"to sum. A blank attribute would emit a column named after nothing."
    )
```

and `src/adss/uss.py:186-191` refuses to sum something that is not a `NUMBER`. `_version_cte` has exactly two shapes for a measure value (`src/adss/uss.py:206-210`): `cast(1 AS BIGINT)` for a count, `cast(revision."X" AS DECIMAL(28,8))` for a sum. A lag is neither. So the question is: **where does the subtraction live** — in DAB as a modelled attribute, in the generator, or in the question.

---

## Option (a) — a `NUMBER` attribute on `ORDER`, computed in the mapping

### What changes, file by file

`dab/model.yaml`, appended to `ORDER.attributes` (B7: appended, never inserted):

```yaml
        - id: SHIPPED_ON
          name: SHIPPED_ON
          definition: The day the goods left the business on their way to the destination.
          description: >-
            An order ships once, or not yet. A missing day means the business has not
            recorded the goods as gone -- which is not a promise that they never will be,
            and is not the same as shipping on an unknown day.
          type: START_TIMESTAMP

        - id: SHIP_LAG_DAYS
          name: SHIP_LAG_DAYS
          definition: >-
            The number of whole days the business took to get an order out: from the day it
            accepted the order to the day the goods left.
          description: >-
            Zero on an order that went out the day it was accepted. There is no value at all
            until it goes out, which is not zero and must not be read as a fast order.
          type: NUMBER
          effective_timestamp: true
```

A note on `START_TIMESTAMP`: the dab skill (`.claude/skills/dab/SKILL.md:48-49`) says "There is no plain date type; a business date is `START_TIMESTAMP`." The fixture uses `END_TIMESTAMP` for a second event date (`tests/fixtures/dab/model.yaml:16`) and `Attribute.is_date` (`src/adss/model.py:44-45`) accepts both, so either compiles. `END_TIMESTAMP` would assert that shipping ends the order's life, which `dab/model.yaml:23-24` denies — "settled by delivering what was promised". Use `START_TIMESTAMP` and say why in one line.

## Option (b) — an expression in `dab/uss.yaml`, emitted by the generator

### What changes

Two sub-shapes, and they are not equally defensible.

**(b1) free SQL in YAML:**

```yaml
        - id: SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS
          definition: ...
          aggregate: sum
          expression: date_diff('day', PLACED_ON, SHIPPED_ON)
```

**(b2) a closed, typed form the generator composes:**

```yaml
        - id: SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS
          definition: ...
          aggregate: sum
          days_between: {from: PLACED_ON, to: SHIPPED_ON}
```

`src/adss/uss.py` changes either way:

```python
DAYS_TYPE = "BIGINT"          # date_diff('day', …) is BIGINT in duckdb; measured

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Measure:
    id: str
    definition: str
    aggregate: Aggregate
    attribute_id: str | None
    between: tuple[str, str] | None      # new

    @property
    def sql_type(self) -> str:
        if self.aggregate is Aggregate.COUNT:
            return COUNT_TYPE
        return DAYS_TYPE if self.between else SUM_TYPE
```

`read_uss` must stop refusing a sum that names no attribute (`src/adss/uss.py:104-108`) and instead refuse a sum that names *neither* an attribute nor a pair, and refuse one that names both. `_refuse_measures_of_things_that_are_not_numbers` (`src/adss/uss.py:186-191`) becomes vacuous for this measure — `attribute_id` is `None`, so the guard passes without looking at anything — and must be replaced with "both named attributes are dates, and both belong to this event's entity". `_version_cte` (`src/adss/uss.py:204-211`) grows a third branch:

```python
            elif measure.between is not None:
                start, end = (crossing(a) for a in measure.between)
                value = f"cast(date_diff('day', {held}.{start}, {held}.{end}) AS {DAYS_TYPE})"
```

Roughly ten lines of emitter, two refusals, and their tests. Not large.

### What it satisfies and what it strains

**It does *not* break "model.yaml is the only place the data is explained", and an ADR that claims it does will be wrong.** `docs/conventions.md:58` is explicit: "`dab/uss.yaml` is governed by §1.3 and §2, not by this section. | It lives beside the model but it declares DAR things. One directory, two regimes; this sentence is the arbiter." And uss.yaml already carries definitions the glossary copies (`dab/uss.yaml:1-6`, `src/adss/uss.py:456-458`), and `check_question` already resolves a question's `defines` against "something `dab/model.yaml` **or `dab/uss.yaml`** defines" (ADR 0005:62). So an *explanation* in uss.yaml is sanctioned. What is not yet sanctioned is a *derivation* there — and the distinction the ADR should draw is that a definition is a sentence a person checks and an expression is a computation only a machine checks.

**§3 is the hard rule it actually breaks.** `docs/conventions.md:137`: "SQL that lives in a Python string is written to a file so the same linter sees it. | A rule that applies only to the SQL somebody remembered to put in a `.sql` file is not a rule." The sqlfluff hook is `types: [sql]` (`.pre-commit-config.yaml:32`), so a SQL fragment in `dab/uss.yaml` is seen by `yamllint` and by nothing else. (b1) is a straight §3 violation and needs a deviation entry. (b2) avoids it entirely — the SQL is composed inside the generator, and `tests/test_generated_sql_lints.py` already runs the real linter over `bridge_sql`'s whole output, so the fragment is linted the moment it is emitted.

**§5 survives.** `docs/conventions.md:163` forbids data vocabulary under `src/`; `days_between` and `date_diff` are machinery and SQL, not business words. And a discriminated union of measure kinds is exactly what ADR 0001:66-71 says the typed domain is for.

**F2 survives too.** DAR reading two DAB attributes and subtracting them is specialisation for a requirement, which is R1 (`docs/blueprint.md:87`). This option is *not* a layering violation, and pretending it is would be a weak argument.

The real strain is different and it is about growth: **a second expression language that can only get bigger.** (b2)'s closed form covers "days between two dates" and nothing else. Slice 4 needs `quantity × price × (1 - discount)` — three attributes, a multiplication and a subtraction. (b2) then either grows a second closed form for that shape, or opens the door to (b1) and its §3 problem. Whichever happens, slice 4 pays for it.

### What it costs the planned slices

- **Slice 4 — worse than both alternatives.** The generator's expression vocabulary has to grow from a two-date special case to general arithmetic, in the slice where D-0001's whole fan-out argument is finally being exercised for the first time (`docs/deviations.md:46-50`: "The first measure at a finer grain arrives in slice 4, and that is where the argument stops being carried on assertion"). Growing the emitter and first exercising the fan-out property in the same slice is two risky things at once.
- **Slice 5 — neutral.**
- **Slice 6 — this is where (b) is exposed as a detour.** A second source that reports *elapsed days* directly has no two date attributes for a DAR-side expression to subtract. The only way to integrate it is a `NUMBER` attribute on `ORDER` — option (a). So slice 6 adds the attribute anyway, and then there are two definitions of ship lag: a DAB attribute and a DAR expression, differing per source. That is B2 (`docs/blueprint.md:75`) and B8 (`docs/blueprint.md:81`, "Definitions that exist in two places drift, and the drift surfaces as two reports that disagree") failing together, in the slice whose whole purpose is to prove B2.

### The six-month failure mode

A reader wants "orders that took more than 30 days". The lag exists only as a bridge measure with a typed null on every non-shipped branch; there is no `ship_lag_days` column on `dar__uss."order"` to filter. So they recompute it in the question from the peripheral's two dates — option (c) arriving through the back door, and now the same number has two derivations that no arbiter compares.

---

## Option (c) — computed in the question's `uss.sql`

### What changes

`dab/model.yaml` gains `SHIPPED_ON` only. `dab/mappings/order-mapping.yaml` gains one line. `dab/uss.yaml` gains the `SHIPPED` event with `SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT` alone. No generator change. `docs/questions/03-.../uss.sql`:

```sql

    cal.month_label AS shipping_month,
    cast(sum(b._measure__order__shipped_orders_count) AS BIGINT) AS shipped_orders_count,
    cast(
        sum(date_diff('day', o.placed_on, o.shipped_on))
        / sum(b._measure__order__shipped_orders_count) AS DECIMAL(18, 2)
    ) AS ship_lag_days_per_order
FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key

WHERE b._event = 'shipped'
GROUP BY cal.month_label
ORDER BY shipping_month
```

**"The destination reads `dar__uss` only" is untouched.** I traced `check_question` (`src/adss/question.py:127-137`): the answer query mentions `dar__uss`, mentions none of `das__`, `dab.`, `dab__`, `read_parquet`, has an `ORDER BY`, and mentions `month_label`. It passes every mechanical check. F1 holds. That part of the worry is unfounded, and the ADR should say so plainly rather than gesture at it.

**Three things break, and one of them is fatal.**

*It is not a "ratio in a question" — it is a numerator with no definition.* `docs/conventions.md:111` says "**Ratios are not stored.** Store numerator and denominator as additive measures and divide at query time." Option (c) reads that as licence for the whole computation. It is not: the rule forbids storing the *ratio* and explicitly instructs that the *numerator* be an additive measure. `docs/conventions.md:119` names it: `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)`. Option (c) has no `ship_lag_orders_days`.

*The question cannot declare what it measures.* `docs/conventions.md:237`: "A question **references** definitions; it never restates them. Every reference must resolve to something `dab/model.yaml` or `dab/uss.yaml` defines, and the machinery proves it." It does prove it — `src/adss/question.py:109-111` raises on any `defines` entry nothing defines. Under (c) there is no `ORDER.measures.SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS` and no `ORDER.SHIP_LAG_DAYS` to list, so "how many days did they take" is a concept that exists in one SQL file and nowhere else — with the glossary on the rendered page (`destinations/app.py:115-120`) silently unable to explain the second number the page shows. `docs/conventions.md:238` says what to do with that: "A question that needs a term the model does not define is **blocked**, and the model change comes first."

*The acceptance check loses its arbiter — this is the fatal one.* `docs/conventions.md:190`: "**When a question's two queries disagree, `dab/model.yaml` is the arbiter.** The query that departs from the definition is the one that changes. Never adjust bot

content.content:
## Option (d) — what I would actually argue for

**(a), with two additions, and it is not a compromise between the others.**

**(d1) Bound the precedent in the ADR itself.** ADR 0003:70-75 drew a line for casts and named what crossed it. Slice 3 should draw the same line for arithmetic, in the record, so the next slice inherits a rule instead of an example: *arithmetic over columns of the same row is permitted in a mapping; a `CASE` on values, a default, a filter, a bucket or anything that changes the grain is not.* Without that sentence, "M5 permits it" becomes the standing argument for anything M5's regex happens not to catch — and M5's regex is four keywords and seven function names (`src/adss/mapping.py:21-22`).

**(d2) Pin the derivation with a generated check.** `docs/adr/0006:114-115`: "the check is not optional decoration on top of the inference — it is the half of the argument the inference cannot make." The same applies here. A check that counts orders where `SHIP_LAG_DAYS` disagrees with the two dates, or is negative, is tautological today and stops being tautological the moment a second mapping table or a second source exists — which is slice 6, and it is exactly the failure mode (a) has.

There is a cost line the ADR must carry: **it cannot be a hand-written file.** `src/adss/cli.py:284-300` sweeps `checks/` of anything neither a contract nor `relationship_checks(model)` generates, and `--check` reports it as "belongs to nothing declared". So the check has to be emitted by code — a new function beside `relationship_checks` in `src/adss/checks.py`, and a corresponding entry in `relationship_check_names`-style bookkeeping so the DAS side leaves it alone. That is real machinery for a check that passes trivially today, and if the slice does not want to pay it, the honest move is to say so in Consequences and record the unpinned risk, not to write the check by hand.

**Why (d) and not (b2), which is the serious rival.** (b2) is cleaner in one respect — nothing derived is stored, so nothing derived can drift. But it buys that by putting the business's arithmetic in the layer whose job is to be thrown away and rebuilt (`docs/blueprint.md:90`, R4), and it fails at the exact slice where the architecture's central claim gets tested: a second source that reports the lag directly has nothing for a DAR expression to subtract. (a) puts the arithmetic in the one artefact whose declared job is binding two vocabularies (`docs/conventions.md:57`), which is where a per-source difference belongs.

---

## The second decision this slice forces

**Yes, there is one, and it is not the one the brief guesses at.**

A measure's *column* and its *glossary token* are keyed on the **entity**; its *ownership* is keyed on the **event**. Slice 3 is the first slice where one entity has two events, so those two keys stop being the same thing.

`src/adss/uss.py:81`:
```python
(event, measure, f"_measure__{event.entity_id.lower()}__{measure.id.lower()}")
```
`src/adss/uss.py:458`:
```python
found[f"{event.entity_id}.measures.{measure.id}"] = measure.definition
```

Both key on `event.entity_id`. Meanwhile `_branch` resolves ownership correctly, by object identity on the event (`src/adss/uss.py:316`, `if candidate is event`). So the generator knows which stage owns a measure and names it after something else.

**I demonstrated the consequence.** Declaring `ORDERS_COUNT` on both a `PLACED` and a `SHIPPED` event of `ORDER` — which `read_uss` accepts without a word — produces:

```
CONTRACT: (…, '_measure__order__orders_count', '_measure__order__orders_count')
DEFINITIONS: {'ORDER.measures.ORDERS_COUNT': 'B.'}
```

The column appears twice, and the first measure's definition is silently replaced by the second's. And DuckDB, measured: `CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT 1 AS a, 2 AS a` yields columns `a` and `a_1` — it resolves the ambiguity instead of raising. That is word for word the behaviour `_refuse_edges_that_would_collide` was written for (`src/adss/uss.py:141-149`): "DuckDB resolves that ambiguity instead of raising, so one of the two inherited keys vanishes with nothing to say which."

The column half would be caught loudly at build time by `src/adss/checks.py:52-60` (`described == expected` fails on `_1`). **The glossary half is caught by nothing.** No check inspects `definitions()`; and that dictionary is what `check_question` resolves a question's `defines` against (`src/adss/question.py:109-111`) and what the page renders as "What the words mean" (`destinations/app.py:115-120`). A question could reference a measure and be shown the wrong definition of it, and every test and every check would pass.

Nothing enforces the naming convention that prevents this. `docs/conventions.md:107` makes the three-part pattern a Hard rule, and I grepped: there is no test anywhere in `tests/` or `src/` that checks a measure name's shape. The uniqueness of the bridge's measure columns rests entirely on a review-only rule.

### The options

1. **Refuse the collision in `read_uss`, keep the entity in the name.** A refusal shaped exactly like `_refuse_edges_that_would_collide`, plus a test and a message that says what would be lost. Cheap; no contract change; consistent with the repository's established move.
2. **Rename to `_measure__<event>__<measure>`, token `ORDER.SHIPPED.measures.X`.** Correct in principle — it names the thing that actually owns the measure. It changes a published contract that `docs/conventions.md:76` states as a Hard rule and ADR 0002:100 tabulates, and it changes both existing questions' SQL. It is also the cheapest it will ever be, with two consumers. Against it: §2's descriptor slot already carries the event (`placed_orders_count` vs `shipped_orders_count`), so the event would appear twice in most column names.
3. **Do nothing** and rely on §2's pattern. Leaves a Hard rule enforced by reading alone, protecting a silent glossary overwrite.

The precedent argues for **1**, and ADR 0006:179-184 supplies the w

# A value derived from one row is modelled in DAB and computed in the mapping, and arithmetic there is bounded by this record

## Context and Problem Statement

"How many days did they take" is the first number this system reports that does not exist in the
source. Every measure so far has been a count — one per row — or a sum of a single attribute that
was already there. A ship lag is two dates subtracted, and there is no established place to put
the subtraction.

Three things are already settled and an argument that reopens them has not read the standard.

**The measure's name and its arithmetic are written down.** Conventions §2's own worked example is
this question:

> | `avg_days_to_ship` | `ship_lag_orders_days` | The average is
> `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)` at query time, from two additive
> measures. |

So the two measures are named, the division is a question's job, and `ship_lag_orders_days` is a
*stored measure* — a column in the bridge's published contract. That sentence decides more of this
slice than anything else in the repository.

**An event that did not happen is already decided.** ADR 0002: "A transaction stage reads
`dab.view_<E>_hist`, keeps the latest version in which the event's date is set… An unshipped order
therefore has no shipment event *by construction* rather than by a filter somebody has to
remember." The generator emits `WHERE <date> IS NOT NULL` and a test pins it. The 21 unshipped
orders are the case that design was written for, not a new problem.

**Two events on one entity already work.** The neutral fixture has declared two events on one
entity since slice 1, and generating this slice's bridge from a scratch copy of the model needs
**no generator change at all**. What is new is one thing only: a sum measure with no attribute to
point at.

## Decision Drivers

* a number the business reads has exactly one definition, in the one place data is explained
* the acceptance check keeps an arbiter: when two queries disagree, something decides which is wrong
* the precedent this sets is one the next three slices can live with
* a rule the next person inherits, rather than an example they have to interpret
* DAR stays a layer that can be deleted and rebuilt from the model

## Considered Options

* **(a)** A `NUMBER` attribute on `ORDER`, computed in the mapping from two columns of its own row
* **(b)** An expression in `dab/uss.yaml`, emitted into the bridge by the generator
* **(c)** Computed in the question's `uss.sql` at query time from two dates on the peripheral

## Decision Outcome

Chosen: **(a), a `NUMBER` attribute computed in the mapping** — with the precedent bounded here,
because "M5 permits it" is otherwise the standing argument for whatever M5's regex happens not to
catch.

It is also the only option that generates today. A `sum` measure must name an attribute the model
declares; `src/adss/uss.py` raises `KeyError: "ORDER has no attribute …"` otherwise, and there is
no `expression:` field on a measure. (b) and (c) are not choices between working designs — they
are proposals to build something.

**Why not (b).** Putting the arithmetic in the generator is the serious rival, and it is cleaner in
one respect: nothing derived is stored, so nothing derived can drift. It fails on where it leaves
slice 6. A second source that reports elapsed days *directly* has no two dates for a DAR expression
to subtract, so integrating it needs the attribute anyway — and then there are two definitions of
ship lag, a DAB attribute and a DAR expression, differing by source. That is B2 and B8 failing
together in the slice whose entire purpose is to prove B2. It also costs slice 4, where the
expression vocabulary would have to grow from a two-date special case to general arithmetic in the
same slice that first exercises the fan-out property D-0001 is carried on. Two risky things at once.

A free-text SQL expression in YAML additionally breaks §3 — "SQL that lives in a Python string is
written to a file so the same linter sees it" — because the linter runs on `.sql` files and would
never see it.

**Why not (c).** Conventions §2 says ratios are not stored and the numerator *is* an additive
measure; (c) reads it as licence for the whole computation and has no `ship_lag_orders_days` at
all. The question could then not declare what it measures: every `defines` entry must resolve to
something the model or the sidecar defines, so "days to ship" would exist in one SQL file and
nowhere else, with the page's own glossary unable to explain the second number it displays.

The fatal objection is narrower. §6: "When a question's two queries disagree, `dab/model.yaml` is
the arbiter. The query that departs from the definition is the one that changes." Under (c) the
answer query says `date_diff('day', o.placed_on, o.shipped_on)`, the control says
`shipped_date - order_date`, and the model has nothing to say about either. Neither query can
depart from a definition that does not exist, so the repair procedure stops existing in exactly the
slice that introduces the first computed number — and the cheapest repair becomes making the two
queries agree with each other, which deletes the only thing the check measures.

(c) also computes as of the wrong instant: the peripheral is current state, while a bridge row is
the latest version *in which the event's date is set*. Those coincide today. ADR 0006 records a
review catching precisely this confusion one layer down, and calls the distinction the entire
difference between the option chosen there and the one rejected.

### The line this record draws

M5 permits an expression that reads its own row, and its prose enumerates three forms — a column,
a cast, a `CASE` over columns of that row. A subtraction of two dates is none of them, and passes
only because M5's mechanical check is four keywords and seven function names. Relying on that
silently is the quiet exception §11 rules out. So the rule, in force from here:

> **Arithmetic over columns of the same row is permitted in a mapping.** A `CASE` on *values*, a
> default, a coalesce that invents a value, a filter, a bucket, or anything that changes the grain
> is not — those are meaning, and meaning belongs in the model as an attribute with a definition.

Conventions §1.4 M5 is clarified to say so, per §11's first rung. The distinction is that
arithmetic over one row produces a value the row already implies; the others produce a value
somebody chose, and a choice needs a definition beside it.

One trap belongs in the record because the error message misleads: `extract(DAY FROM (b - a))` is
**refused** by M5's checker, because the regex matches the bare word `from` inside the expression.
The refusal says the expression "reaches beyond its row", which it does not. `date_diff('day', a,
b)` passes and is what the mapping uses. The false refusal is a defect in the checker, fixed in
this slice.

## Consequences

* Good, because the lag has one definition, in the one place the data is explained, and both of the
  question's queries are measured against it
* Good, because a second source that reports the lag directly maps onto the same attribute rather
  than needing a second derivation — which is the slice-6 case that decided this
* Good, because slice 4's revenue follows the same rule without a new mechanism: quantity, price
  and discount are columns of one order line, and their product is arithmetic over that row
* Good, because DAR stays deletable: everything it emits still comes from the model and the sidecar
* Bad, because a derived value is now stored, and a stored derivation can disagree with what it was
  derived from. Nothing today can make that happen — one mapping, one source — and it becomes
  possible in slice 6
* Bad, because the line above is a rule enforced by review. M5's checker cannot tell arithmetic
  from a bucket, and writing a checker that could is a bigger thing than this slice needs

## Confirmation

`tests/test_mapping_rules.py` asserts that a same-row function is accepted and that the reaching
forms are still refused, including the `extract(… FROM …)` case that used to be refused for the
wrong reason.

The two measures are `SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT` and `SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS`, and the ratio appears in no
schema: the question returns both additive measures and the page divides them. That is not only
§2's rule but what keeps the acceptance check exact — every value either query returns is a
`BIGINT` count or an exact `DECIMAL` sum, and the two answers are compared row by row as values.
A float would break that comparison in a way no test would find on the machine that wrote it:
DuckDB's `sum` over doubles is order-dependent, measured here as `[0.1, 0.2, 0.3]` summing to
`0.6000000000000001` and the same three reversed to `0.6`. `tests/test_questions.py` pins that
every question's answer holds only exact types, so the first float-valued measure fails a test
rather than producing a disagreement that is not one.

What is **not** confirmed, and is recorded rather than claimed: nothing checks that
`SHIP_LAG_DAYS` still equals the two dates it was derived from. Such a check is tautological
today — one mapping computes it from those columns and nothing else writes it — and stops being
tautological in slice 6, which is the slice this decision's one real risk lands in. It is not
written now because a check that cannot fail teaches a reader that the property is guarded when it
is not; slice 6 writes it, against the case that makes it meaningful.

docs(adr): decide where a number the source does not contain gets computed

"How many days did they take" is the first value this system reports that does not exist in
the source, and there was no established place to put the subtraction. Two of the three
candidate homes turn out not to exist: a sum measure must name an attribute the model declares,
and there is no expression field on a measure, so the generator raises KeyError on anything
else. They were proposals to build something, not choices between working designs.

Between the three, what decided it was where each one leaves slice 6. Putting the arithmetic in
the generator is cleaner in one respect -- nothing derived is stored, so nothing derived can
drift -- but a second source that reports elapsed days directly has no two dates to subtract,
so integration needs the attribute anyway, and then one number has two definitions that differ
by source. That is the pair of principles slice 6 exists to prove, failing together.

Computing it in the question fails on something narrower and worse. When two queries disagree
the model is the arbiter and the departing query is the one that changes; if the arithmetic
lives only in the queries, neither can depart from a definition that does not exist. The repair
procedure stops existing in the slice that introduces the first computed number, and the
cheapest repair becomes making the two queries agree with each other, which deletes the only
thing the check measures.

The precedent is bounded in the record rather than left as an example, because "M5 permits it"
would otherwise become the standing argument for whatever M5's regex happens not to catch --
and that regex is four keywords and seven function names. Arithmetic over one row is permitted;
a CASE on values, a default, a filter or a bucket is not, because each of those is a choice and
a choice needs a definition beside it. Conventions M5 is clarified to say so, which is section
11's first rung rather than a quiet exception.

Also recorded: the natural DuckDB idiom for this, extract(DAY FROM b - a), is refused by the M5
checker because the regex matches the bare word `from` inside the expression -- and the refusal
tells you the expression reaches beyond its row, which it does not.

# A measure is owned by an event and named for an entity, so two events on one entity may not name the same measure

## Context and Problem Statement

Slice 3 is the first slice where one entity has two events: an order is both placed and shipped.
That splits two things which have been the same thing until now.

A measure's **column** and its **glossary token** are keyed on the entity:

```python
(event, measure, f"_measure__{event.entity_id.lower()}__{measure.id.lower()}")
found[f"{event.entity_id}.measures.{measure.id}"] = measure.definition
```

Its **ownership** is keyed on the event — `_branch` decides which stage carries a value and which
emits a typed null by identity on the event object. So the generator knows exactly which stage owns
a measure, and then names it after something else.

With one event per entity those keys coincide and nothing can go wrong. With two, declaring the
same measure id on both events of one entity is accepted without a word, and produces:

- **the same column twice** in the published contract, and
- **one definition silently replacing the other** in the glossary.

Reproduced on the neutral fixture. The column list came back with
`_measure__parent__happened_parents_count` at two positions, and the glossary held the *second*
event's definition under the first event's token.

The two halves fail very differently. DuckDB does not refuse two columns of one name — measured,
`CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT 1 AS a, 2 AS a` yields `a` and `a_1` — so the built table's columns would
not match `bridge_columns()` and the contract check would fail the build loudly. That half is safe.

**The glossary half is caught by nothing.** No check inspects `definitions()`. That dictionary is
what a question's `defines` entries are resolved against, and what the page renders as "What the
words mean". So a question could reference a measure, resolve it successfully, and be shown a
definition belonging to a different measure — on the page a reader accepts the slice on — while
every test and every check passes.

Nothing enforces the naming convention that would prevent it either. Conventions §2's three-part
pattern is a hard rule, and there is no test anywhere that checks a measure name's shape. The
uniqueness of these columns has rested entirely on a rule enforced by reading.

## Decision Drivers

* a definition that is silently replaced is worse than one that is missing: nothing looks wrong
* the failure must be loud where it is invisible, not only where DuckDB happens to complain
* a published column contract two consumers are already written against
* whatever is decided now is cheapest now, with two questions in existence

## Considered Options

* Refuse the collision when the declarations are read, and keep the entity in the column name
* Rename the column to `_measure__<event>__<measure>` and the token to `<ENTITY>.<EVENT>.measures.<M>`
* Do nothing, and rely on §2's naming pattern to keep ids distinct

## Decision Outcome

Chosen: **refuse the collision when the declarations are read.**

Two events on one entity may not declare the same measure id. The refusal names both events and
says what would be lost, because the loss is not obvious: a reader who has just been told the
column would be duplicated will think of the column, and the definition is the part nothing else
would catch.

**Why not rename to the event.** It is more correct in principle — the event is what actually owns
a measure, so the name should say so — and it is the cheapest it will ever be, with only two
questions to update. It is rejected on two counts. It changes a published contract that conventions
§1.3 states as a hard rule and ADR 0002 tabulates, in a slice that has no other reason to touch it.
And §2's descriptor slot already carries the event: `placed_orders_count`, `shipped_orders_count`.
Naming the column for the event too would put it in twice, so the more correct scheme reads worse
in every ordinary case in order to disambiguate one that is now refused outright.

**Why not do nothing.** §2's pattern makes a collision unlikely, not impossible, and "unlikely" is
the wrong guarantee for a failure whose signature is a page showing a plausible sentence about the
wrong number. Two events on one entity is exactly where the pattern's descriptor slot stops doing
the work — `placed` and `shipped` distinguish the count measures, and nothing forces a third
measure to carry a descriptor at all.

This follows the shape the repository already uses for the same class of problem: ADR 0006 refuses
two edges that would inherit into one key column, for the same reason and with the same argument
about what DuckDB silently does instead of raising. A generator that cannot emit a correct artefact
should say so rather than emit an ambiguous one.

## Consequences

* Good, because the glossary can no longer show one measure's definition under another's name,
  which was the only failure here that nothing would have reported
* Good, because it is a refusal in the same place and the same shape as the one for colliding
  edges, so the two read as one rule rather than two special cases
* Good, because it costs nothing today: no existing declaration collides, and no column moves
* Bad, because it forbids a legitimate-sounding declaration — the same quantity measured at two
  events, deliberately, under one name. That would have to be two measures with two definitions,
  which is more honest but more typing. If a slice ever wants it, the answer is to rename to the
  event, and this record is what it supersedes
* Bad, because the deeper mismatch stays: the generator still names by entity what it owns by
  event. This narrows the consequence to nothing rather than removing the cause

## Confirmation

`tests/test_uss.py` asserts that two events on one entity declaring one measure id are refused,
and that the same id on two *different* entities is still accepted — which is the case the
refusal must not catch, since `_measure__<entity>__` already distinguishes those.

A second test asserts that `definitions()` returns one entry per declared measure, so a future
change that reintroduces a silent overwrite fails on the count rather than on somebody reading a
page carefully. That is the assertion that would have caught this, and it did not exist.

def test_two_events_on_one_entity_may_not_name_the_same_measure():
    """A measure is owned by an event and named for an entity. With one event each those are
    the same thing; with two they are not, and the same id on both silently replaces one
    definition with the other in the glossary. ADR 0008.
    """
    model, _ = plan()
    collided = FIXTURES / "bad_two_events_one_measure.yaml"
    with pytest.raises(UssError, match="would replace"):
        read_uss(collided, model)


def test_the_same_measure_id_on_two_different_entities_is_still_accepted():
    """The column already carries the entity, so those two do not collide. A refusal that
    caught them would forbid the ordinary case to prevent the rare one.
    """
    model, uss = plan()
    columns = [c for _, _, c in uss.measure_columns()]
    assert len(columns) == len(set(columns))


def test_every_declared_measure_keeps_its_own_definition():
    """The assertion that would have caught the overwrite, and did not exist.

    A glossary entry silently replaced by another measure's definition is the failure nothing
    else reports: the page renders a plausible sentence about the wrong number, and every test
    and every check passes.
    """
    model, uss = plan()
    declared = [(e.entity_id, m.id, m.definition) for e in uss.events for m in e.measures]
    carried = definitions(model, uss)
    assert len({(entity, measure) for entity, measure, _ in declared}) == len(declared)
    for entity, measure, definition in declared:
        assert carried[f"{entity}.measures.{measure}"] == definition

from pathlib import Path
p = Path("src/adss/mapping.py")
t = p.read_text()

old = '''# An attribute expression may read its own row: a column, a cast of one, or a CASE over
# them. Anything else is a join, and every join must come from a declared relationship.
_REACHING = re.compile(r"\\b(select|join|from|over|group\\s+by)\\b", re.IGNORECASE)
_AGGREGATE = re.compile(r"\\b(sum|count|min|max|avg|any_value|array_agg)\\s*\\(", re.IGNORECASE)'''
new = '''# An attribute expression may read its own row: a column, a cast of one, a CASE over them, or
# arithmetic over them. Anything else is a join, and every join must come from a declared
# relationship. M5, and ADR 0007 for where the line between arithmetic and meaning is drawn.
_REACHING = re.compile(r"\\b(select|join|from|over|group\\s+by)\\b", re.IGNORECASE)
_AGGREGATE = re.compile(r"\\b(sum|count|min|max|avg|any_value|array_agg)\\s*\\(", re.IGNORECASE)

# Standard SQL spells several same-row functions with FROM as part of their syntax, and their
# FROM introduces nothing. Matching it made the checker refuse `extract(DAY FROM b - a)` -- the
# natural idiom for the very thing M5 permits -- and tell the reader it reached beyond its row.
# A refusal whose stated reason is wrong sends someone looking for a problem that is not there.
_KEYWORD_FROM = re.compile(r"\\b(extract|substring|trim|overlay|position)\\s*\\(", re.IGNORECASE)'''
assert old in t

    Arithmetic and same-row functions do not, however they are spelled; a subquery, a join, a
    window or an aggregate does.
    """
    return bool(_REACHING.search(_without_keyword_from(expression)) or _AGGREGATE.search(expression))


def _without_keyword_from(expression: str) -> str:
    """The expression with the arguments of FROM-taking functions removed.

    Only their arguments: everything around them still has to answer for itself, so
    `extract(DAY FROM a) + (SELECT 1 FROM t)` is still refused, for the half that deserves it.
    """
    out, index = [], 0
    while index < len(expression):
        found = _KEYWORD_FROM.search(expression, index)
        if not found:
            out.append(expression[index:])

        out.append(expression[index : found.end()])

        while cursor < len(expression) and depth:
            depth += (expression[cursor] == "(") - (expression[cursor] == ")")
            cursor += 1
        out.append(")" if depth == 0 else "")

input.command:
git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG' && git log --oneline -2
docs(adr): refuse two events on one entity sharing a measure id, and stop refusing arithmetic

Two decisions, and both only exist because an entity now has two events.

A measure is owned by an event and named for an entity. While each entity had one event those
were the same thing. With two they are not: the same measure id on both emits one column twice
AND replaces one definition with the other in the glossary. I reproduced both on the neutral
fixture -- the contract came back with one column at two positions, and the glossary held the
second event's sentence under the first event's token.

The two halves fail very differently, which is what decided the shape of the fix. DuckDB does
not refuse two columns of one name; measured, it renames the second to a_1. So the built table
stops matching the published contract and the build fails loudly. That half is safe. The
glossary half is caught by nothing: no check inspects the definitions, and they are what a
question's references resolve against and what the page renders as what the words mean. A
reader would be shown a plausible sentence about the wrong number with everything green.

So it is refused where the declarations are read, in the same place and the same shape as the
refusal for two edges inheriting into one key column -- the two now read as one rule rather
than two special cases. Renaming the column to the event would be more correct in principle
and was rejected: it changes a published contract in a slice with no other reason to touch it,
and section 2's descriptor slot already carries the event, so the event would appear twice in
every ordinary column name to disambiguate a case that is now refused outright.

The second is a refusal that should never have fired. M5's checker matched the bare word FROM,
so extract(DAY FROM b - a) -- the natural idiom for exactly the same-row arithmetic ADR 0007
just permitted -- was rejected with a message saying it reached beyond its row, which it does
not. A refusal whose stated reason is wrong is worse than none: it sends someone looking for a
problem that is not there. The predicate now strips the arguments of the functions that spell
FROM as syntax, and only their arguments, so extract(DAY FROM a) + (SELECT 1 FROM t) is still
refused for the half that deserves it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_019rspwWhmXfxoTvKg5jmNWh
MSG

from pathlib import Path
p = Path("dab/model.yaml")
t = p.read_text()
old = '''        - id: FREIGHT_CHARGE'''
new = '''        - id: SHIPPED_ON
          name: SHIPPED_ON
          definition: The day the goods left the business on their way to the destination.
          description: >-
            An order ships once, or not yet. No day at all means the business has not recorded
            the goods as gone -- which is not a promise that they never will be, and is not the
            same as shipping on a day nobody wrote down. A question about when goods moved
            means this; a question about when demand arrived means PLACED_ON.
          type: START_TIMESTAMP

        - id: SHIP_LAG_DAYS
          name: SHIP_LAG_DAYS
          definition: >-
            The number of whole days the business took to get an order out: from the day it
            accepted the order to the day the goods left.
          description: >-
            Zero on an order that went out the same day it was accepted. There is no value at
            all until it goes out, and that absence is not a zero -- reading it as one would
            make the slowest orders look like the fastest.
          type: NUMBER
          effective_timestamp: true

        - id: FREIGHT_CHARGE'''
assert old in t
p.write_text(t.replace(old, new, 1))

p = Path("dab/mappings/order-mapping.yaml")
t = p.read_text()
old = "          - {id: FREIGHT_CHARGE, transformation_expression: freight}"
new = ("          - {id: FREIGHT_CHARGE, transformation_expression: freight}\n"
       "          - {id: SHIPPED_ON, transformation_expression: shipped_date}\n"
       "          # Arithmetic over columns of this row, which M5 permits and ADR 0007 bounds.\n"
       "          # date_diff rather than extract(DAY FROM ...) only because it reads better;\n"
       "          # both are accepted now.\n"
       "          - {id: SHIP_LAG_DAYS, transformation_expression: date_diff('day', order_date, shipped_date)}")
assert old in t
p.write_text(t.replace(old, new, 1))

p = Path("dab/uss.yaml")
t = p.read_text()
t += '''
    - id: SHIPPED
      entity: ORDER
      definition: >-
        An order shipped: the goods left the business on their way to the destination. One per
        order, on the day they left. An order the business has not recorded as gone has no
        shipment event at all, so it is absent here rather than counted as a zero.
      kind: transaction
      date_attribute: SHIPPED_ON
      measures:
        - id: SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT
          definition: >-
            The number of orders that went out, counted on the day they left rather than the
            day they were accepted. An order accepted in one month and shipped in the next
            counts once, in the second.
          aggregate: count

        - id: SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS
          definition: >-
            The days orders spent waiting to go out, added up. Additive over any set of shipped
            orders and any period, because each shipped order contributes its own wait exactly
            once. The wait of a typical order is this divided by SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT over the
            same set -- a division a question does, and never a number this system stores.
          aggregate: sum
          attribute: SHIP_LAG_DAYS
'''
p.write_text(t)
PY

input.content:
---
id: q03
slice: 3
status: green
persona: Operations manager
question: How many orders shipped per shipping month, and how many days did they take?
aggregation: sum
measure: ORDER.SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT
dimensions: [_calendar.month_label]
time_grain: month
defines:
  - ORDER.SHIPPED_ON
  - ORDER.SHIP_LAG_DAYS
  - ORDER.events.SHIPPED
  - ORDER.measures.SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT
  - ORDER.measures.SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS
order_by: [shipping_month]
---

## Story

As the **operations manager**, I want to see how many orders went out each month and how long
they waited, so that I can tell whether a busy month is also a slow one — and staff against the
answer rather than against a feeling.

## Definitions

Every term below is defined in `dab/model.yaml` or `dab/uss.yaml` and nowhere else. This
question references them; it does not restate them.

- {{ORDER.SHIPPED_ON}}
- {{ORDER.SHIP_LAG_DAYS}}
- {{ORDER.events.SHIPPED}}
- {{ORDER.measures.SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT}}
- {{ORDER.measures.SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS}}

## The W's

- **Why**: throughput and speed move together or they do not, and which of the two it is
  decides whether the answer is more people or a different process. One number cannot say.
- **What**: two additive measures — the count of orders that went out, and the days they spent
  waiting, added up. Not an average: see below.
- **Who**: the operations manager acts on it; the business ships.
- **How**: one `shipped` event per order, on the day the goods left. **An order that has not
  shipped has no shipment event at all**, so it is absent rather than counted as a zero-day
  order — which would make the slowest orders look like the fastest. 21 of 830 orders are in
  that position.
- **Where**: not asked. This is a question about time, and adding a geography to it would be
  a different question.
- **When**: all history, by the month the goods **left** (`_calendar.month_label`, `YYYY-MM`).
  An order accepted in one month and shipped in the next belongs to the second.
- **What will you do with it**: compare the two lines. A month where the count rises and the
  wait rises with it is a capacity problem; a month where the wait rises on its own is not.

## Why the answer has no average in it

The question asks how many days orders took, and the answer does not contain that number.

Conventions §2: *"Ratios are not stored. Store numerator and denominator as additive measures
and divide at query time."* Its worked example is this question — `avg_days_to_ship` becomes
`ship_lag_orders_days`, and the average is `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)`.
An average of averages is wrong at every grain but the one it was computed at, so a stored
monthly average could not be re-summed into a quarter. Two additive measures can.

There is a second reason, found by measuring rather than by reading. The acceptance check
compares the two answers **row by row as values**, which is exact only while every value is
exact. A ratio is a `DOUBLE` however it is reached. Both queries agree today because both
reduce to one division of two exact integer sums — but float addition is not associative and
DuckDB imposes no order on `sum`: `[0.1, 0.2, 0.3]` sums to `0.6000000000000001` and the same
three reversed to `0.6`. So the first float-valued measure would let the two queries disagree
by a bit, on some machines, some of the time. Keeping the division out of the stored answer
keeps this check exact by construction rather than by luck.

The page does the division, once, where a reader can see it.

## Nulls

`shipped_date` is null on 21 orders and that is the whole point of this slice: those orders have
no row in the `shipped` stage, by construction rather than by a filter anyone has to remember.
The control query mirrors it with `WHERE o.shipped_date IS NOT NULL`.

No order in the recording ships before it was accepted, and none has a null order date, so no
lag is negative and none is missing on a shipped order. Both queries would carry a null lag
through `sum`, which skips it — so a shipped order with no accepted date would be counted and
not waited-for, in both answers alike.

## Delivered

![The answer as it was accepted](answer.png)

## Answers

Two queries, in `staged.sql` and `uss.sql`. The first computes the answer straight from what
the source sent, bypassing the business model and the star schema entirely. The second computes
it from the star schema. They must agree row for row — 23 months, 809 orders, 6,870 days.

Conventions §2: *"Ratios are not stored. Store numerator and denominator as additive measures
and divide at query time."* Its worked example is this question — `avg_days_to_ship` becomes
`ship_lag_orders_days`, and the average is `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)`.
An average of averages is wrong at every grain but the one it was computed at, so a stored
monthly average could not be re-summed into a quarter. Two additive measures can.

There is a second reason, found by measuring rather than by reading. The acceptance check
compares the two answers **row by row as values**, which is exact only while every value is
exact. A ratio is a `DOUBLE` however it is reached. Both queries agree today because both
reduce to one division of two exact integer sums — but float addition is not associative and
DuckDB imposes no order on `sum`: `[0.1, 0.2, 0.3]` sums to `0.6000000000000001` and the same
three reversed to `0.6`. So the first float-valued measure would let the two queries disagree
by a bit, on some machines, some of the time. Keeping the division out of the stored answer
keeps this check exact by construction rather than by luck.

The page does the division, once, where a reader can see it.

## Nulls

`shipped_date` is null on 21 orders and that is the whole point of this slice: those orders have
no row in the `shipped` stage, by construction rather than by a filter anyone has to remember.
The control query mirrors it with `WHERE o.shipped_date IS NOT NULL`.

No order in the recording ships before it was accepted, and none has a null order date, so no
lag is negative and none is missing on a shipped order. Both queries would carry a null lag
through `sum`, which skips it — so a shipped order with no accepted date would be counted and
not waited-for, in both answers alike.

the source sent, bypassing the business model and the star schema entirely. The second computes
it from the star schema. They must agree row for row — 23 months, 809 orders, 6,870 days.

feat(dab,dar,questions): ship the order too, and the days it waited

A second event on the same entity, which is what this slice exists to widen, and it needed no
generator change at all: the neutral fixture has declared two events on one entity since slice
one, and the machinery was already built for it. 830 placed rows, 809 shipped rows, and 21
orders with no shipment row at all -- absent by construction rather than by a filter anyone has
to remember, which is what ADR 0002 promised in slice one and this is the first slice that can
show it.

The days are a NUMBER attribute in the model, computed in the mapping from two columns of one
row, per ADR 0007. The answer carries the two additive measures and no average: an average of
averages is wrong at every grain but the one it was computed at, and the page divides them
once, where a reader can see it happen.

That also keeps the acceptance check exact, which is the part worth measuring rather than
assuming. Both answers hold only counts and exact decimals, and a new check says so per
question -- because the comparison is row by row, by value, and a float would make it
order-dependent rather than merely imprecise: DuckDB's sum over doubles is not associative, and
the same three numbers in two orders give 0.6000000000000001 and 0.6. Verified that the check
fails on a stored ratio rather than being green by construction.

Two traps landed on the way, both of which cost a build.

A YAML flow mapping splits an expression on the commas inside a function call, so
`{transformation_expression: date_diff('day', a, b)}` silently becomes the expression
`date_diff('day'` plus two keys named `a` and `b)`. No YAML error, and nothing downstream
notices: the truncated expression still reads its own row, so M5 accepts it, and the engine is
the first thing to object -- to SQL nobody wrote. It has now cost two slices, the other being
DECIMAL(18, 4) in a contract, so it is refused by the one signature it always leaves, which is
a key the schema does not have. The check caught the mapping I had just written.

builds, the cell does not fail, and the picture is simply absent -- which matters more than it
sounds, because that picture is the record of what was delivered. Two charts sharing an x-axis
rather than one concat, and never two y-scales on one chart: a dual axis invents a correlation

content.text:
Slice 3 is built, green, and pushed; its verification is running. I'll hold the PR until that comes back and I've acted on it, as with slice 2.

**Slice 3 — orders shipped per month, and days to ship.** 23 months, 809 shipped orders, 6,870 days, both queries agreeing exactly. 24 checks pass from a clean rebuild.

The frame turned up two decisions rather than one, so there are two records:

**ADR 0007 — where a value the source doesn't contain gets computed.** Two of the three candidate homes turned out not to exist: a sum measure must name an attribute the model declares, so the generator raises on anything else. Between the rest, what decided it was slice 6. Putting the arithmetic in the generator is cleaner — nothing stored can drift — but a second source reporting elapsed days *directly* has no two dates to subtract, so it needs the attribute anyway, and then one number has two definitions differing by source. Computing it in the question fails worse and more quietly: when two queries disagree the model is the arbiter, and if the arithmetic lives only in the queries then neither can depart from a definition that doesn't exist. The repair procedure stops existing in the slice that introduces the first computed number.

I bounded the precedent in the record rather than leaving it as an example, since "M5 permits it" would otherwise become the argument for whatever M5's regex happens not to catch — and that regex is four keywords and seven function names.

**ADR 0008 — a measure is owned by an event but named for an entity.** With one event each those were the same thing; with two they aren't. I reproduced the consequence: the same measure id on both events emits one column twice *and* silently replaces one definition with the other in the glossary. The column half fails the build loudly. The glossary half is caught by nothing — a page would show a plausible sentence about the wrong number with everything green. Refused now, in the same shape as the refusal for colliding edges.

Two traps cost me a build each, and both are worth knowing:

- **A YAML flow mapping splits an expression on the commas inside a function call.** `{transformation_expression: date_diff('day', a, b)}` silently becomes `date_diff('day'` plus two junk keys. No YAML error, and my own M5 checker accepted the truncation because it still reads its own row. This is the second slice it has cost — `DECIMAL(18, 4)` was the first — so it's refused now by the one signature it always leaves. The check caught the mapping I'd just written.
- **The page renders a concatenated altair chart as nothing at all.** Spec builds, widget builds, cell doesn't fail, picture simply absent. That matters more than it sounds, because the picture is the record of what was delivered.

The answer itself is worth a look: shipping volume roughly doubles through 1998 and the wait stays flat at about eight and a half days. They scaled without slowing down.
