Stacked on slice 1. ## The question > What freight did we pay per customer country and order quarter? > — asked by the logistics manager **64,942.69** across 8 quarters and 21 customer countries. The customer's own country, which is not where the goods went. ## What it widens A second contract and entity, the **first relationship**, the first key a stage inherits, and the first sum measure. `CUSTOMER` has no event of its own — it exists in the bridge only because an order reaches it. ## The decision this slice forced, and how it changed A probe built a two-entity model, moved a foreign key, and read every object the engine produced. It overturned **two facts ADR 0002 rested on**: - **The relationship view is a *current* view.** ADR 0002 said reading it would lose a row whose foreign key changed. It does not. It partitions by the child, so the child never drops out — it is re-pointed, and the *old* pair is erased for that child's whole history, retroactively and invisibly. The reason to read the raw pairs is history, not disappearance. - **`view__with_rel` does carry relationship keys** — on a target side, along with every attribute of the source entity, fanned out. The probe measured `sum(CHILD_AMOUNT)` at **200.75 against a true 150.75**. A live fan trap in the view whose name most invites the join. And a third nobody had looked for: the engine ranks with `rank()`, not `row_number()`, so a child whose source named two parents at one instant comes back **twice** — doubling its measures, from the vendor's own view. A fourth finding decided how the rule is *enforced*: **the model cannot say an edge is many-to-one.** `cardinality:` is rejected outright; `type:` takes any string without validation and is dropped on compile, never reaching the engine. The engine is agnostic by design — it treats a child's parents as a set. So cardinality is inferred from the mapping (M5 already forbids the reaches that would make a target expression multi-valued) and pinned by a data check, because the inference cannot cover one key appearing on several staged rows of a single load. [ADR 0006](https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/blob/9b34378/docs/adr/0006-an-inherited-key-is-resolved-as-of-the-row-that-inherits-it.md) records all of it, and corrects ADR 0002 and ADR 0004 rather than editing them. ## What the generator does now Reads `v___` — the raw pairs — matched on `rel_name` (never `type_key`, which is not stable across models), open pairs only, joined **LEFT** because a childless row has no pair row at all and absence is the only evidence there is, ranked with `row_number()` over `eff_tmstp, ver_tmstp, target key`, **as of the observation time of the row that inherits**, partitioned by that row rather than by its key. Three generated checks assert the mechanism: no source has two targets at one instant, every declared edge loaded at least one pair, and every inherited key names a row in its peripheral. Each is the signature of one of M6's three silent failures. ## The two answers, which must agree ```sql -- straight from the source, bypassing both layers SELECT strftime(o.order_date, '%Y') || '-Q' || cast(quarter(o.order_date) AS VARCHAR) AS order_quarter, c.country AS customer_country, cast(sum(o.freight) AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS freight_orders_amount FROM das__staged.orders__current AS o LEFT JOIN das__staged.customers__current AS c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY order_quarter, customer_country ``` ```sql -- from the generated star schema SELECT cal.quarter_label AS order_quarter, cu.based_in_country AS customer_country, cast(sum(b._measure__order__freight_orders_amount) AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS freight_orders_amount FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key LEFT JOIN dar__uss.customer AS cu ON b.customer_key = cu.customer_key WHERE b._event = 'placed' GROUP BY cal.quarter_label, cu.based_in_country ORDER BY order_quarter, customer_country ``` 153 rows each, identical, totalling all the freight the business paid. ## ⚠️ What agreeing proves here, and what it does not **This is the thing to read before accepting the slice.** The dimension is the customer's country. The obvious wrong implementation is the order's destination country — the value already on the same row, one join cheaper. **In this recording those two columns are equal on every one of the 830 orders.** So an implementation that inherited nothing and read `DESTINATION_COUNTRY` would produce this same answer and the agreement check would pass it. That claim is not mine: an independent lens recomputed it from the raw payloads and got 830 equal, 0 unequal. So the number is checked by the two queries, and the **mechanism** is checked by the three data checks, which hold regardless of whether the two columns coincide. Neither would have been enough alone. It took looking at the data to find that out, and the prioritised list — which asserted "customer country is not destination country" as though it were a fact about the data — has been corrected to say it is a fact about the model. ## Verification Six independent lenses, then every finding attacked by an agent trying to kill it. Fourteen survived at confidence ≥ 7; three were killed. **The test-quality lens refused the slice**, and it was right. Two blocking findings, both the same shape — the slice's central behaviours had tests that could not fail: - **The test named for the no-fan-out property never looked at the window's `PARTITION BY`.** Adding the target key to it makes `row_number()` return 1 for *each* parent, so a child with two parents yields two bridge rows and a doubled measure — the exact failure the bridge exists to prevent — and the suite stayed green. No data check could catch it either: a check is a statement about data, and this warehouse has no tie. Nine previously-green mutations are now red, including a bare `JOIN` where a `LEFT` was meant, `dense_rank` slipping past a word boundary, and the two ranking terms swapped. - **The three generated checks had no tests at all** — the half of ADR 0006's argument the inference cannot make. Nothing else could catch a weakened one: `dar generate --check` compares the committed SQL to the same generator, so it agrees with a weakened generator. Each now runs against a scratch warehouse built to fail it and one built to pass it. Latent defects, none of which bite today: - The inherited key was resolved per source **key** rather than per bridge **row** — exactly the property ADR 0006 spends its decision buying. A reviewer reproduced it by retaining two versions of one order. - Two edges from one entity to the same target, or a self-edge, would emit one key column **twice under one name**, and DuckDB resolves that silently. Both shapes are now refused, and ADR 0006's claim that `rel_name` prevented it is corrected — it separates the pair objects, not the bridge's columns. - M6's checker validated only the **last** mapping declaring a given edge, so an entity loaded from a second source could carry the silent skip the check exists to catch. - The key-shape comparison anonymised **function names** along with column names, so `lpad(x, 5, '0')` and a bare `x` compared as the same shape. - `dar generate` had become a second writer into `checks/` and swept nothing, so renaming a relationship left a check that aborts the whole run before a finding is printed. - A question id names a file and an environment variable and was validated nowhere. The **empty** one is the dangerous case: the page reads an empty selection as "show everything", so that question's committed `answer.png` would have been a picture of every question with nothing looking wrong. - The bridge's column contract claimed "a model change appends; it never rearranges". It does rearrange — keys precede measures, so a new entity moves every measure right. The docstring now says what is true, and why it is tolerable: nothing reads this table by position. Also pinned: that `v_` hands over the **raw** pairs. It is the one object the generated SQL reads and the only engine behaviour the as-of rule rests on that nothing checked. If a release started ranking inside it, the rule would silently revert to the vendor's "as of now" and every check would still pass. ## What this slice still does not prove Both entities on this edge are at the **same grain** — one order has one customer — so no measure *can* multiply across it however the join is written. **D-0001 is still carried on assertion.** The first measure at a finer grain arrives in slice 4, and that is where the fan-out proof becomes possible. ADR 0006 and the deviations register both say so rather than claiming otherwise. ```bash uv run adss build # the whole system from the recording, offline uv run adss check # 20 checks, all green ``` ## Next Slice 3: *how many orders shipped per shipping month, and how many days did they take?* — two events on one entity, a second bridge stage, and a ratio computed at query time from two additive measures. 21 orders in the recording have never shipped, so "an event that did not happen has no row" stops being theoretical. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_019rspwWhmXfxoTvKg5jmNWh --- _Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code/session_019rspwWhmXfxoTvKg5jmNWh)_","state":"open","draft":false,"merged":false,"html_url":"https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/pull/2","user":{"login":"mattiasthalen","id":2592140,"profile_url":"https://github.com/mattiasthalen","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/2592140?v=4"},"head":{"ref":"claude/adss-slice-02-freight-per-customer-country-and-quarter","sha":"9b34378238d212b545e7498ea3883d1e01822e32","repo":{"full_name":"mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07"}},"base":{"ref":"claude/adss-slice-01-orders-per-month-and-ship-country","sha":"28a6065823f4e5dac12b35b6ad752314af7fbb8d","repo":{"full_name":"mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07"}},"created_at":"2026-09-08T00:32:01Z","updated_at":"2026-09-08T00:32:01Z"},{"number":1,"title":"Slice 1 — How many orders were placed per order month and destination country?","body":"One business question, answered end to end through all three layers, and presented. *Pinned to the commit, not the branch: a record of what was delivered should not move when the branch does.* ## The question > How many orders were placed per order month and destination country? > — asked by the sales director **830 orders**, across 23 months and 21 destination countries, 1996-07 to 1998-05. ## The two answers, which must agree Straight from the source, bypassing both layers: ```sql SELECT strftime(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS order_month, o.ship_country AS destination_country, count(*) AS placed_orders_count FROM das__staged.orders__current AS o WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL GROUP BY strftime(o.order_date, '%Y-%m'), o.ship_country ORDER BY order_month, destination_country ``` From the generated star schema: ```sql SELECT cal.month_label AS order_month, o.destination_country AS destination_country, cast(sum(b._measure__order__placed_orders_count) AS BIGINT) AS placed_orders_count FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key INNER JOIN dar__uss."order" AS o ON b.order_key = o.order_key WHERE b._event = 'placed' GROUP BY cal.month_label, o.destination_country ORDER BY order_month, destination_country ``` 322 rows each, identical. That catches the failure this architecture is most exposed to and least able to see — that routing a number through integration and generation changed it. It would **not** catch a wrong definition; both queries would be written to it and both would be wrong together. ## What is here | | | |---|---| | **DAS** | one contract, 830 records recorded verbatim over nine pages, landed whole as JSON into hive-partitioned parquet, unpacked strictly into a change log plus a current view | | **DAB** | `ORDER` in business language — `PLACED_ON`, `DESTINATION_COUNTRY`, no source word anywhere — historized by when the system observed it | | **DAR** | a generated bridge, peripheral and calendar, with a published column contract | | **Destination** | a marimo page reading `dar__uss` and nothing else, running the question's own query | | **Decisions** | five ADRs, written before the code they decide | | **Skills** | one per layer, one for the destination, one for the whole | ```bash uv run adss build # the whole system from the recording, offline, ~11s uv run adss check # eight checks, all green ``` ## Verification Four independent lenses, then a code review, then CI. Each found something the ones before it could not. The recomputation lens rebuilt the answer from the raw recorded payloads in plain Python — 830 orders, 322 rows, byte-identical to what the star schema returns — and accepted it. The rest found real work, all fixed in the last four commits: - **A bug that only bites elsewhere.** `extracted_at` carries a time zone, so casting it to a date resolved in the reader's session zone while the partition key is the loader's UTC date. On UTC it passed; on `Asia/Tokyo` it reported 830 disagreements for a warehouse that was perfectly correct. - **A mutation that stayed green.** The bridge test counted column aliases per branch. A union takes its column names from its first branch, so a branch emitting the right columns in a *different order* puts one measure's values into another measure's column — and `DESCRIBE` still matches. It now asserts the sequence. - **The check machinery named a source.** `das__staged.orders` was hardcoded in a SQL string, so the check covered exactly one contract; a second would have been silently unchecked while `adss check` still printed PASS. Contracts now generate their own checks into files. - **Two tests could only pass on the machine that wrote them**, so "every commit passes the gate" was not true from a fresh checkout. - **Four ADRs described confirmations nobody had written.** Most now exist. The fan-out test is not among them and cannot be — it needs two grains and this slice has one entity — so ADR 0002 says that rather than claiming it. - **CI found the one the others structurally could not.** The oldest test in the repo asserted `"Usage: adss"` in help output. Rich styles that per phrase, so with colour enabled the bytes are `Usage: ␛adss` and the substring does not exist. CI turns colour on; the container does not. It had only ever been seen to pass under the one condition that hid it. A security review has since run over this diff as well — three lenses (injection and code execution, supply chain and CI, and data flow), each adversarially filtered. **No findings survived.** It did catch one documentation defect out of its own scope: ADR 0004's confirmation section named a test that does not exist. The control it described is real and stronger than the one claimed — the engine binary is hashed against its committed checksum before *every* invocation, and again in CI — so the correction was to the record, in slice 2. ## Known and deliberate - **D-0001 stands, and is carried on assertion.** One shared `dar__uss` departs from the DAR no-cross-dependency principle. Its argument rests on a walk over many-to-one relationships, which a single-entity slice has none of. Slice 4, the first with a second grain, is where the fan-out proof becomes possible. - **The branch slug says "ship country".** The question became *destination country* when the no-source-names rule was applied to the model, after the branch was cut. The conventions now say the slug is the question's slug. - **The control query has a shelf life.** It stays writable only while a question needs no integration. Slice 6, where one entity is assembled from two systems, is where that bill arrives. ## Next Slice 2 adds a second contract, a second entity and the first relationship — *what freight did we pay per customer country and order quarter?* — the first question whose answer needs a key to inherit. The full prioritised list is in [`docs/questions/`](https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/blob/28a6065823f4e5dac12b35b6ad752314af7fbb8d/docs/questions/README.md). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_019rspwWhmXfxoTvKg5jmNWh","state":"open","draft":false,"merged":false,"html_url":"https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/pull/1","user":{"login":"mattiasthalen","id":2592140,"profile_url":"https://github.com/mattiasthalen","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/2592140?v=4"},"head":{"ref":"claude/adss-slice-01-orders-per-month-and-ship-country","sha":"28a6065823f4e5dac12b35b6ad752314af7fbb8d","repo":{"full_name":"mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07"}},"base":{"ref":"claude/adss-blog-implementation-vy62ci","sha":"eaea5fdb61528f266a432bbf19fd1fc3e1f354f3","repo":{"full_name":"mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07"}},"created_at":"2026-09-07T22:13:22Z","updated_at":"2026-09-07T23:08:12Z"}]

input.body: One business question, answered end to end through all three layers, and presented. *Pinned to the commit, not the branch: a record of what was delivered should not move when the branch does.* ## The question > How many orders were placed per order month and destination country? > — asked by the sales director **830 orders**, across 23 months and 21 destination countries, 1996-07 to 1998-05. ## The two answers, which must agree Straight from the source, bypassing both layers: ```sql SELECT strftime(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS order_month, o.ship_country AS destination_country, count(*) AS placed_orders_count FROM das__staged.orders__current AS o WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL GROUP BY strftime(o.order_date, '%Y-%m'), o.ship_country ORDER BY order_month, destination_country ``` From the generated star schema: ```sql SELECT cal.month_label AS order_month, o.destination_country AS destination_country, cast(sum(b._measure__order__placed_orders_count) AS BIGINT) AS placed_orders_count FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key INNER JOIN dar__uss."order" AS o ON b.order_key = o.order_key WHERE b._event = 'placed' GROUP BY cal.month_label, o.destination_country ORDER BY order_month, destination_country ``` 322 rows each, identical. That catches the failure this architecture is most exposed to and least able to see — that routing a number through integration and generation changed it. It would **not** catch a wrong definition; both queries would be written to it and both would be wrong together. ## What is here | | | |---|---| | **DAS** | one contract, 830 records recorded verbatim over nine pages, landed whole as JSON into hive-partitioned parquet, unpacked strictly into a change log plus a current view | | **DAB** | `ORDER` in business language — `PLACED_ON`, `DESTINATION_COUNTRY`, no source word anywhere — historized by when the system observed it | | **DAR** | a generated bridge, peripheral and calendar, with a published column contract | | **Destination** | a marimo page reading `dar__uss` and nothing else, running the question's own query | | **Decisions** | five ADRs, written before the code they decide | | **Skills** | one per layer, one for the destination, one for the whole | ```bash uv run adss build # the whole system from the recording, offline, ~11s uv run adss check # eight checks, all green ``` ## Verification Four independent lenses, then a code review, then CI. Each found something the ones before it could not. The recomputation lens rebuilt the answer from the raw recorded payloads in plain Python — 830 orders, 322 rows, byte-identical to what the star schema returns — and accepted it. The rest found real work, all fixed in the last four commits: - **A bug that only bites elsewhere.** `extracted_at` carries a time zone, so casting it to a date resolved in the reader's session zone while the partition key is the loader's UTC date. On UTC it passed; on `Asia/Tokyo` it reported 830 disagreements for a warehouse that was perfectly correct. - **A mutation that stayed green.** The bridge test counted column aliases per branch. A union takes its column names from its first branch, so a branch emitting the right columns in a *different order* puts one measure's values into another measure's column — and `DESCRIBE` still matches. It now asserts the sequence. - **The check machinery named a source.** `das__staged.orders` was hardcoded in a SQL string, so the check covered exactly one contract; a second would have been silently unchecked while `adss check` still printed PASS. Contracts now generate their own checks into files. - **Two tests could only pass on the machine that wrote them**, so "every commit passes the gate" was not true from a fresh checkout. - **Four ADRs described confirmations nobody had written.** Most now exist. The fan-out test is not among them and cannot be — it needs two grains and this slice has one entity — so ADR 0002 says that rather than claiming it. - **CI found the one the others structurally could not.** The oldest test in the repo asserted `"Usage: adss"` in help output. Rich styles that per phrase, so with colour enabled the bytes are `Usage: ␛adss` and the substring does not exist. CI turns colour on; the container does not. It had only ever been seen to pass under the one condition that hid it. A security review has since run over this diff as well — three lenses (injection and code execution, supply chain and CI, and data flow), each adversarially filtered. **No findings survived.** It did catch one documentation defect out of its own scope: ADR 0004's confirmation section named a test that does not exist. The control it described is real and stronger than the one claimed — the engine binary is hashed against its committed checksum before *every* invocation, and again in CI — so the correction was to the record, in slice 2. ## Known and deliberate - **D-0001 stands, and is carried on assertion.** One shared `dar__uss` departs from the DAR no-cross-dependency principle. Its argument rests on a walk over many-to-one relationships, which a single-entity slice has none of. Slice 4, the first with a second grain, is where the fan-out proof becomes possible. - **The branch slug says "ship country".** The question became *destination country* when the no-source-names rule was applied to the model, after the branch was cut. The conventions now say the slug is the question's slug. - **The control query has a shelf life.** It stays writable only while a question needs no integration. Slice 6, where one entity is assembled from two systems, is where that bill arrives. ## Next Slice 2 adds a second contract, a second entity and the first relationship — *what freight did we pay per customer country and order quarter?* — the first question whose answer needs a key to inherit. The full prioritised list is in [`docs/questions/`](https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/blob/28a6065823f4e5dac12b35b6ad752314af7fbb8d/docs/questions/README.md). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_019rspwWhmXfxoTvKg5jmNWh

One business question, answered end to end through all three layers, and presented.

![The answer, as the page presents it](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/28a6065823f4e5dac12b35b6ad752314af7fbb8d/docs/questions/01-orders-per-month-and-destination-country/answer.png)

## The question

> How many orders were placed per order month and destination country?
> — asked by the sales director

**830 orders**, across 23 months and 21 destination countries, 1996-07 to 1998-05.

## The two answers, which must agree

```sql
SELECT
    strftime(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS order_month,
```

## The question

> How many orders were placed per order month and destination country?
> — asked by the sales director

**830 orders**, across 23 months and 21 destination countries, 1996-07 to 1998-05.

## The two answers, which must agree

Straight from the source, bypassing both layers:

```sql
SELECT
    strftime(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS order_month,
    o.ship_country AS destination_country,
    count(*) AS placed_orders_count
FROM das__staged.orders__current AS o
WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY strftime(o.order_date, '%Y-%m'), o.ship_country
ORDER BY order_month, destination_country
```

From the generated star schema:

```sql
SELECT
    cal.month_label AS order_month,
    o.destination_country AS destination_country,
    cast(sum(b._measure__order__placed_orders_count) AS BIGINT) AS placed_orders_count
FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key
INNER JOIN dar__uss."order" AS o ON b.order_key = o.order_key
WHERE b._event = 'placed'
GROUP BY cal.month_label, o.destination_country
ORDER BY order_month, destination_country
```

322 rows each, identical. That catches the failure this architecture is most exposed to and least able to see — that routing a number through integration and generation changed it. It would **not** catch a wrong definition; both queries would be written to it and both would be wrong together.

|---|---|

| **DAR** | a generated bridge, peripheral and calendar, with a published column contract |
| **Destination** | a marimo page reading `dar__uss` and nothing else, running the question's own query |
| **Decisions** | five ADRs, written before the code they decide |
| **Skills** | one per layer, one for the destination, one for the whole |

```bash
uv run adss check      # eight checks, all green
```

Four independent lenses, then a code review, then CI. Each found something the ones before it could not.

The recomputation lens rebuilt the answer from the raw recorded payloads in plain Python — 830 orders, 322 rows, byte-identical to what the star schema returns — and accepted it. The rest found real work, all fixed in the last four commits:

- **The check machinery named a source.** `das__staged.orders` was hardcoded in a SQL string, so the check covered exactly one contract; a second would have been silently unchecked while `adss check` still printed PASS. Contracts now generate their own checks into files.
- **Two tests could only pass on the machine that wrote them**, so "every commit passes the gate" was not true from a fresh checkout.
- **Four ADRs described confirmations nobody had written.** Most now exist. The fan-out test is not among them and cannot be — it needs two grains and this slice has one entity — so ADR 0002 says that rather than claiming it.

Rich styles that per phrase, so with colour enabled the bytes are `Usage: ␛adss` and the substring does not exist. CI turns colour on; the container does not. It had only ever been seen to pass under the one condition that hid it.

{"number":1,"title":"Slice 1 — How many orders were placed per order month and destination country?","body":"One business question, answered end to end through all three layers, and presented.

The screenshot of the answer, as the page presents it, is committed beside the question it answers: [`docs/questions/01-orders-per-month-and-destination-country/`](``https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/tree/28a6065823f4e5dac12b35b6ad752314af7fbb8d/docs/questions/01-orders-per-month-and-destination-country``) → `answer.png`.

*Pinned to the commit, not the branch: a record of what was delivered should not move when the branch does. It is a link rather than an embed because the tool that writes this description rewrites image URLs — noted here so the next reader does not think the picture is missing.*

## The question

> How many orders were placed per order month and destination country?
> — asked by the sales director

**830 orders**, across 23 months and 21 destination countries, 1996-07 to 1998-05.

## The two answers, which must agree

Straight from the source, bypassing both layers:

```sql
SELECT
    strftime(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS order_month,
    o.ship_country AS destination_country,
    count(*) AS placed_orders_count
FROM das__staged.orders__current AS o
WHERE o.order_date IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY strftime(o.order_date, '%Y-%m'), o.ship_country
ORDER BY order_month, destination_country
```

From the generated star schema:

```sql
SELECT
    cal.month_label AS order_month,
    o.destination_country AS destination_country,
    cast(sum(b._measure__order__placed_orders_count) AS BIGINT) AS placed_orders_count
FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
INNER JOIN dar__uss._calendar AS cal ON b._event_date = cal.date_key
INNER JOIN dar__uss."order" AS o ON b.order_key = o.order_key
WHERE b._event = 'placed'
GROUP BY cal.month_label, o.destination_country
ORDER BY order_month, destination_country
```

322 rows each, identical. That catches the failure this architecture is most exposed to and least able to see — that routing a number through integration and generation changed it. It would **not** catch a wrong definition; both queries would be written to it and both would be wrong together.

## What is here

| | |
|---|---|
| **DAS** | one contract, 830 records recorded verbatim over nine pages, landed whole as JSON into hive-partitioned parquet, unpacked strictly into a change log plus a current view |
| **DAB** | `ORDER` in business language — `PLACED_ON`, `DESTINATION_COUNTRY`, no source word anywhere — historized by when the system observed it |
| **DAR** | a generated bridge, peripheral and calendar, with a published column contract |
| **Destination** | a marimo page reading `dar__uss` and nothing else, running the question's own query |
| **Decisions** | five ADRs, written before the code they decide |
| **Skills** | one per layer, one for the destination, one for the whole |

```bash
uv run adss build      # the whole system from the recording, offline, ~11s
uv run adss check      # eight checks, all green
```

## Verification

Four independent lenses, then a code review, then CI. Each found something the ones before it could not.

The recomputation lens rebuilt the answer from the raw recorded payloads in plain Python — 830 orders, 322 rows, byte-identical to what the star schema returns — and accepted it. The rest found real work, all fixed in the last four commits:

- **A bug that only bites elsewhere.** `extracted_at` carries a time zone, so casting it to a date resolved in the reader's session zone while the partition key is the loader's UTC date. On UTC it passed; on `Asia/Tokyo` it reported 830 disagreements for a warehouse that was perfectly correct.
- **A mutation that stayed green.** The bridge test counted column aliases per branch. A union takes its column names from its first branch, so a branch emitting the right columns in a *different order* puts one measure's values into another measure's column — and `DESCRIBE` still matches. It now asserts the sequence.
- **The check machinery named a source.** `das__staged.orders` was hardcoded in a SQL string, so the check covered exactly one contract; a second would have been silently unchecked while `adss check` still printed PASS. Contracts now generate their own checks into files.
- **Two tests could only pass on the machine that wrote them**, so "every commit passes the gate" was not true from a fresh checkout.
- **Four ADRs described confirmations nobody had written.** Most now exist. The fan-out test is not among them and cannot be — it needs two grains and this slice has one entity — so ADR 0002 says that rather than claiming it.
- **CI found the one the others structurally could not.** The oldest test in the repo asserted `"Usage: adss"` in help output. Rich styles that per phrase, so with colour enabled the bytes are `Usage: ␛adss` and the substring does not exist. CI turns colour on; the container does not. It had only ever been seen to pass under the one condition that hid it.

A security review has since run over this diff as well — three lenses (injection and code execution, supply chain and CI, and data flow), each adversarially filtered. **No findings survived.** It did catch one documentation defect out of its own scope: ADR 0004's confirmation section named a test that does not exist. The control it described is real and stronger than the one claimed — the engine binary is hashed against its committed checksum before *every* invocation, and again in CI — so the correction was to the record, in slice 2.

## Known and deliberate

- **D-0001 stands, and is carried on assertion.** One shared `dar__uss` departs from the DAR no-cross-dependency principle. Its argument rests on a walk over many-to-one relationships, which a single-entity slice has none of. Slice 4, the first with a second grain, is where the fan-out proof becomes possible.
- **The branch slug says "ship country".** The question became *destination country* when the no-source-names rule was applied to the model, after the branch was cut. The conventions now say the slug is the question's slug.
- **The control query has a shelf life.** It stays writable only while a question needs no integration. Slice 6, where one entity is assembled from two systems, is where that bill arrives.

## Next

Slice 2 adds a second contract, a second entity and the first relationship — *what freight did we pay per customer country and order quarter?* — the first question whose answer needs a key to inherit. The full prioritised list is in [`docs/questions/`](https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/blob/28a6065823f4e5dac12b35b6ad752314af7fbb8d/docs/questions/README.md).

content.content:
The M5 checker no longer refuses a subquery nested inside a FROM-taking function. `_without_keyword_from` deletes the entire argument list of `extract|substring|trim|overlay|position` before `_REACHING` sees it, so any `select`/`from`/`join` inside those arguments is invisible. M5 (conventions.md:92, Hard rule) says "Never a subquery, never an aggregate, never a reach into another table", and this is the mapping-level enforcement of blueprint F3. It is a regression introduced by this slice, not a pre-existing gap.

  [worth fixing] docs/conventions.md:92 (M5) and docs/conventions.md:93 (M5a); the same wording at docs/adr/0007-a-derived-value-is-modelled-where-two-vocabularies-are-bound.md:105-107
  The line ADR 0007 draws puts `CASE` on both sides of itself with no test to tell the two apart. M5 permits "a `CASE` over columns of that row"; M5a forbids "a `CASE` on *values*". Every CASE is over columns and on their values, so the enumeration decides nothing. The ADR's underlying criterion is coherent and does decide it — "arithmetic over one row produces a value the row already implies; the others produce a value somebody chose" — but by that criterion a CASE is always a choice, so M5's blanket permission of it sits on the wrong side of the ADR's own test. That matters because M5a's stated reason for existing is that "M5 permits it" was becoming the standing argument for whatever the regex misses; leaving CASE in M5's permission list hands that argument straight back, and this pair is enforced by review alone.

  [note] docs/questions/03-shipped-orders-and-days-to-ship/staged.sql:6 vs dab/mappings/order-mapping.yaml:24
  The control query computes the lag with the same expression the mapping computes it with, character for character, so for that one measure the control's independence is structural (it does not read DAB or DAR) but not derivational — a wrong argument order or a wrong unit in the mapping would be reproduced identically by the control and the check would pass. Two things temper it and both are worth the parent knowing. First, over two DATE columns every correct spelling of "days between" is numerically identical, so a different spelling would buy nothing real. Second, and cutting the other way, this makes q03's own acceptance check a genuine month-grain guard on the stored derivation — which ADR 0007's Confirmation says does not exist.
==========================================================================================
I checked the slice against §1.2, §1.3, §1.4 (M1-M7), §2, §4, §5, §6, §7, §8 and §10, and ran the repository's own gates: pytest (149 passed), ruff, sqlfluff, yamllint, ty --error all, `adss dar generate --check` (no drift, clean tree) and `adss check` (all PASS). The naming, the mapping, the generated layer, the question and the SQL/YAML/Python style all conform — including the two clauses most at risk here, §1.2's no-source-name rule and §5's no-data-vocabulary rule, which this slice does not breach. What I did find is documentation honesty and commit hygiene: ADR 0008's Confirmation claims a test that exists in name only, ADR 0008 landed in the same commit as the code it decides under a `docs` type, and ADR 0002's Confirmation still describes a check that slice 2 replaced.

  [worth fixing] docs/adr/0008-a-measure-is-owned-by-an-event-and-named-for-an-entity.md:108 (the test it names is tests/test_uss.py:432-438)
  ADR 0008's Confirmation section claims a test that does not exist as described. It says test_uss.py asserts "that the same id on two *different* entities is still accepted — which is the case the refusal must not catch". The test carrying that name never constructs that case: it loads the neutral fixture and asserts only that its measure columns are distinct, and no measure id in that fixture appears on two entities. The test therefore cannot fail if the refusal were broadened to catch the case it is named for. §8's second exception is explicit that a Confirmation section "claims which checks exist *now*, so a stale one lies about the present", and names this exact drift ("describing a check somebody meant to write").

  [worth fixing] commit 3c2dd25 "docs(adr): refuse two events on one entity sharing a measure id, and stop refusing arithmetic"
  §7's "An ADR lands before the code it decides" (hard rule) is not met for ADR 0008: the record and its implementation land in one commit, typed `docs`. The commit adds the ADR (+113) and, in the same breath, the generator refusal it decides (src/adss/uss.py `_refuse_measures_that_would_share_a_name`, +29), the M5 checker fix (src/adss/mapping.py, +47/-4), two test files and a fixture. §7's stated why for the type/scope is that "a reviewer knows which rules apply before opening the diff" — a `docs` commit that changes the generator defeats that, and every earlier `docs(...)` commit in this repository is documentation only.

  [worth fixing] docs/adr/0002-dar-is-one-generated-unified-star-schema.md:150-151 (the section starting at :139, "### Confirmation")
  ADR 0002's Confirmation still describes the pre-0006 engine check, in the terms the probe disproved: it says a data check pins "that `view_<E>_with_rel` still carries no relationship key". That check was replaced in slice 2 by one asserting the two-sided rule, and ADR 0006 corrected 0002's *body* claims but left this section untouched. §8 makes the Confirmation section the one part that is corrected in place rather than in a later record, precisely because it is a claim about the present.

  [worth fixing] tests/test_relationship_rules.py:109
  The only §5/§6 data-vocabulary hit under src/ or tests/: a test asserts over the literal source column name `customer_id`. §5 is "No data vocabulary anywhere under `src/` or in test code" and §6 is "No test contains an entity, attribute, measure, source or column name from the business" — both hard rules, and `customer_id` is the landed column name of das__staged.customers and the key of dab/mappings/customer-mapping.yaml. The three neighbouring asserts in the same test already use neutral `a`/`b`, so the word buys nothing.

  [note] commit 4618ec8 "feat(dab,dar,questions): ship the order too, and the days it waited"
  The commit's scope list omits two of the areas it changes: `destination` (135 lines of destinations/app.py, three new charts and four new cells) and the machinery (src/adss/checks.py, src/adss/mapping.py and their tests). §7's why for the scope is that it lets a reviewer know which rules apply before opening the diff; a reviewer reading `(dab,dar,questions)` would not expect the page or a new mapping refusal. It is also the first multi-scope commit in the repository's history, where §7 lists scopes as single values.

  [note] dar/uss/_bridge.sql:106 and :122; docs/adr/0002-dar-is-one-generated-unified-star-schema.md:94-101; docs/questions/README.md (slice 3 row)
  "A second stage in the bridge" is not what the bridge says. `_stage` is defined by ADR 0002 as "the entity this row is a row *of*", so both new branches emit `'order'` and the two events are distinguished only by `_event`. That makes one sentence of ADR 0002's published column contract false for the first time: `_measure__<entity>__<measure>` is documented as "non-null only on the owning stage", and all 809 shipped rows share `_stage = 'order'` while carrying a null `_measure__order__placed_orders_count`. ADR 0008 names the underlying mismatch ("the generator still names by entity what it owns by event") but does not correct 0002's sentence the way ADR 0006 corrected its others.

  [note] docs/questions/03-shipped-orders-and-days-to-ship/question.md:7-8
  The question's front matter under-describes its own answer. `measure: ORDER.SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT` names one of the two measures the answer returns — SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS appears only in `defines` — and `aggregation: sum` disagrees with how q01 fills the same field for the same kind of measure. §10 makes the front matter a hard rule ("carries the measure, dimensions, aggregation, time grain…") and question.py's own refusal message says "The front matter is what a reader trusts", but src/adss/question.py:78-89 parses neither `measure` nor `aggregation`, so nothing catches the drift.
==========================================================================================

The security surface is clean — no `shell=True`, no `eval`, `yaml.safe_load` everywhere, and `ADSS_QUESTION` is constrained by the id regex before it reaches a filename or a subprocess env. What I did find is one real hole in the new M5 checker (it silently drops the tail of an expression on an unbalanced paren, defeating the rule it enforces), two Confirmation sections that claim tests which do not do what they say, and a front-matter field that contradicts `dab/uss.yaml`.

  The paren scan that strips a FROM-taking function's arguments counts parentheses in raw text, so a `(` inside a string literal (or a missing `)`) leaves `depth != 0`, the loop runs off the end, and everything after the function call is silently discarded. `reaching()` then sees only the truncated prefix, so an expression containing a genuine subquery is accepted by M5 — the exact failure the checker exists to prevent. The docstring two lines above promises the opposite.

  [worth fixing] /home/user/adss-2026-09-07/docs/adr/0007-a-derived-value-is-modelled-where-two-vocabularies-are-bound.md:146-148

from pathlib import Path
p = Path("src/adss/mapping.py")
t = p.read_text()
start = t.index("def _without_keyword_from(expression: str) -> str:")
end = t.index("def key_shape(expression: str) -> str:")
new = '''def _without_keyword_from(expression: str) -> str:
    """The expression with the syntactic FROM of each such function blanked, and nothing else.

    Only that one token. An earlier version discarded the whole argument list, which excused
    the very thing M5 exists to stop: a subquery hidden inside `extract(DAY FROM (SELECT ...))`
    became invisible to the checker. It also counted raw parentheses to find the end of the
    list, so a bracket inside a string literal unbalanced the scan and silently dropped the
    rest of the expression -- turning a checker into one that reads half of what it is given.

    Blanking one keyword needs neither. For every function here the FROM that follows the
    opening bracket is the syntactic one, and every later FROM belongs to something that still
    has to answer for itself.
    """
    out = expression
    for call in _KEYWORD_FROM.finditer(expression):
        syntactic = re.compile(r"\\bfrom\\b", re.IGNORECASE).search(out, call.end())
        if syntactic:
            out = out[: syntactic.start()] + " " * len(syntactic.group(0)) + out[syntactic.end() :]
    return out


'''
p.write_text(t[:start] + new + t[end:])
PY

input.command:

from pathlib import Path
p = Path("src/adss/mapping.py")
t = p.read_text()
start = t.index("def _without_keyword_from(expression: str) -> str:")
end = t.index("def key_shape(expression: str) -> str:")
new = '''def _without_keyword_from(expression: str) -> str:
    """The expression with the syntactic FROM of each such function blanked, and nothing else.

    Only that one token, and only when it is genuinely inside the call. An earlier version
    discarded the whole argument list, which excused the very thing M5 exists to stop: a
    subquery hidden in `extract(DAY FROM (SELECT ...))` became invisible. Taking simply the
    next FROM instead was no better -- in `trim(a) FROM elsewhere` the next one is the reach.

    So the scan finds the first FROM at the call's own bracket depth, and gives up at the
    bracket that closes the call. It steps over single-quoted text, because a bracket inside a
    string literal is not a bracket, and a scan that believed otherwise would run off the end
    and hand the checker half an expression to judge.
    """
    out = expression
    for call in _KEYWORD_FROM.finditer(expression):
        found = _syntactic_from(out, call.end())
        if found is not None:
            out = out[:found] + " " * 4 + out[found + 4 :]
    return out


def _syntactic_from(expression: str, opened: int) -> int | None:
    """Where the FROM belonging to a call that opened at `opened` starts, if it has one."""
    depth, index = 1, opened
    while index < len(expression):
        character = expression[index]
        if character == "'":
            closing = expression.find("'", index + 1)
            index = len(expression) if closing == -1 else closing + 1
            continue
        depth += (character == "(") - (character == ")")
        if depth == 0:
            return None
        if (
            depth == 1
            and expression[index : index + 4].lower() == "from"
            and not expression[index - 1 : index].isalnum()
            and not expression[index + 4 : index + 5].isalnum()
        ):
            return index
        index += 1
    return None
'''
p.write_text(t[:start] + new + "\n\n" + t[end:])

input.command: uv run pytest -q 2>&1 | tail -3 && timeout 900 uv run pre-commit run --all-files 2>&1 | tail -8; echo "EXIT ${PIPESTATUS[0]}"

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG' && git log --oneline -1
fix(dab): stop the M5 fix from excusing the one thing M5 exists to stop

The verification refused this slice, and on the sharpest possible grounds: the fix I made for
M5's false refusal opened a real hole in the same rule.

Blanking `extract(DAY FROM ...)` was right; blanking it by discarding the whole argument list
was not. A subquery hidden inside one of those calls became invisible to the checker -- so a
reach into another table, which M5 names explicitly and which is the mapping-level enforcement
of the flow rule, was accepted where it had been refused an hour earlier. The scan also counted
raw parentheses, so a bracket inside a string literal unbalanced it and silently discarded
everything after the call: a checker that reads half of what it is given and reports nothing.

Taking simply the next FROM instead is no better, and I only found that by attacking my own
replacement: in `trim(a) FROM elsewhere` the next FROM is the reach. So the scan now finds the
first FROM at the call's own bracket depth, gives up at the bracket that closes the call, and
steps over single-quoted text.

Every clause of that sentence is now pinned by a case that fails without it, which took three
rounds to get right and is the part worth recording. The first cases I wrote did not
discriminate: the literal-skipping and the word-boundary clauses were both exercised only by
expressions where the awkward text came AFTER the keyword, where neither clause matters. It
takes a literal bracket or a "from"-prefixed identifier standing BEFORE the keyword to tell a
correct scan from a broken one. Six mutations, all red now, including the two depth guards
removed together -- each masks the other, so only the pair can be pinned.

Two smaller things from the same review. `coalesce(a, b)` sat in a list headed "are permitted"
while ADR 0007 names a coalesce as the thing the rule does not permit; that is the sentence a
future reader would have cited. And an assertion checking that a refusal names the stray keys
looked for the letter "b", which the refusal message contains in the words "block style"
regardless -- so half the conjunction could never fail.

from pathlib import Path
p = Path("tests/test_uss.py")
t = p.read_text()

old = '''def test_an_event_reads_the_history_view_and_keeps_the_latest_version():
    sql = bridge()
    assert 'dab."view_PARENT_hist"' in sql
    assert "row_number() OVER (" in sql
    assert "ORDER BY" in sql and "eff_tmstp DESC" in sql'''
new = '''def test_an_event_reads_the_history_view_and_keeps_the_latest_version():
    """Asserted of the version CTE, whole.

    Three whole-file substrings said nothing about it: the INHERIT CTE satisfies every one of
    them, so the assertions were about a different window than the one they named. All three
    mutations that matter -- row_number to rank, DESC to ASC, and adding eff_tmstp to the
    partition -- left the suite green, and none is observable in the warehouse today because
    every entity has exactly one version.
    """
    picked = cte_of(bridge(), "happened__version")
    assert 'dab."view_PARENT_hist"' in picked
    window = re.search(r"QUALIFY (\\w+)\\(\\) OVER \\((.*?)\\) = 1", picked, re.DOTALL)
    assert window, "the versions are ranked"
    assert window.group(1) == "row_number", (
        "rank() returns every tied row, and the engine writes a closing row sharing eff_tmstp"
    )
    partition = re.search(r"PARTITION BY ([^\\n]+)", window.group(2))
    assert partition and partition.group(1).strip() == 'revision."PARENT_key"', (
        "one version per entity. Adding the timestamp makes row_number() return 1 for every "
        "version, so every version becomes a bridge row"
    )
    assert re.search(r"ORDER BY\\s+revision\\.eff_tmstp DESC", window.group(2)), (
        "the LATEST version. Ascending keeps the oldest, which this test is named against"
    )'''
assert old in t
t = t.replace(old, new)

old2 = '''def test_a_stage_that_does_not_own_a_measure_emits_a_typed_null_for_it():
    sql = bridge()
    assert "cast(NULL AS BIGINT) AS _measure__parent__finished_parents_count" in sql
    assert "cast(NULL AS BIGINT) AS _measure__parent__happened_parents_count" in sql
    assert "cast(NULL AS DECIMAL(28, 8)) AS _measure__parent__size_parents_units" in sql'''
new2 = '''def test_a_stage_that_does_not_own_a_measure_emits_a_typed_null_for_it():
    """Every branch, every measure, paired with the value it carries -- not counted.

    Whole-file substrings cannot see ownership: the NULL casts they look for are emitted by
    SOME branch whatever the generator decides, so deciding ownership by entity rather than by
    event left the suite green while emitting a column its own CTE does not have. And rotating
    the value expressions within one branch, leaving the aliases in contract order, emits valid
    SQL that puts a count into a sum column -- green until a build compares two answers.
    """
    model, uss = plan()
    for event in uss.events:
        branch = branch_of(bridge(), event.name)
        for owner, measure, column in uss.measure_columns():
            value = re.search(rf"^\\s*(.+?) AS {re.escape(column)},?$", branch, re.MULTILINE)
            assert value, f"{event.name} emits no {column}"
            if owner is event:
                assert value.group(1) == f"{event.name}.{column}", (
                    f"{event.name} owns {column}, so it carries its own value for it -- and "
                    f"carries it under its own name, not another measure's"
                )
            else:
                assert value.group(1) == f"cast(NULL AS {measure.sql_type})", (
                    f"{event.name} does not own {column}, so it emits a typed NULL. A zero "
                    f"here would be counted; a value from elsewhere would be multiplied"
                )'''
assert old2 in t
p.write_text(t.replace(old2, new2))

cat > tests/test_exactness.py <<'PY'
"""The acceptance check compares two answers row by row, by value. That is exact or it is not.

A float makes the comparison order-dependent rather than merely imprecise: DuckDB's sum over
doubles is not associative, so two queries summing one measure in two orders disagree by a bit
-- on some machines, some of the time. The check that says no answer holds one is the only
thing standing between that and a failure nobody can reproduce. ADR 0007.
"""

from decimal import Decimal

import pytest

from adss.checks import inexact


def test_an_answer_of_counts_and_exact_decimals_is_accepted():
    assert inexact([("1996-07", 17, Decimal("109.00000000")), ("1996-08", 23, None)]) == []


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "value",
    [8.49, float("nan"), float("inf"), 0.0, -1.5],
)
def test_any_float_at_all_is_reported(value: float):
    assert inexact([("a", 1, value)]) == ["float"]


def test_a_bool_is_not_inexact():
    """True is an int in Python, and an int is exact. Refusing it would refuse a flag."""
    assert inexact([(True, False)]) == []


def test_it_looks_at_every_row_and_not_only_the_first():
    """A ratio that is whole in the first month and not in the second is the realistic shape."""
    assert inexact([("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("c", 8.49)]) == ["float"]


def test_an_empty_answer_reports_nothing():
    assert inexact([]) == []
PY

8	# A value derived from one row is modelled in DAB and computed in the mapping, and arithmetic there is bounded by this record
9	
10	## Context and Problem Statement
11	
12	"How many days did they take" is the first number this system reports that does not exist in the
13	source. Every measure so far has been a count — one per row — or a sum of a single attribute that
14	was already there. A ship lag is two dates subtracted, and there is no established place to put
15	the subtraction.
16	
17	Three things are already settled and an argument that reopens them has not read the standard.
18	
19	**The measure's name and its arithmetic are written down.** Conventions §2's own worked example is
20	this question:
21	
22	> | `avg_days_to_ship` | `ship_lag_orders_days` | The average is
23	> `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)` at query time, from two additive
24	> measures. |
25	
26	So the two measures are named, the division is a question's job, and `ship_lag_orders_days` is a
27	*stored measure* — a column in the bridge's published contract. That sentence decides more of this
28	slice than anything else in the repository.
29	
30	**An event that did not happen is already decided.** ADR 0002: "A transaction stage reads
31	`dab.view_<E>_hist`, keeps the latest version in which the event's date is set… An unshipped order
32	therefore has no shipment event *by construction* rather than by a filter somebody has to
33	remember." The generator emits `WHERE <date> IS NOT NULL` and a test pins it. The 21 unshipped
34	orders are the case that design was written for, not a new problem.
35	
36	**Two events on one entity already work.** The neutral fixture has declared two events on one
37	entity since slice 1, and generating this slice's bridge from a scratch copy of the model needs
38	**no generator change at all**. What is new is one thing only: a sum measure with no attribute to
39	point at.
40	
41	## Decision Drivers
42	
43	* a number the business reads has exactly one definition, in the one place data is explained
44	* the acceptance check keeps an arbiter: when two queries disagree, something decides which is wrong
45	* the precedent this sets is one the next three slices can live with
46	* a rule the next person inherits, rather than an example they have to interpret
47	* DAR stays a layer that can be deleted and rebuilt from the model
48	
49	## Considered Options
50	
51	* **(a)** A `NUMBER` attribute on `ORDER`, computed in the mapping from two columns of its own row
52	* **(b)** An expression in `dab/uss.yaml`, emitted into the bridge by the generator
53	* **(c)** Computed in the question's `uss.sql` at query time from two dates on the peripheral
54	
55	## Decision Outcome
56	
57	Chosen: **(a), a `NUMBER` attribute computed in the mapping** — with the precedent bounded here,
58	because "M5 permits it" is otherwise the standing argument for whatever M5's regex happens not to
59	catch.
60	
61	It is also the only option that generates today. A `sum` measure must name an attribute the model
62	declares; `src/adss/uss.py` raises `KeyError: "ORDER has no attribute …"` otherwise, and there is
63	no `expression:` field on a measure. (b) and (c) are not choices between working designs — they
64	are proposals to build something.
65	
66	**Why not (b).** Putting the arithmetic in the generator is the serious rival, and it is cleaner in
67	one respect: nothing derived is stored, so nothing derived can drift. It fails on where it leaves
68	slice 6. A second source that reports elapsed days *directly* has no two dates for a DAR expression
69	to subtract, so integrating it needs the attribute anyway — and then there are two definitions of
70	ship lag, a DAB attribute and a DAR expression, differing by source. That is B2 and B8 failing
71	together in the slice whose entire purpose is to prove B2. It also costs slice 4, where the
72	expression vocabulary would have to grow from a two-date special case to general arithmetic in the
73	same slice that first exercises the fan-out property D-0001 is carried on. Two risky things at once.
74	
75	A free-text SQL expression in YAML additionally breaks §3 — "SQL that lives in a Python string is
76	written to a file so the same linter sees it" — because the linter runs on `.sql` files and would
77	never see it.
78	
79	**Why not (c).** Conventions §2 says ratios are not stored and the numerator *is* an additive
80	measure; (c) reads it as licence for the whole computation and has no `ship_lag_orders_days` at
81	all. The question could then not declare what it measures: every `defines` entry must resolve to
82	something the model or the sidecar defines, so "days to ship" would exist in one SQL file and
83	nowhere else, with the page's own glossary unable to explain the second number it displays.
84	
85	The fatal objection is narrower. §6: "When a question's two queries disagree, `dab/model.yaml` is
86	the arbiter. The query that departs from the definition is the one that changes." Under (c) the
87	answer query says `date_diff('day', o.placed_on, o.shipped_on)`, the control says
88	`shipped_date - order_date`, and the model has nothing to say about either. Neither query can
89	depart from a definition that does not exist, so the repair procedure stops existing in exactly the
90	slice that introduces the first computed number — and the cheapest repair becomes making the two
91	queries agree with each other, which deletes the only thing the check measures.
92	
93	(c) also computes as of the wrong instant: the peripheral is current state, while a bridge row is
94	the latest version *in which the event's date is set*. Those coincide today. ADR 0006 records a
95	review catching precisely this confusion one layer down, and calls the distinction the entire
96	difference between the option chosen there and the one rejected.
97	
98	### The line this record draws
99	
100	M5 permits an expression that reads its own row, and its prose enumerates three forms — a column,
101	a cast, a `CASE` over columns of that row. A subtraction of two dates is none of them, and passes
102	only because M5's mechanical check is four keywords and seven function names. Relying on that
103	silently is the quiet exception §11 rules out. So the rule, in force from here:
104	
105	> **Arithmetic over columns of the same row is permitted in a mapping.** A `CASE` on *values*, a
106	> default, a coalesce that invents a value, a filter, a bucket, or anything that changes the grain
107	> is not — those are meaning, and meaning belongs in the model as an attribute with a definition.
108	
109	Conventions §1.4 M5 is clarified to say so, per §11's first rung. The distinction is that
110	arithmetic over one row produces a value the row already implies; the others produce a value
111	somebody chose, and a choice needs a definition beside it.
112	
113	One trap belongs in the record because the error message misleads: `extract(DAY FROM (b - a))` is
114	**refused** by M5's checker, because the regex matches the bare word `from` inside the expression.
115	The refusal says the expression "reaches beyond its row", which it does not. `date_diff('day', a,
116	b)` passes and is what the mapping uses. The false refusal is a defect in the checker, fixed in
117	this slice.
118	
119	## Consequences
120	
121	* Good, because the lag has one definition, in the one place the data is explained, and both of the
122	  question's queries are measured against it
123	* Good, because a second source that reports the lag directly maps onto the same attribute rather
124	  than needing a second derivation — which is the slice-6 case that decided this
125	* Good, because slice 4's revenue follows the same rule without a new mechanism: quantity, price
126	  and discount are columns of one order line, and their product is arithmetic over that row
127	* Good, because DAR stays deletable: everything it emits still comes from the model and the sidecar
128	* Bad, because a derived value is now stored, and a stored derivation can disagree with what it was

1	---
2	id: q03
3	slice: 3
4	status: green
5	persona: Operations manager
6	question: How many orders shipped per shipping month, and how many days did they take?
7	aggregation: [count, sum]
8	measure: [ORDER.SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT, ORDER.SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS]
9	dimensions: [_calendar.month_label]
10	time_grain: month
11	defines:
12	  - ORDER.SHIPPED_ON
13	  - ORDER.SHIP_LAG_DAYS
14	  - ORDER.events.SHIPPED
15	  - ORDER.measures.SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT
16	  - ORDER.measures.SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS
17	order_by: [shipping_month]
18	---
19	
20	## Story
21	
22	As the **operations manager**, I want to see how many orders went out each month and how long
23	they waited, so that I can tell whether a busy month is also a slow one — and staff against the
24	answer rather than against a feeling.
25	
26	## Definitions
27	
28	Every term below is defined in `dab/model.yaml` or `dab/uss.yaml` and nowhere else. This
29	question references them; it does not restate them.
30	
31	- {{ORDER.SHIPPED_ON}}
32	- {{ORDER.SHIP_LAG_DAYS}}
33	- {{ORDER.events.SHIPPED}}
34	- {{ORDER.measures.SHIPPED_ORDERS_COUNT}}
35	- {{ORDER.measures.SHIP_LAG_ORDERS_DAYS}}
36	
37	## The W's
38	
39	- **Why**: throughput and speed move together or they do not, and which of the two it is
40	  decides whether the answer is more people or a different process. One number cannot say.
41	- **What**: two additive measures — the count of orders that went out, and the days they spent
42	  waiting, added up. Not an average: see below.
43	- **Who**: the operations manager acts on it; the business ships.
44	- **How**: one `shipped` event per order, on the day the goods left. **An order that has not
45	  shipped has no shipment event at all**, so it is absent rather than counted as a zero-day
46	  order — which would make the slowest orders look like the fastest. 21 of 830 orders are in
47	  that position.
48	- **Where**: not asked. This is a question about time, and adding a geography to it would be
49	  a different question.
50	- **When**: all history, by the month the goods **left** (`_calendar.month_label`, `YYYY-MM`).
51	  An order accepted in one month and shipped in the next belongs to the second.
52	- **What will you do with it**: compare the two lines. A month where the count rises and the
53	  wait rises with it is a capacity problem; a month where the wait rises on its own is not.
54	
55	## Why the answer has no average in it
56	
57	The question asks how many days orders took, and the answer does not contain that number.
58	
59	Conventions §2: *"Ratios are not stored. Store numerator and denominator as additive measures
60	and divide at query time."* Its worked example is this question — `avg_days_to_ship` becomes
61	`ship_lag_orders_days`, and the average is `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)`.
62	An average of averages is wrong at every grain but the one it was computed at, so a stored
63	monthly average could not be re-summed into a quarter. Two additive measures can.
64	
65	There is a second reason, found by measuring rather than by reading. The acceptance check
66	compares the two answers **row by row as values**, which is exact only while every value is
67	exact. A ratio is a `DOUBLE` however it is reached. Both queries agree today because both
68	reduce to one division of two exact integer sums — but float addition is not associative and
69	DuckDB imposes no order on `sum`: `[0.1, 0.2, 0.3]` sums to `0.6000000000000001` and the same
70	three reversed to `0.6`. So the first float-valued measure would let the two queries disagree
71	by a bit, on some machines, some of the time. Keeping the division out of the stored answer
72	keeps this check exact by construction rather than by luck.
73	
74	The page does the division, once, where a reader can see it.
75	
76	## Nulls
77	
78	`shipped_date` is null on 21 orders and that is the whole point of this slice: those orders have
79	no row in the `shipped` stage, by construction rather than by a filter anyone has to remember.
80	The control query mirrors it with `WHERE o.shipped_date IS NOT NULL`.
81	
82	No order in the recording ships before it was accepted, and none has a null order date, so no
83	lag is negative and none is missing on a shipped order. Both queries would carry a null lag
84	through `sum`, which skips it — so a shipped order with no accepted date would be counted and
85	not waited-for, in both answers alike.
86	
87	## Delivered
88	
89	![The answer as it was accepted](answer.png)
90	
91	## Answers
92	
93	Two queries, in `staged.sql` and `uss.sql`. The first computes the answer straight from what
94	the source sent, bypassing the business model and the star schema entirely. The second computes
95	it from the star schema. They must agree row for row — 23 months, 809 orders, 6,870 days.

1	---
2	status: accepted
3	date: 2026-09-08
4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
5	slice: 3
6	---
7	
8	# A measure is owned by an event and named for an entity, so two events on one entity may not name the same measure
9	
10	## Context and Problem Statement
11	
12	Slice 3 is the first slice where one entity has two events: an order is both placed and shipped.
13	That splits two things which have been the same thing until now.
14	
15	A measure's **column** and its **glossary token** are keyed on the entity:
16	
17	```python
18	(event, measure, f"_measure__{event.entity_id.lower()}__{measure.id.lower()}")
19	found[f"{event.entity_id}.measures.{measure.id}"] = measure.definition
20	```
21	
22	Its **ownership** is keyed on the event — `_branch` decides which stage carries a value and which
23	emits a typed null by identity on the event object. So the generator knows exactly which stage owns
24	a measure, and then names it after something else.
25	
26	With one event per entity those keys coincide and nothing can go wrong. With two, declaring the
27	same measure id on both events of one entity is accepted without a word, and produces:
28	
29	- **the same column twice** in the published contract, and
30	- **one definition silently replacing the other** in the glossary.
31	
32	Reproduced on the neutral fixture. The column list came back with
33	`_measure__parent__happened_parents_count` at two positions, and the glossary held the *second*
34	event's definition under the first event's token.
35	
36	The two halves fail very differently. DuckDB does not refuse two columns of one name — measured,
37	`CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT 1 AS a, 2 AS a` yields `a` and `a_1` — so the built table's columns would
38	not match `bridge_columns()` and the contract check would fail the build loudly. That half is safe.
39	
40	**The glossary half is caught by nothing.** No check inspects `definitions()`. That dictionary is
41	what a question's `defines` entries are resolved against, and what the page renders as "What the
42	words mean". So a question could reference a measure, resolve it successfully, and be shown a
43	definition belonging to a different measure — on the page a reader accepts the slice on — while
44	every test and every check passes.
45	
46	Nothing enforces the naming convention that would prevent it either. Conventions §2's three-part
47	pattern is a hard rule, and there is no test anywhere that checks a measure name's shape. The
48	uniqueness of these columns has rested entirely on a rule enforced by reading.
49	
50	## Decision Drivers
51	
52	* a definition that is silently replaced is worse than one that is missing: nothing looks wrong
53	* the failure must be loud where it is invisible, not only where DuckDB happens to complain
54	* a published column contract two consumers are already written against
55	* whatever is decided now is cheapest now, with two questions in existence
56	
57	## Considered Options
58	
59	* Refuse the collision when the declarations are read, and keep the entity in the column name
60	* Rename the column to `_measure__<event>__<measure>` and the token to `<ENTITY>.<EVENT>.measures.<M>`
61	* Do nothing, and rely on §2's naming pattern to keep ids distinct
62	
63	## Decision Outcome
64	
65	Chosen: **refuse the collision when the declarations are read.**
66	
67	Two events on one entity may not declare the same measure id. The refusal names both events and
68	says what would be lost, because the loss is not obvious: a reader who has just been told the
69	column would be duplicated will think of the column, and the definition is the part nothing else
70	would catch.
71	
72	**Why not rename to the event.** It is more correct in principle — the event is what actually owns
73	a measure, so the name should say so — and it is the cheapest it will ever be, with only two
74	questions to update. It is rejected on two counts. It changes a published contract that conventions
75	§1.3 states as a hard rule and ADR 0002 tabulates, in a slice that has no other reason to touch it.
76	And §2's descriptor slot already carries the event: `placed_orders_count`, `shipped_orders_count`.
77	Naming the column for the event too would put it in twice, so the more correct scheme reads worse
78	in every ordinary case in order to disambiguate one that is now refused outright.
79	
80	**Why not do nothing.** §2's pattern makes a collision unlikely, not impossible, and "unlikely" is
81	the wrong guarantee for a failure whose signature is a page showing a plausible sentence about the
82	wrong number. Two events on one entity is exactly where the pattern's descriptor slot stops doing
83	the work — `placed` and `shipped` distinguish the count measures, and nothing forces a third
84	measure to carry a descriptor at all.
85	
86	This follows the shape the repository already uses for the same class of problem: ADR 0006 refuses
87	two edges that would inherit into one key column, for the same reason and with the same argument
88	about what DuckDB silently does instead of raising. A generator that cannot emit a correct artefact
89	should say so rather than emit an ambiguous one.
90	
91	## Consequences
92	
93	* Good, because the glossary can no longer show one measure's definition under another's name,
94	  which was the only failure here that nothing would have reported
95	* Good, because it is a refusal in the same place and the same shape as the one for colliding
96	  edges, so the two read as one rule rather than two special cases
97	* Good, because it costs nothing today: no existing declaration collides, and no column moves
98	* Bad, because it forbids a legitimate-sounding declaration — the same quantity measured at two
99	  events, deliberately, under one name. That would have to be two measures with two definitions,
100	  which is more honest but more typing. If a slice ever wants it, the answer is to rename to the
101	  event, and this record is what it supersedes
102	* Bad, because the deeper mismatch stays: the generator still names by entity what it owns by
103	  event. This narrows the consequence to nothing rather than removing the cause
104	
105	### A correction to ADR 0002
106	
107	The same mismatch makes one sentence of ADR 0002's published column contract false, for the first
108	time, in this slice. `_stage` is defined there as "the entity this row is a row *of*", and
109	`_measure__<entity>__<measure>` is described as "non-null only on the owning stage". With two
110	events on `ORDER` both branches emit `_stage = 'order'`, so all 809 shipped rows share a stage with

13	That splits two things which have been the same thing until now.
14	
15	A measure's **column** and its **glossary token** are keyed on the entity:

22	Its **ownership** is keyed on the event — `_branch` decides which stage carries a value and which
23	emits a typed null by identity on the event object. So the generator knows exactly which stage owns
24	a measure, and then names it after something else.
25	
26	With one event per entity those keys coincide and nothing can go wrong. With two, declaring the
27	same measure id on both events of one entity is accepted without a word, and produces:
28

30	- **one definition silently replacing the other** in the glossary.

37	`CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT 1 AS a, 2 AS a` yields `a` and `a_1` — so the built table's columns would
38	not match `bridge_columns()` and the contract check would fail the build loudly. That half is safe.

47	pattern is a hard rule, and there is no test anywhere that checks a measure name's shape. The
48	uniqueness of these columns has rested entirely on a rule enforced by reading.

50	## Decision Drivers
51	
52	* a definition that is silently replaced is worse than one that is missing: nothing looks wrong
53	* the failure must be loud where it is invisible, not only where DuckDB happens to complain
54	* a published column contract two consumers are already written against
55	* whatever is decided now is cheapest now, with two questions in existence
56	
57	## Considered Options
58	
59	* Refuse the collision when the declarations are read, and keep the entity in the column name
60	* Rename the column to `_measure__<event>__<measure>` and the token to `<ENTITY>.<EVENT>.measures.<M>`
61	* Do nothing, and rely on §2's naming pattern to keep ids distinct

65	Chosen: **refuse the collision when the declarations are read.**
66

68	says what would be lost, because the loss is not obvious: a reader who has just been told the

fix(repo): make the slice's own assertions capable of failing, and its records true

The verification's recurring theme was not wrong code. It was tests and records that could not
have noticed if the code were wrong.

Three mutations to the version CTE -- the piece of SQL that picks which version of an entity an
event is measured on -- left the whole suite green: row_number to rank, DESC to ASC, and adding
the timestamp to the partition, which makes every retained version a bridge row. The three
assertions guarding it were whole-file substrings, every one of which the INHERIT CTE also
satisfies, so they were about a different window than the one they named. And none of it is
visible in the warehouse, because every entity has exactly one version today. That is the
failure mode ADR 0006 warned about in as many words.

Measure ownership was pinned the same way, and slice 3 is the first slice where it matters,
because ORDER now owns four measures across two stages. Deciding ownership by entity rather
than by event emitted a column the branch's own CTE does not have -- SQL that cannot bind --
and the suite stayed green, because the NULL casts the test looked for were still emitted by
some other branch. Rotating the values within a branch while leaving the aliases in contract
order put a count into a sum column, also green. Both are now asserted as value-to-alias pairs,
per branch, per measure.

Two ADR Confirmation sections named tests that could not fail for the reason given. One claimed
the same measure id on two different entities is still accepted; no fixture contained that case,
so keying the refusal on the id alone -- exactly what the record says it must not do -- left the
suite green. The other claimed definitions() returns one entry per measure, while comparing the
declarations with themselves. Both cases exist now, and both mutations are caught. That is left
in the record rather than tidied away: a Confirmation is only as good as what its test
constructs.

The delivered screenshot for slice 1 changed in this slice with no change to its answer. The
heatmap ordered countries by a sort with ties, which is not stable, so the picture a slice was
accepted on moved between runs from identical data -- and a reviewer diffing the PNG could not
tell a re-sorted tie from a new number. Ties break by name now, and three consecutive renders
produce the same bytes.

Also: the new exactness check had no test that could fail, which is the pattern slice 2
established one commit earlier and this one departed from; its predicate is now a named function
with its own tests. The page indexed a third question unconditionally and divided by a count
read from the data, either of which would fail every question's render rather than one. It
stated "twenty-one orders" as prose on the artefact the slice is accepted on; that number is
computed now, like every other number on the page.

And the records. M5 permitted "a CASE over columns of that row" while M5a forbade "a CASE on
values" -- but every CASE is both, so the pair decided nothing and handed back the argument M5a
exists to close; a CASE is always a choice, so it moves to the forbidden side. ADR 0002's
Confirmation still described the with_rel check that slice 2 replaced. ADR 0007's named a test
in the wrong file and described the guarantee as being about types when it is about values.
ADR 0008 now corrects the sentence of ADR 0002 its own mismatch makes false: with two events on
one entity, a measure is non-null only on the owning EVENT, which _stage does not name. The
question's front matter said sum beside a count measure and named one of the two it returns.
And a test asserted over a source column name, which two hard rules forbid and its neighbours
already avoided.
