content.text: Nearly all of those were reproduced against the pre-fix commits and are now closed. Two remain. Let me address the sentinel-date one honestly:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("docs/questions/03-shipped-orders-and-days-to-ship/question.md")
t = p.read_text()
old = """No order in the recording ships before it was accepted, and none has a null order date, so no
lag is negative and none is missing on a shipped order. Both queries would carry a null lag
through `sum`, which skips it — so a shipped order with no accepted date would be counted and
not waited-for, in both answers alike."""
new = """No order in the recording ships before it was accepted, and none has a null order date, so no
lag is negative and none is missing on a shipped order. Both queries would carry a null lag
through `sum`, which skips it — so a shipped order with no accepted date would be counted and
not waited-for, in both answers alike.

**What the absence rests on, exactly.** "Has not shipped" is *the DAB attribute is null*, and
nothing more. That is structural with respect to this system — the filter is generated from the
event's `date_attribute`, so nobody can forget it — but not with respect to the source. An empty
string fails loudly at the cast, which is fine. A **sentinel date** would not fail at all: it
produces a shipment event, and both of this question's queries agree on it, because both derive
from the same sentinel. Its one signature is a lag that is negative or absurd, and nothing here
checks for that; the paragraph above is prose, not a check. Verified by substituting `1900-01-01`
for the 21 nulls in a scratch copy — 830 shipped rows, both queries agreeing, every gate green.
It is recorded rather than guarded because a check would have to know what a plausible lag is,
which is a business fact this model does not yet state."""
assert old in t
p.write_text(t.replace(old, new))
PY

docs(questions): say what "has not shipped" actually rests on

The slice's headline property is that an unshipped order has no shipment row, by construction.
That is true of this system -- the filter is generated from the event's date attribute, so
nobody can forget it -- and the verification asked the sharper question: is it true of the
source?

It is not, and the gap has one shape. "Has not shipped" means the DAB attribute is null and
nothing else. An empty string fails loudly at the cast. A sentinel date does not fail at all: it
produces a shipment event, and both of this question's queries agree on it, because both derive
from the same sentinel. Substituting 1900-01-01 for the 21 nulls in a scratch copy gives 830
shipped rows, two agreeing answers and a green gate.

Its only signature is an absurd lag, and the paragraph claiming there is none was prose rather
than a check. It stays prose, and now says so: a check would have to know what a plausible lag
is, and that is a business fact this model does not state yet. Recording the gap is worth more
than a check that guesses at the threshold.

input.title: Slice 3 — How many orders shipped per shipping month, and how many days did they take?
input.head: claude/adss-slice-03-shipped-orders-and-days-to-ship
input.body: Two events on one entity, and the first number this system reports that the source does not contain. Stacked on slice 2. ## The question > How many orders shipped per shipping month, and how many days did they take? > — asked by the operations manager **809 orders out, 8.5 days each**, across 23 months. **21 orders are missing entirely** because they have never shipped — absent rather than counted as having taken no time. The answer is worth reading: shipping volume roughly doubles through 1998 while days-per-order stays flat near 8. They scaled without slowing down. ## What it widens A **second event on the same entity** — an order is both placed and shipped — so a second stage in the bridge. It needed **no generator change at all**: the neutral fixture has declared two events on one entity since slice 1. This is also the first slice where an event **did not happen** for some entities. ADR 0002 claimed in slice 1 that such an entity has no row "by construction rather than by a filter somebody has to remember". 830 placed rows, 809 shipped rows, zero shipment rows for the 21 — the claim holds, and this is the first slice that could show it. ## The decisions **[ADR 0007](https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/blob/27d76ed/docs/adr/0007-a-derived-value-is-modelled-where-two-vocabularies-are-bound.md) — where a value the source does not contain gets computed.** Two of the three candidate homes turned out not to exist: a sum measure must name an attribute the model declares, so the generator raises on anything else. Between the rest, what decided it was slice 6. Putting the arithmetic in the generator is cleaner — nothing stored can drift — but a second source reporting elapsed days *directly* has no two dates to subtract, so it needs the attribute anyway, and then one number has two definitions differing by source. Computing it in the question fails worse and more quietly: when two queries disagree the model is the arbiter, and if the arithmetic lives only in the queries then **neither can depart from a definition that does not exist**. The repair procedure stops existing in the slice that introduces the first computed number. The precedent is bounded in the record rather than left as an example, because "M5 permits it" would otherwise become the argument for whatever M5's regex happens not to catch — and that regex is four keywords and seven function names. **[ADR 0008](https://github.com/mattiasthalen/adss-2026-09-07/blob/27d76ed/docs/adr/0008-a-measure-is-owned-by-an-event-and-named-for-an-entity.md) — a measure is owned by an event but named for an entity.** With one event each those were the same thing. With two they are not: the same measure id on both events emits one column twice *and* silently replaces one definition with the other in the glossary. The column half fails the build loudly (DuckDB renames the second to `a_1`, so the table stops matching its contract). **The glossary half is caught by nothing** — a page would show a plausible sentence about the wrong number with everything green. Refused now, in the same shape as slice 2's refusal for colliding edges. ## Why the answer has no average in it Conventions §2's own worked example is this question: `avg_days_to_ship` becomes `ship_lag_orders_days`, and the average is `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)` at query time. An average of averages is wrong at every grain but the one it was computed at. There is a second reason, found by measuring. The acceptance check compares two answers **row by row as values**, which is exact only while every value is exact. A ratio is a `DOUBLE` however it is reached — but the hazard is the *sum*, not the division: float addition is not associative and DuckDB imposes no order, so `[0.1, 0.2, 0.3]` sums to `0.6000000000000001` and the same three reversed to `0.6`. The first float-valued measure would let the two queries disagree by a bit, on some machines, some of the time. The page does the division, once, where a reader can see it. ## Two traps that each cost a build - **A YAML flow mapping splits an expression on the commas inside a function call.** `{transformation_expression: date_diff('day', a, b)}` silently becomes `date_diff('day'` plus two junk keys. No YAML error, and the M5 checker accepted the truncation because it still reads its own row. Second slice this has cost — `DECIMAL(18, 4)` was the first — so it is refused now by the one signature it always leaves. The check caught the mapping I had just written. - **The page renders a concatenated altair chart as nothing at all.** Spec builds, widget builds, cell does not fail, picture simply absent. That matters because the picture is the record of what was delivered. ## Verification Six lenses, then every finding attacked by an agent trying to kill it. The recomputation lens **accepted** the numbers. The layering lens **refused the slice**, and on the sharpest possible grounds: my own fix for M5's false refusal had opened a hole in M5. **The blocking finding.** Blanking `extract(DAY FROM …)` was right; blanking it by discarding the whole argument list was not — a subquery hidden inside one of those calls became invisible, so a reach into another table was accepted where it had been refused an hour earlier. The scan also counted raw parentheses, so a bracket in a string literal unbalanced it and silently discarded the rest of the expression. Taking simply the *next* `FROM` instead is no better, which I only found by attacking my own replacement: in `trim(a) FROM elsewhere` the next one is the reach. It now finds the first `FROM` at the call's own bracket depth, gives up at the closing bracket, and steps over quoted text — every clause pinned by a case that fails without it, which took three rounds because the first cases only exercised awkward text *after* the keyword, where none of the clauses matter. **The recurring theme was assertions that could not fail.** Not wrong code — tests and records that would not have noticed if the code were wrong: - Three mutations to the **version CTE** left the suite green: `row_number`→`rank`, `DESC`→`ASC`, and adding the timestamp to the partition (which makes every retained version a bridge row). The guards were whole-file substrings that the *inherit* CTE also satisfies, so they were about a different window than the one they named — and none of it is visible in the warehouse, because every entity has one version today. Exactly what ADR 0006 warned about. - **Measure ownership** was pinned the same way, and this is the first slice where it matters, because `ORDER` now owns four measures across two stages. Deciding ownership by entity rather than event emitted a column the branch's own CTE does not have — SQL that cannot bind — and stayed green. So did rotating values within a branch, putting a count into a sum column. - **Two ADR Confirmation sections named tests that could not fail for the reason given.** One claimed the same measure id on two different entities is accepted; no fixture contained that case, so keying the refusal on the id alone — what the record explicitly forbids — left the suite green. The other compared the declarations with themselves. Both cases exist now, both mutations caught, and the record says so rather than tidying it away. - **Slice 1's delivered screenshot changed in this slice with no change to its answer.** The heatmap ordered countries by a sort with ties, which is not stable, so the picture a slice was accepted on moved between runs from identical data. Ties break by name now; three consecutive renders produce identical bytes. ## Known, and recorded rather than fixed - **`extract(DAY FROM b - a)` used to be refused with a wrong reason** — the checker matched the bare word `from` and told you the expression reached beyond its row. A refusal whose stated reason is wrong sends someone looking for a problem that is not there. - **"Has not shipped" means the DAB attribute is null, and nothing more.** Structural with respect to this system, not with respect to the source: an empty string fails loudly, but a **sentinel date** produces a shipment event that both queries agree on, because both derive from the same sentinel. Verified — `1900-01-01` for the 21 nulls gives 830 shipped rows and a green gate. Its only signature is an absurd lag, and that stays prose rather than a check, because a check would have to know what a plausible lag is and the model does not say yet. - **A process failure of mine.** ADR 0008 landed in the *same commit* as the code it decides, typed `docs`. The rule is that an ADR lands before its code, and ADR 0007 did. I am not rewriting history to hide it. - **D-0001 is still carried on assertion.** Both stages here are on one entity at one grain, so nothing can multiply. Slice 4 is where the fan-out proof becomes possible. ```bash uv run adss build # the whole system from the recording, offline uv run adss check # 24 checks, all green ``` ## Next Slice 4: *what revenue did we take per order month?* — a third entity at a **finer grain**, a derived measure, and the fan-out proof that freight must not multiply across an order's lines. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_019rspwWhmXfxoTvKg5jmNWh

content.text:
Slice 4 is framed and running. It turns out to carry more than the plan anticipated — three things land at once, and I found two of them by reading the source metadata rather than the plan:

**The fan-out proof.** This is the one the architecture has been deferring to since slice 1. D-0001 puts every process in one shared `dar__uss`, departing from a DAR principle, and its entire justification is that a measure cannot multiply across a many-to-one walk. Slices 1–3 couldn't test it — every entity sat at one grain. Order lines are finer than orders, so freight and revenue become the first two measures at different grains in one bridge. The deviations register says in as many words that this is where the argument stops being carried on assertion.

**A composite source key.** `OrderDetails` is keyed on `(OrderId, ProductId)`. Convention M2 permits exactly one `primary_keys` entry and allows "a concat of casts with a separator", warning that a concat *without* one makes `'A1'+'23'` and `'A12'+'3'` the same key. That clause has been review-only since slice 1 because nothing had a composite key — and with integer ids the collision is live: order 121 product 3 versus order 12 product 13.

**A float in the source.** `Discount` is `Edm.Single`, and revenue is quantity × price × (1 − discount). # DECISION B — how the fan-out proof is actually made

## B.1 The two queries, on the real two-grain bridge

Ground truth, straight from `das__staged`, bypassing both layers: freight **64,942.69**, revenue **1,265,793.0395**, 2155 lines, 830 orders.

**What the bridge returns — every shape I could think of:**

```
sum(freight measure) over the WHOLE bridge, no filter        64942.69000000   ✓
sum(revenue measure) over the WHOLE bridge, no filter      1265793.03950000   ✓
both at once, one scan, no filter, no join                 64942.69 / 1265793.0395   ✓
both per order month, joined to _calendar (3794 rows)      64942.69 / 1265793.0395   ✓
```

That is the first demonstration in this repository's history of the property `ADR 0002:61-64` states and `deviations.md:19` is carried on. 2155 line rows carry `order_key`, and freight does not move.

**The query that COULD multiply — and does.** It is not a self-join anyone would be ashamed of; it is one join, and the join is the same one q01 and q02 already write:

```sql
SELECT cast(sum(o.freight_charge) AS DECIMAL(28,8))
FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
INNER JOIN dar__uss."order" AS o ON b.order_key = o.order_key
WHERE b._event = 'ordered';
-- 207306.10000000  against a true 64942.69.  3.19x, once per LINE.
```

`freight_charge` is a **published column of the order peripheral** (`dar/uss/order.sql:11`), and `revenue` is likewise published on the line peripheral. Three more measurements:

| query | freight | rows |
|---|---|---|
| bridge ⨝ order peripheral, `_event='ordered'`, sum the **attribute** | **207,306.10** | 2155 |
| bridge ⨝ bridge on `order_key` (placed × ordered) | **207,306.10** (revenue correct — half right, which is worse) | 2155 |
| bridge ⨝ order peripheral, no event filter, sum the **attribute** | **336,203.81** | 3794 |
| same shape, sum the **measure column** | **64,942.69** ✓ | 3794 |

**This was already live at slice 3** and nobody noticed. On the untouched warehouse: `sum(o.freight_charge)` over `_bridge ⨝ order` with two events is **128,897.71** against 64,942.69. Slice 4 does not introduce the trap; it makes it 3.19× instead of 1.98× and, for the first time, reachable *from another entity's stage*, which is what "fan trap" actually means.

## B.2 The test — it belongs in `tests/`, and here it is

`conventions.md:176` puts machinery in `tests/` as "pure functions over data files. No warehouse, no network, no binary", and checks in `checks/` as "assertions about what the built warehouse actually contains". The fan-out property is a property of the **generator**, not of the data, so it is machinery. The precedent for running SQL there already exists: `tests/test_relationship_checks.py:35-53` fabricates `dab."v_<edge>"` and `dar__uss._bridge` in a scratch DuckDB, and `tests/test_das_executes.py:3-5` says in as many words that a machinery test may build "a synthetic lake it builds itself". §6's stub prohibition (`conventions.md:187`) is aimed at *data checks*, not at these.

And the neutral fixture is already the shape ADR 0002 promised: `tests/fixtures/dab/model.yaml` has PARENT (with `SIZE_PARENTS_UNITS`) and CHILD (with `WEIGHT_CHILDREN_UNITS`) on a `CHILD_POINTS_AT_PARENT` edge. Nothing new is needed.

Drafted, written to `…/s4/test_fan_out.py`, and **run**: 4 passed.

```python

B.3 Is the property true of the design, or only of the data?

**True of the design, for the measure columns.** `src/adss/uss.py:345-348` decides ownership by event identity and emits `cast(NULL AS <sql_type>)` on every other branch; `_stage_cte` (`:314-322`) joins only CTEs that are one row per inheriting row, so no join in the bridge can fan out. That is structural, not incidental.

**False for the peripherals**, and that is the shape in which it fails — measured above at 207,306.10 and 336,203.81. State it plainly:

> Any `NUMBER` attribute that is also a measure's source appears **twice** in `dar__uss` — once as an additive measure on its owning stage, once as a plain attribute on its peripheral. Only the first is protected. `FREIGHT_CHARGE`, `SHIP_LAG_DAYS` and `REVENUE` are all in that position today.

There is a second shape, which is why D5 below matters: because the walk is one hop, an entity two edges away carries `NULL`, and a reader who joins around that null through the peripherals reconstructs the fan by hand.

## B.4 What stops a bad reader — and D-0001's status

Nothing does. A bridge does not stop a bad query; it makes the good query natural, and the honest form of that claim is narrower than it sounds:

- `sum(_measure__…)` is right at **every** shape I could construct, including no filter and a peripheral join. That is a strong \"natural\".
- `sum(<peripheral>.<attribute>)` is wrong at any shape with more than one bridge row per entity — which is now every shape, because ORDER has two events *and* an inbound edge.
- `conventions.md:137` (\"No `SELECT *` in anything a consumer reads\") makes the wrong column something a reader had to type deliberately. `ADR 0002:112-114` already publishes two query-time rules; neither covers this one.

**My recommendation: D-0001 does not close.** Its exit condition (`deviations.md:19`) is *\"A second consumer needs isolation\"*, and that has not happened — closing it now on the strength of a demonstration would be closing it for a reason that is not its own exit condition. But the review clause (`deviations.md:44-53`) says an open entry is checked \"against whether its argument is still being carried on assertion\", and after this slice it is not: the argument is demonstrated by `test_fan_out.py` and by six data checks. So the entry's **Why** column should be edited to say the property is proved and to name what it does *not* cover — the peripheral's attribute columns — and a third query-time rule should be added to `ADR 0002`'s contract section:

> A number on a peripheral is that e

DECISION C — the float discount

## C.1 What type DAS should give it, and where the float stops

`Edm.Single` is a 32-bit float. The contract vocabulary (`src/adss/contract.py:23-38`) has `DOUBLE` and `DECIMAL` and no `REAL`/`FLOAT`, so neither candidate is a transcription of `Edm.Single`; both are a choice.

**Verified: a `NUMBER` attribute is `DECIMAL(28,8)`.** The dab skill's claim (`SKILL.md:81`) holds at every layer of the engine — `dab.\"view_ORDER_LINE_hist\"` gives `QUANTITY`, `UNIT_PRICE`, `DISCOUNT_RATE`, `REVENUE` all `DECIMAL(28,8)`; so do `dab.ORDER_LINE_desc.val_num` and every `dab__stage.type_*` table.

**The float stops at `dab__stage.type_reader.val_num` / `dab.<E>_desc.val_num` — a `DECIMAL(28,8)` column, coerced silently by the engine.** Nobody in this repository wrote that cast and nothing names it. I proved it by building the whole slice twice, once with `discount: DOUBLE` and once with `discount: DECIMAL(18,4)`:

| | DECIMAL build | DOUBLE build |
|---|---|---|
| `das__staged.order_details.discount` | `DECIMAL(18,4)` | `DOUBLE` |
| `dab…hist.DISCOUNT_RATE` | `DECIMAL(28,8)` | `DECIMAL(28,8)` |
| distinct `discount_rate` in DAR | `0E-8 … 0.25000000` | **byte-identical** |
| per-line `revenue` rows differing | — | **0 of 2155** |
| q04 control vs answer | agree | agree |

## C.2 Is the product exact?

`typeof(quantity * unit_price * (1 - discount))` is `DECIMAL(18,8)` when the discount is decimal, `DOUBLE` when it is not. Landing either into `DECIMAL(28,8)` is a widening today.

**On this data, exact either way.** Revenue uses at most **4** decimal places (1243 lines at 0 dp, … 21 lines at 4 dp; widest `929.09250000`). `DECIMAL(28,8)` holds every value with four places to spare, and the DOUBLE path's error (~1e-12 at these magnitudes) is absorbed by the 1e-8 quantum.

**Not exact in general, and I found the boundary.** Same expression, larger magnitude:

```
97 * 1234567.8901 * (1 - 0.06)
  via DOUBLE  -> 112567900.21931798
  via DECIMAL -> 112567900.21931800     <- they differ
```

**Order-dependence, measured on the real revenue values as DOUBLEs:**

```
ORDER BY order_id, product_id            -> 1265793.0395000004
ORDER BY product_id DESC, order_id DESC  -> 1265793.0394999993
ORDER BY unit_price, quantity            -> 1265793.0395000007
```

Three orders, three answers. `ADR 0007:151-152`'s `[0.1, 0.2, 0.3]` witness also still reproduces on DuckDB 1.5.5 (`0.6000000000000001` forward, `0.6` reversed, from a table with an `ORDER BY` — it constant-folds if written as a literal list). So the ADR is right and slice 4 supplies a much better witness: the failure it predicts is live on this slice's own measure.

## C.3 Does slice 3's exactness check catch it? At which layer?

**No — not as the question would naturally be written.** `inexact()` (`src/adss/checks.py:38-47`) inspects *returned values*, and it is applied to both answers in `run_checks` (`:183`). Both sides launder the float:

- the **answer** side is always `DECIMAL(28,8)`, because DAB widens `NUMBER` and `_version_cte` casts to `SUM_TYPE` — so a float can never reach it, whatever DAS does;
- the **control** side reads `das__staged` where the discount would be `DOUBLE`, but every existing control query already wraps the sum in `cast(… AS DECIMAL(28,8))` (`02/staged.sql:7`, `03/staged.sql:6`), which converts the float to a `Decimal` before `inexact()` ever sees it.

Measured, with the DOUBLE contract:

```
control with the cast, answer from the bridge:  agree row for row = True,  inexact() = []
control WITHOUT the cast:                       inexact() = ['float'],  first row ('1996-07', 27861.894999999997)
```

So the check fires **only if the question's author omits a cast**, which is a coin flip. It is not a defence against a float in the source; it is a defence against a float in an answer. `ADR 0007`'s Confirmation is accurate about this (\"it fails on the *values* returned rather than on a column's declared type\") — the point for slice 4 is that the values are laundered twice before they get there, so the check is silent on the very hazard this slice was expected to trip it on.

**There is a second, sharper asymmetry the check also cannot see.** The two sides round at *different points*: the control sums doubles over a month then rounds once; the answer rounds each line at the DAB landing then sums exactly. On this data those coincide, row for row, on all 23 months. They are not the same operation, and at C.2's magnitudes they diverge.

| `NaN` in the payload | `Conversion Error: Could not

# Slice 4 pre-flight audit — what already binds, and what it breaks

Baseline verified: `pytest` 169 passed, `adss check` all PASS (24 findings), against `warehouse.duckdb` as committed.

**H1 — a line has no date, and the generator can only date a stage by an attribute of its own entity.** This is a blocker, not a wrinkle. Verified by construction against a scratch copy of the model:

```

`read_uss` → `_refuse_measures_of_things_that_are_not_numbers` does `entity = model.entity(event.entity_id); entity.attribute(event.date_attribute_id)` (`src/adss/uss.py:210-214`), and `Entity.attribute` raises a bare `KeyError` (`src/adss/model.py:72`) — not a `UssError`, so the failure has no explanation attached to it. `_version_cte` then dates the row `cast(revision.\"<DATE>\" AS DATE)` from that same entity's history view (`uss.py:223-252`). The walk inherits **keys only** and is **one hop** (`_stage_cte`, `uss.py:295-326`, iterating `model.edges_from(entity.id)`); it never carries a date.

The source confirms there is nothing to map from — live `$metadata`, fetched just now:

```xml
<EntityType Name=\"OrderDetail\">
  <Key><PropertyRef Name=\"OrderId\"/><PropertyRef Name=\"ProductId\"/></Key>
  <Property Name=\"OrderId\" Type=\"Edm.Int32\"/><Property Name=\"ProductId\" Type=\"Edm.Int32\"/>
  <Property Name=\"UnitPrice\" Type=\"Edm.Decimal\" Nullable=\"false\" Scale=\"Variable\"/>
  <Property Name=\"Quantity\" Type=\"Edm.Int16\" Nullable=\"false\"/>
  <Property Name=\"Discount\" Type=\"Edm.Single\" Nullable=\"false\"/>
```

No date. And none of the three layers may go and get one: M1 forbids a join or subquery in `table:`; M5 forbids \"a reach into another table\" (`conventions.md:88,92`); a DAS contract has no key for an expression or a join (`contract.py:43-45`, ADR 0003). A second mapped table on the ORDER_LINE entity cannot help either — it would be keyed by `order_id`, which is not a line.

|---|---|
| generator learns to date a stage by a date reached along the walk | new DAR mechanism, new neutral fixture, new ADR — **exactly** what ADR 0007 refused to put in this slice: *\"It also costs slice 4, where the expression vocabulary would have to grow … in the same slice that first exercises the fan-out property D-0001 is carried on. | question joins `dar__uss.\"order\"` and groups on `o.placed_on`, no calendar | the line event still needs *some* non-null date, so this does not actually escape; and ADR 0007 rejected the peripheral-as-of-now reasoning explicitly (`0007…md:93-96`) |

Whatever is chosen, it must be decided and recorded **before** the code (`conventions.md:202`), and slice 5 (\"line to product to category\", `questions/README.md:21`) inherits it.

**H2 — D-0001's exit condition cannot be met by slice 4.** Detail in §1 below.

**H3 — the composite-key collision the brief calls \"live\" is invisible in this data.** Measured over all 2155 real order lines: distinct keys *with* a separator = 2155; distinct keys *without* = 2155. OrderIds are 10248–11077 (five digits), ProductIds 1–77 (one or two), so no collision is reachable. A separator-less key passes every gate, every data check and both acceptance queries. Detail in §3.

Every knowing departure from a principle in [blueprint.md](blueprint.md) or a hard rule in

The register exists because an unregistered exception is indistinguishable from a mistake. Once

content.text:
The frame found a blocker the plan didn't anticipate, and it needs your call before I build.

**An order line has no date.** `OrderDetail` carries only `OrderId`, `ProductId`, `UnitPrice`, `Quantity`, `Discount` — verified against the live `$metadata`. The generator can only date a stage by an attribute of the stage's own entity (`KeyError: ORDER_LINE has no attribute 'PLACED_ON'`), and no layer may go and fetch one: M1 forbids a join in a mapping's `table:`, M5 forbids a reach into another table, and a DAS contract has no key for a join. So "revenue per order month" can't be built as briefed.

Two other things the frame established that you should know before choosing:

**The fan trap is already live, at slice 3, and nothing caught it.** On the warehouse as it stands, `sum(o.freight_charge)` over `_bridge ⨝ order` returns **128,897.71** against a true 64,942.69. That isn't a contrived query — it's the same join q01 and q02 already write, and `freight_charge` is a published column of the order peripheral. The bridge protects the *measure* column structurally; it does not protect the *attribute* column published beside it. Every `NUMBER` that is also a measure's source is in that position: freight, ship lag, and revenue when it lands.

**D-0001 will not close in slice 4.** Its exit condition is "a second consumer needs isolation", and a fourth persona reading the same page isn't that. What changes is that its argument stops being carried on assertion — I have a fan-out test that I mutation-killed (150.75 → 501.50, and moving with the child count).

questions.question: An order line has no date of its own, so the bridge can't date its stage. How should slice 4 get one?

options.label: Generator dates along the walk (recommended)
options.description: The bridge already walks many-to-one edges to inherit keys; it would carry the parent's event date along that same walk, so an ORDER_LINE stage is dated by the order's PLACED_ON. This is Puppini's standard pattern — a line belongs to the order process and takes its date. One definition, one home: PLACED_ON stays on ORDER. Cost: a new DAR mechanism in the slice that also carries the fan-out proof, which ADR 0007 warned against — though its warning was about growing an *expression* vocabulary, and dating is narrower and reuses the existing walk. Slices 5 and 6 inherit it.

options.label: Record the order date onto the line in DAS
options.description: Recording OrderDetails with $expand=Order so the landed line record carries the order's date, then mapping it to an ORDER_LINE attribute. No generator change at all. Cost: a new contract capability ($expand, plus an Endpoint field), and it lands the same fact twice — ORDER.PLACED_ON and ORDER_LINE.ORDERED_ON would be two definitions of one thing, which is the smell B8 exists to prevent, in the layer B8 governs.

options.label: Change the question so a line needs no date
options.description: Re-cut slice 4 to ask something an order line can date itself, or move revenue onto the ORDER stage. Cost: revenue is a line-grain fact, so putting it on the order means pre-aggregating in DAB, which B5 forbids — and the finer grain is the entire point of this slice, since it is what makes the fan-out proof possible at all. I think this loses the slice.

questions.question: The bridge protects measure columns but not the same number published as a peripheral attribute. What should I do about it?

options.label: Stop publishing it, and record why (recommended)
options.description: A NUMBER attribute that is a measure's source stops appearing on its peripheral — it is already in the bridge as a protected measure, so the peripheral copy adds nothing but a way to get a wrong number. Removes the trap by construction rather than by asking readers to be careful. Cost: it changes the published peripheral contract, and a reader wanting the per-order freight of one order has to read the bridge.

options.label: Keep it, add a query-time rule and a check
options.description: Leave the attribute published, add a third query-time rule to ADR 0002 ('a number on a peripheral is that row's own, and summing it across bridge rows multiplies it'), and generate a data check per measure. Cost: the trap stays reachable — a bridge makes the good query natural, it cannot make the bad one impossible — and the rule is enforced by reading.

options.label: Record it and leave it for now
options.description: Write it into ADR 0002 and the deviations register as a known, measured hole, and decide in a later slice. Cost: the wrong number stays one plausible join away, and it is already reachable today.

20	## Story
21	
22	As the **operations manager**, I want to see how many orders went out each month and how long
23	they waited, so that I can tell whether a busy month is also a slow one — and staff against the
24	answer rather than against a feeling.
25

27	
28	Every term below is defined in `dab/model.yaml` or `dab/uss.yaml` and nowhere else. This
29	question references them; it does not restate them.
30	
31	- {{ORDER.SHIPPED_ON}}

37	## The W's
38	
39	- **Why**: throughput and speed move together or they do not, and which of the two it is
40	  decides whether the answer is more people or a different process. One number cannot say.

4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]

8	# A measure is owned by an event and named for an entity, so two events on one entity may not name the same measure
9	
10	## Context and Problem Statement
11	
12	Slice 3 is the first slice where one entity has two events: an order is both placed and shipped.
13	That splits two things which have been the same thing until now.
14	
15	A measure's **column** and its **glossary token** are keyed on the entity:
16	
17	```python
18	(event, measure, f"_measure__{event.entity_id.lower()}__{measure.id.lower()}")
19	found[f"{event.entity_id}.measures.{measure.id}"] = measure.definition
20	```
21	
22	Its **ownership** is keyed on the event — `_branch` decides which stage carries a value and which
23	emits a typed null by identity on the event object. So the generator knows exactly which stage owns
24	a measure, and then names it after something else.
25	
26	With one event per entity those keys coincide and nothing can go wrong. With two, declaring the
27	same measure id on both events of one entity is accepted without a word, and produces:
28	
29	- **the same column twice** in the published contract, and
30	- **one definition silently replacing the other** in the glossary.
31	
32	Reproduced on the neutral fixture. The column list came back with
33	`_measure__parent__happened_parents_count` at two positions, and the glossary held the *second*
34	event's definition under the first event's token.
35	
36	The two halves fail very differently. DuckDB does not refuse two columns of one name — measured,
37	`CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT 1 AS a, 2 AS a` yields `a` and `a_1` — so the built table's columns would
38	not match `bridge_columns()` and the contract check would fail the build loudly. That half is safe.
39	
40	**The glossary half is caught by nothing.** No check inspects `definitions()`. That dictionary is
41	what a question's `defines` entries are resolved against, and what the page renders as "What the
42	words mean". So a question could reference a measure, resolve it successfully, and be shown a
43	definition belonging to a different measure — on the page a reader accepts the slice on — while
44	every test and every check passes.
45	
46	Nothing enforces the naming convention that would prevent it either. Conventions §2's three-part
47	pattern is a hard rule, and there is no test anywhere that checks a measure name's shape. The
48	uniqueness of these columns has rested entirely on a rule enforced by reading.
49	
50	## Decision Drivers
51	
52	* a definition that is silently replaced is worse than one that is missing: nothing looks wrong
53	* the failure must be loud where it is invisible, not only where DuckDB happens to complain
54	* a published column contract two consumers are already written against
55	* whatever is decided now is cheapest now, with two questions in existence
56	
57	## Considered Options
58	
59	* Refuse the collision when the declarations are read, and keep the entity in the column name
60	* Rename the column to `_measure__<event>__<measure>` and the token to `<ENTITY>.<EVENT>.measures.<M>`
61	* Do nothing, and rely on §2's naming pattern to keep ids distinct
62	
63	## Decision Outcome
64	
65	Chosen: **refuse the collision when the declarations are read.**
66	
67	Two events on one entity may not declare the same measure id. The refusal names both events and
68	says what would be lost, because the loss is not obvious: a reader who has just been told the
69	column would be duplicated will think of the column, and the definition is the part nothing else
70	would catch.
71	
72	**Why not rename to the event.** It is more correct in principle — the event is what actually owns
73	a measure, so the name should say so — and it is the cheapest it will ever be, with only two
74	questions to update. It is rejected on two counts. It changes a published contract that conventions
75	§1.3 states as a hard rule and ADR 0002 tabulates, in a slice that has no other reason to touch it.
76	And §2's descriptor slot already carries the event: `placed_orders_count`, `shipped_orders_count`.
77	Naming the column for the event too would put it in twice, so the more correct scheme reads worse
78	in every ordinary case in order to disambiguate one that is now refused outright.
79	
80	**Why not do nothing.** §2's pattern makes a collision unlikely, not impossible, and "unlikely" is
81	the wrong guarantee for a failure whose signature is a page showing a plausible sentence about the
82	wrong number. Two events on one entity is exactly where the pattern's descriptor slot stops doing
83	the work — `placed` and `shipped` distinguish the count measures, and nothing forces a third
84	measure to carry a descriptor at all.
85	
86	This follows the shape the repository already uses for the same class of problem: ADR 0006 refuses
87	two edges that would inherit into one key column, for the same reason and with the same argument
88	about what DuckDB silently does instead of raising. A generator that cannot emit a correct artefact
89	should say so rather than emit an ambiguous one.
90	
91	## Consequences
92	
93	* Good, because the glossary can no longer show one measure's definition under another's name,
94	  which was the only failure here that nothing would have reported
95	* Good, because it is a refusal in the same place and the same shape as the one for colliding
96	  edges, so the two read as one rule rather than two special cases
97	* Good, because it costs nothing today: no existing declaration collides, and no column moves
98	* Bad, because it forbids a legitimate-sounding declaration — the same quantity measured at two
99	  events, deliberately, under one name. That would have to be two measures with two definitions,
100	  which is more honest but more typing. If a slice ever wants it, the answer is to rename to the
101	  event, and this record is what it supersedes
102	* Bad, because the deeper mismatch stays: the generator still names by entity what it owns by
103	  event. This narrows the consequence to nothing rather than removing the cause
104	
105	### A correction to ADR 0002
106	
107	The same mismatch makes one sentence of ADR 0002's published column contract false, for the first
108	time, in this slice. `_stage` is defined there as "the entity this row is a row *of*", and
109	`_measure__<entity>__<measure>` is described as "non-null only on the owning stage". With two
110	events on `ORDER` both branches emit `_stage = 'order'`, so all 809 shipped rows share a stage with
111	the placed rows while carrying a null `_measure__order__placed_orders_count`. The column is
112	non-null only on the owning **event**, which `_event` names and `_stage` does not. The contract's
113	behaviour is right; that sentence describing it is not.
114	
115	## Confirmation
116	
117	`tests/test_uss.py` asserts that two events on one entity declaring one measure id are refused,
118	and that the same id on two *different* entities is still accepted — which is the case the
119	refusal must not catch, since `_measure__<entity>__` already distinguishes those.
120	
121	A second test asserts that `definitions()` returns one entry per declared measure, counting what
122	the glossary returns rather than the declarations twice, so a silent overwrite fails on the count
123	rather than on somebody reading a page carefully. That is the assertion that would have caught
124	this, and it did not exist.
125	
126	Both of these were written wrong the first time and a review caught them, which is worth leaving in
127	the record: the first named an acceptance case no fixture contained, and the second compared a list
128	with itself. A Confirmation section that names a test is only as good as what the test actually
129	constructs, and neither of these could have failed for the reason it was written down for.

9

11	
12	"How many days did they take" is the first number this system reports that does not exist in the
13	source. Every measure so far has been a count — one per row — or a sum of a single attribute that
14	was already there. A ship lag is two dates subtracted, and there is no established place to put
15	the subtraction.
16	
17	Three things are already settled and an argument that reopens them has not read the standard.
18	
19	**The measure's name and its arithmetic are written down.** Conventions §2's own worked example is
20	this question:
21	
22	> | `avg_days_to_ship` | `ship_lag_orders_days` | The average is
23	> `sum(ship_lag_orders_days) / sum(shipped_orders_count)` at query time, from two additive
24	> measures. |
25	
26	So the two measures are named, the division is a question's job, and `ship_lag_orders_days` is a
27	*stored measure* — a column in the bridge's published contract. That sentence decides more of this
28	slice than anything else in the repository.
29	
30	**An event that did not happen is already decided.** ADR 0002: "A transaction stage reads
31	`dab.view_<E>_hist`, keeps the latest version in which the event's date is set… An unshipped order

37	entity since slice 1, and generating this slice's bridge from a scratch copy of the model needs
38	**no generator change at all**. What is new is one thing only: a sum measure with no attribute to
39	point at.

58	because "M5 permits it" is otherwise the standing argument for whatever M5's regex happens not to
59	catch.

62	declares; `src/adss/uss.py` raises `KeyError: "ORDER has no attribute …"` otherwise, and there is
63	no `expression:` field on a measure. (b) and (c) are not choices between working designs — they
64	are proposals to build something.

67	one respect: nothing derived is stored, so nothing derived can drift. It fails on where it leaves
68	slice 6. A second source that reports elapsed days *directly* has no two dates for a DAR expression
69	to subtract, so integrating it needs the attribute anyway — and then there are two definitions of
70	ship lag, a DAB attribute and a DAR expression, differing by source. That is B2 and B8 failing
71	together in the slice whose entire purpose is to prove B2. It also costs slice 4, where the
72	expression vocabulary would have to grow from a two-date special case to general arithmetic in the
73	same slice that first exercises the fan-out property D-0001 is carried on. Two risky things at once.

75	A free-text SQL expression in YAML additionally breaks §3 — "SQL that lives in a Python string is
76	written to a file so the same linter sees it" — because the linter runs on `.sql` files and would
77	never see it.

90	slice that introduces the first computed number — and the cheapest repair becomes making the two
91	queries agree with each other, which deletes the only thing the check measures.

95	review catching precisely this confusion one layer down, and calls the distinction the entire
96	difference between the option chosen there and the one rejected.

102	only because M5's mechanical check is four keywords and seven function names. Relying on that
103	silently is the quiet exception §11 rules out. So the rule, in force from here:

106	> default, a coalesce that invents a value, a filter, a bucket, or anything that changes the grain
107	> is not — those are meaning, and meaning belongs in the model as an attribute with a definition.

109	Conventions §1.4 M5 is clarified to say so, per §11's first rung. The distinction is that
110	arithmetic over one row produces a value the row already implies; the others produce a value

117	always a choice.

120	**refused** by M5's checker, because the regex matches the bare word `from` inside the expression.

122	b)` passes and is what the mapping uses. The false refusal is a defect in the checker, fixed in
123	this slice.

128	  question's queries are measured against it
129	* Good, because a second source that reports the lag directly maps onto the same attribute rather
130	  than needing a second derivation — which is the slice-6 case that decided this

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.

Use when starting work on this repository, adding a slice or a business question, deciding which layer a change belongs in, or when a change seems to need two layers at once.

- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. input.content:
---
status: accepted
date: 2026-09-08
decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
slice: 4
---

# A stage may be dated by a date it inherits along the walk, named where it is inherited from

## Context and Problem Statement

Slice 4 asks for revenue per order **month**. Revenue is measured on an order line — quantity
times price less discount — so the bridge needs a row per line. And **an order line has no
date.** The source's `OrderDetail` has five properties and not one of them is a date; the live
`$metadata` says so, and there is nothing to map from.

The generator can only date a stage by an attribute of the event's own entity. `read_uss`
resolves `date_attribute` against `model.entity(event.entity_id)`, so naming the order's date on
a line event fails with a bare `KeyError: "ORDER_LINE has no attribute 'PLACED_ON'"` — not even a
`UssError`, so the refusal arrives with no explanation attached.

Nor may any layer go and fetch one. M1 forbids a join or a subquery in a mapping's `table:`; M5
forbids a reach into another table; a DAS contract has no key for a join. A second mapped table
on `ORDER_LINE` would be keyed by the order, which is not a line.

So the question the plan wrote down for this slice cannot be built at all without deciding
something the plan did not anticipate.

**What is already true, and is the whole reason this is small.** The walk exists. For every
edge, `_inherit_cte` already resolves the parent **as of the observation time of the row that
inherits** and puts the parent's key on the child's bridge row. ADR 0006 spent its whole decision
on getting that instant right. A date is another column of the row the walk already found.

This is also what a Unified Star Schema does. Puppini's bridge is a row per measurement event;
the event for an order line is the order being placed, on the day it was placed. Dating a line by
its order's date is not an accommodation — it is what the shape means.

## Decision Drivers

* the question is answerable at all, which today it is not
* a bridge row is true as of one instant, and every column on it is true as of that same instant
* a mechanism that already exists, extended, rather than a second one beside it
* the date a reader sees is traceable to a definition in the one place data is explained
* slice 5 walks two hops, and must not need a third mechanism

## Considered Options

* **(a)** The date inherits along the walk, named as `<ENTITY>.<ATTRIBUTE>` in the sidecar
* **(b)** Record `OrderDetails?$expand=Order` so the landed line carries the order's date
* **(c)** Give `ORDER_LINE` its own date attribute, mapped from the order via the source
* **(d)** Drop the calendar and let the question group on the order peripheral's date

## Decision Outcome

Chosen: **(a), the date inherits along the walk**, written in `dab/uss.yaml` as

```yaml
    - id: ORDERED
      entity: ORDER_LINE
      date_attribute: ORDER.PLACED_ON      # qualified: inherited along the edge to ORDER
```

An unqualified `date_attribute` still means an attribute of the event's own entity, which is
every event declared so far and stays the ordinary case. A qualified one names the entity the
date is inherited from, and that entity must be reachable along a declared edge from the event's
entity — otherwise it is refused, by name, with the edges that do exist listed.

The date is resolved **in the same CTE and at the same instant as the key**, because they are the
same row of the same parent. Anything else would put two instants on one bridge row, which is the
confusion ADR 0006 calls the entire difference between the option it chose and the one it
rejected. A line whose order cannot be resolved gets a null date and therefore no bridge row, by
the filter the generator already emits — consistent with how an event that did not happen is
already handled.

**Why not (b), expanding the source record.** It is the cheap-looking one and it is the worst.
`PLACED_ON` would then have two homes — the order's own attribute and a copy on every line — and
B8 says a definition exists exactly once. Two homes is how two reports start disagreeing, and
this one would disagree *silently*, because both copies come from the same load and would agree
until the first time they did not. It also needs a new contract key and a new `Endpoint` field to
build a URL the recorder cannot currently express.

**Why not (c), a mapped date on the line.** Same objection with an extra step: the mapping would
have to reach into another table to get it, which M5 forbids outright.

**Why not (d), grouping on the peripheral.** The stage still needs a non-null date to exist at
all, so it does not escape the problem. And ADR 0007 rejected the peripheral-as-of-now reasoning
already: a peripheral is current state, a bridge row is the version in which the event is dated,
and reading one against the other puts two instants on one answer.

### What this does not become

The temptation this record exists to close is to let `date_attribute` take an expression, or to
let it reach further than one declared edge because "the walk goes there anyway". Neither. The
value is *a date attribute of an entity reached along a declared edge*, resolved exactly as its
key is resolved. Arithmetic on it belongs in the mapping under ADR 0007; anything else is a
second expression language in a file that is not linted, which ADR 0007 refused on §3.

## Consequences

* Good, because the question is answerable, and answerable at the grain it is asked at
* Good, because it reuses the walk rather than adding a mechanism beside it: one more column off
  a row the generator already resolves, at an instant it already got right
* Good, because slice 5's two-hop chain inherits this unchanged — a date reached along two edges
  is the same rule applied twice, and needs no new decision
* Good, because the date on a line is traceable to `ORDER.PLACED_ON`, which has one definition,
  so the page's glossary can explain the axis a reader is looking at
* Bad, because `dab/uss.yaml` now has two shapes for one field, and a reader has to know that a
  dot means "inherited". The alternative — always qualifying — would rewrite three existing
  declarations for no gain, and `<ENTITY>.<ATTRIBUTE>` is the notation the questions already use
* Bad, because a line's date now moves if its order is re-pointed to a different order, which
  cannot happen in this source and is a real property of the design rather than a bug. The
  as-of resolution is what bounds it: the date is the one in force when the line was observed

## Confirmation

# A stage may be dated by a date it inherits along the walk, named where it is inherited from

## Context and Problem Statement

Slice 4 asks for revenue per order **month**. Revenue is measured on an order line — quantity
times price less discount — so the bridge needs a row per line. And **an order line has no
date.** The source's `OrderDetail` has five properties and not one of them is a date; the live
`$metadata` says so, and there is nothing to map from.

The generator can only date a stage by an attribute of the event's own entity. `read_uss`
resolves `date_attribute` against `model.entity(event.entity_id)`, so naming the order's date on
a line event fails with a bare `KeyError: "ORDER_LINE has no attribute 'PLACED_ON'"` — not even a
`UssError`, so the refusal arrives with no explanation attached.

Nor may any layer go and fetch one. M1 forbids a join or a subquery in a mapping's `table:`; M5
forbids a reach into another table; a DAS contract has no key for a join. A second mapped table
on `ORDER_LINE` would be keyed by the order, which is not a line.

So the question the plan wrote down for this slice cannot be built at all without deciding
something the plan did not anticipate.

**What is already true, and is the whole reason this is small.** The walk exists. For every
edge, `_inherit_cte` already resolves the parent **as of the observation time of the row that
inherits** and puts the parent's key on the child's bridge row. ADR 0006 spent its whole decision
on getting that instant right. A date is another column of the row the walk already found.

This is also what a Unified Star Schema does. Puppini's bridge is a row per measurement event;
the event for an order line is the order being placed, on the day it was placed. Dating a line by
its order's date is not an accommodation — it is what the shape means.

## Decision Drivers

* the question is answerable at all, which today it is not
* a bridge row is true as of one instant, and every column on it is true as of that same instant
* a mechanism that already exists, extended, rather than a second one beside it
* the date a reader sees is traceable to a definition in the one place data is explained
* slice 5 walks two hops, and must not need a third mechanism

## Considered Options

* **(a)** The date inherits along the walk, named as `<ENTITY>.<ATTRIBUTE>` in the sidecar
* **(b)** Record `OrderDetails?$expand=Order` so the landed line carries the order's date
* **(c)** Give `ORDER_LINE` its own date attribute, mapped from the order via the source
* **(d)** Drop the calendar and let the question group on the order peripheral's date

## Decision Outcome

Chosen: **(a), the date inherits along the walk**, written in `dab/uss.yaml` as

```yaml
    - id: ORDERED
      entity: ORDER_LINE
      date_attribute: ORDER.PLACED_ON      # qualified: inherited along the edge to ORDER
```

An unqualified `date_attribute` still means an attribute of the event's own entity, which is
every event declared so far and stays the ordinary case. A qualified one names the entity the
date is inherited from, and that entity must be reachable along a declared edge from the event's
entity — otherwise it is refused, by name, with the edges that do exist listed.

The date is resolved **in the same CTE and at the same instant as the key**, because they are the
same row of the same parent. Anything else would put two instants on one bridge row, which is the
confusion ADR 0006 calls the entire difference between the option it chose and the one it
rejected. A line whose order cannot be resolved gets a null date and therefore no bridge row, by
the filter the generator already emits — consistent with how an event that did not happen is
already handled.

**Why not (b), expanding the source record.** It is the cheap-looking one and it is the worst.
`PLACED_ON` would then have two homes — the order's own attribute and a copy on every line — and
B8 says a definition exists exactly once. Two homes is how two reports start disagreeing, and
this one would disagree *silently*, because both copies come from the same load and would agree
until the first time they did not. It also needs a new contract key and a new `Endpoint` field to
build a URL the recorder cannot currently express.

**Why not (c), a mapped date on the line.** Same objection with an extra step: the mapping would
have to reach into another table to get it, which M5 forbids outright.

**Why not (d), grouping on the peripheral.** The stage still needs a non-null date to exist at
all, so it does not escape the problem. And ADR 0007 rejected the peripheral-as-of-now reasoning
already: a peripheral is current state, a bridge row is the version in which the event is dated,
and reading one against the other puts two instants on one answer.

### What this does not become

The temptation this record exists to close is to let `date_attribute` take an expression, or to
let it reach further than one declared edge because "the walk goes there anyway". Neither. The
value is *a date attribute of an entity reached along a declared edge*, resolved exactly as its
key is resolved. Arithmetic on it belongs in the mapping under ADR 0007; anything else is a
second expression language in a file that is not linted, which ADR 0007 refused on §3.

## Consequences

* Good, because the question is answerable, and answerable at the grain it is asked at
* Good, because it reuses the walk rather than adding a mechanism beside it: one more column off
  a row the generator already resolves, at an instant it already got right
* Good, because slice 5's two-hop chain inherits this unchanged — a date reached along two edges
  is the same rule applied twice, and needs no new decision
* Good, because the date on a line is traceable to `ORDER.PLACED_ON`, which has one definition,
  so the page's glossary can explain the axis a reader is looking at
* Bad, because `dab/uss.yaml` now has two shapes for one field, and a reader has to know that a
  dot means "inherited". The alternative — always qualifying — would rewrite three existing
  declarations for no gain, and `<ENTITY>.<ATTRIBUTE>` is the notation the questions already use
* Bad, because a line's date now moves if its order is re-pointed to a different order, which
  cannot happen in this source and is a real property of the design rather than a bug. The
  as-of resolution is what bounds it: the date is the one in force when the line was observed

## Confirmation

`tests/test_uss.py` asserts that a qualified `date_attribute` is resolved from the inherited
entity and not from the event's own; that it is refused, naming the available edges, when the
entity it names is not reachable along one; that an unqualified one still means the event's own
entity; and that the date and the key come from the same CTE, so no bridge row can carry two
instants. The neutral fixture gains an event on `CHILD` dated by `PARENT.HAPPENED_ON`, which is
the shape this record is about and which the fixture did not have.

A data check asserts that every bridge row's `_event_date` for such a stage equals the inherited
entity's own date for the key on that row — the property that would break silently if the two
were ever resolved at different instants.

# A composite source key becomes one key expression, and a check compares it against the parts it was made from

## Context and Problem Statement

The source's order lines are keyed on `(OrderId, ProductId)`. Conventions M2 has permitted
"a `concat` of casts with a separator" since slice 1 and warned that a concat without one makes
`'A1' + '23'` and `'A12' + '3'` the same key — a clause that has been **review-only for three
slices** because nothing had a composite key. This is the slice that has one.

A probe built the whole slice four times over and measured what the rule has been asserting.

**The collision this data can produce: none.** Over all 2155 real order lines, a separator-less
concat yields 2155 distinct keys — because every `OrderId` is exactly five digits, so the split
point is never ambiguous. A separator-less key would pass every gate, every data check and both
acceptance queries. The warning is right in general and unfalsifiable here, which is the most
dangerous shape a rule can have: it looks satisfied whatever you do.

**A separator that can occur in a value does not fix it.** Measured, with `'-'` between
`('A-1','23')` and `('A','1-23')`: five distinct keys from six pairs. With a separator outside
the value domain: six from six. So "the parts are integers, so `-` is fine" is exactly the
reasoning that is *fine today and wrong at the first string key* — and the key cannot be changed
later, so "wrong later" means wrong with the old key already immortal.

**`concat` ignores nulls; `||` does not.** Measured: `concat('1213','-',NULL)` is `'1213-'`, not
null. `concat_ws` drops the separator too. `'1213' || '-' || NULL` is null. The source's metadata
does **not** mark `OrderDetail.OrderId` or `ProductId` `Nullable="false"` — unlike `Order.OrderId`,
which it does — so a null half silently produces a truncated key that collides with a real one.

**M2's stated reason is wrong, and the truth is worse in a different way.** M2 says two entries
are read as alternate identifiers and "that mode cannot be undone once loaded". Measured: two
entries are **refused at deploy**, loudly, unless `allow_multiple_identifiers` is set on the
mapping group. With it set, the entity key becomes a **minted UUID** — not derived from anything
in DAS — so the layer stops being rebuildable from the source, which is a blueprint promise. The
repository already catches that, but under the `_focal`/`_idfr` vendor pins, which name the
wrong cause.

**And the key expression genuinely cannot be changed after loading.** Changing only `'-'` to
`'/'` and re-executing doubled everything: 2155 keys became 4310, and revenue over the bridge
went from 1,265,793.0395 to 2,531,586.079. `adss check` caught it — as
`ORDER_LINE_desc holds no duplicate versions … a growing gap is FULL ingestion duplicating
silently`, which names a cause that has nothing to do with what happened and would cost a reader
an afternoon.

## Decision Drivers

* a key that cannot collide, demonstrated rather than argued from the shape of the data
* a rule that still holds when a later composite key has a string part
* failing closed on a null part, rather than producing a shorter key that collides
* the next person is told the truth about what two entries actually do

## Considered Options

* `concat` of casts with a separator — what M2's text suggests
* `||` of casts with a separator, plus a check comparing the composed key against its parts
* Two `primary_keys` entries with `allow_multiple_identifiers`
* A surrogate minted in DAS

## Decision Outcome

Chosen: **`||` of casts with a separator, and a generated check that the composed key has exactly
as many distinct values as the source's own composite key.**

```yaml
primary_keys: ["cast(order_id AS VARCHAR) || '-' || cast(product_id AS VARCHAR)"]
```

The check is the part that matters, and it is what turns three slices of asserted reasoning into
something falsifiable. Whatever separator is chosen and whatever the parts turn out to be, the
composed key must not collapse two source rows into one — and that is directly countable against
the contract's own `primary_keys`, which DAS already records as a composite. A separator argument
is a prediction; this is a measurement, and it fires on the data that actually landed.

`||` rather than `concat`, because `concat` is null-blind: it turns a missing half into a shorter
key that can collide with a real one, silently. `||` yields null, and a null key fails at the
engine rather than in a report six months later. The dab skill recommends `concat`; that
recommendation is wrong for a composite key and is corrected.

**Why not two entries.** Not because M2's stated reason is right — it is not — but because what
actually happens is worse: the entity key becomes a minted UUID with nothing in DAS to recompute
it from, so DAB stops being rebuildable from the source. M2's text is corrected to say what the
engine really does.

**Why not a surrogate in DAS.** It would be minted there instead, with the same rebuildability
problem one layer earlier, and DAS's job is to record what a source sent rather than to invent an
identifier it did not.

### On the separator, honestly

`'-'` is chosen for readability — `10248-11` is a key a person can recognise in a screenshot —
and it is safe here only because both parts are non-negative integers. That is not a general
guarantee and this record does not pretend it is. **A composite key with a part that is not a
non-negative integer is a new decision**, not an application of this one: the separator has to be
chosen against that part's value domain, and the check below is what would catch a wrong choice.

## Consequences

* Good, because the property M2 has asserted for three slices is now measured on every build,
  against the source's own key rather than against an argument about digits
* Good, because a null part fails rather than producing a key that is quietly one character short
* Good, because the check is generated per contract, so a later composite key is checked without
  anything else changing
* Bad, because the key is not a number the business uses. `10248-11` is this system's identifier
  for a line, and no order form has ever carried it. If a question ever needs "which product", the
  answer is a `PRODUCT` peripheral reached along an edge — slice 5's content — and **never**
  splitting this string back apart, which would be a reach into a key's internals from a layer
  that must not know it has any
* Bad, because re-keying an entity after it is loaded doubles its history, and the check that
  notices names the wrong cause. That is recorded here and left alone: the right repair is to drop
  the schemas and rebuild, which the build already supports, and a check that explained it
  properly would have to know what a re-key looks like

# A composite source key becomes one key expression, and a check compares it against the parts it was made from

## Context and Problem Statement

The source's order lines are keyed on `(OrderId, ProductId)`. Conventions M2 has permitted
"a `concat` of casts with a separator" since slice 1 and warned that a concat without one makes
`'A1' + '23'` and `'A12' + '3'` the same key — a clause that has been **review-only for three
slices** because nothing had a composite key. This is the slice that has one.

A probe built the whole slice four times over and measured what the rule has been asserting.

**The collision this data can produce: none.** Over all 2155 real order lines, a separator-less
concat yields 2155 distinct keys — because every `OrderId` is exactly five digits, so the split
point is never ambiguous. A separator-less key would pass every gate, every data check and both
acceptance queries. The warning is right in general and unfalsifiable here, which is the most
dangerous shape a rule can have: it looks satisfied whatever you do.

**A separator that can occur in a value does not fix it.** Measured, with `'-'` between
`('A-1','23')` and `('A','1-23')`: five distinct keys from six pairs. With a separator outside
the value domain: six from six. So "the parts are integers, so `-` is fine" is exactly the
reasoning that is *fine today and wrong at the first string key* — and the key cannot be changed
later, so "wrong later" means wrong with the old key already immortal.

**`concat` ignores nulls; `||` does not.** Measured: `concat('1213','-',NULL)` is `'1213-'`, not
null. `concat_ws` drops the separator too. `'1213' || '-' || NULL` is null. The source's metadata
does **not** mark `OrderDetail.OrderId` or `ProductId` `Nullable="false"` — unlike `Order.OrderId`,
which it does — so a null half silently produces a truncated key that collides with a real one.

**M2's stated reason is wrong, and the truth is worse in a different way.** M2 says two entries
are read as alternate identifiers and "that mode cannot be undone once loaded". Measured: two
entries are **refused at deploy**, loudly, unless `allow_multiple_identifiers` is set on the
mapping group. With it set, the entity key becomes a **minted UUID** — not derived from anything
in DAS — so the layer stops being rebuildable from the source, which is a blueprint promise. The
repository already catches that, but under the `_focal`/`_idfr` vendor pins, which name the
wrong cause.

**And the key expression genuinely cannot be changed after loading.** Changing only `'-'` to
`'/'` and re-executing doubled everything: 2155 keys became 4310, and revenue over the bridge
went from 1,265,793.0395 to 2,531,586.079. `adss check` caught it — as
`ORDER_LINE_desc holds no duplicate versions … a growing gap is FULL ingestion duplicating
silently`, which names a cause that has nothing to do with what happened and would cost a reader
an afternoon.

## Decision Drivers

* a key that cannot collide, demonstrated rather than argued from the shape of the data
* a rule that still holds when a later composite key has a string part
* failing closed on a null part, rather than producing a shorter key that collides
* the next person is told the truth about what two entries actually do

## Considered Options

* `concat` of casts with a separator — what M2's text suggests
* `||` of casts with a separator, plus a check comparing the composed key against its parts
* Two `primary_keys` entries with `allow_multiple_identifiers`
* A surrogate minted in DAS

## Decision Outcome

Chosen: **`||` of casts with a separator, and a generated check that the composed key has exactly
as many distinct values as the source's own composite key.**

```yaml
primary_keys: ["cast(order_id AS VARCHAR) || '-' || cast(product_id AS VARCHAR)"]
```

The check is the part that matters, and it is what turns three slices of asserted reasoning into
something falsifiable. Whatever separator is chosen and whatever the parts turn out to be, the
composed key must not collapse two source rows into one — and that is directly countable against
the contract's own `primary_keys`, which DAS already records as a composite. A separator argument
is a prediction; this is a measurement, and it fires on the data that actually landed.

`||` rather than `concat`, because `concat` is null-blind: it turns a missing half into a shorter
key that can collide with a real one, silently. `||` yields null, and a null key fails at the
engine rather than in a report six months later. The dab skill recommends `concat`; that
recommendation is wrong for a composite key and is corrected.

**Why not two entries.** Not because M2's stated reason is right — it is not — but because what
actually happens is worse: the entity key becomes a minted UUID with nothing in DAS to recompute
it from, so DAB stops being rebuildable from the source. M2's text is corrected to say what the
engine really does.

**Why not a surrogate in DAS.** It would be minted there instead, with the same rebuildability
problem one layer earlier, and DAS's job is to record what a source sent rather than to invent an
identifier it did not.

### On the separator, honestly

`'-'` is chosen for readability — `10248-11` is a key a person can recognise in a screenshot —
and it is safe here only because both parts are non-negative integers. That is not a general
guarantee and this record does not pretend it is. **A composite key with a part that is not a
non-negative integer is a new decision**, not an application of this one: the separator has to be
chosen against that part's value domain, and the check below is what would catch a wrong choice.

## Consequences

* Good, because the property M2 has asserted for three slices is now measured on every build,
  against the source's own key rather than against an argument about digits
* Good, because a null part fails rather than producing a key that is quietly one character short
* Good, because the check is generated per contract, so a later composite key is checked without
  anything else changing
* Bad, because the key is not a number the business uses. `10248-11` is this system's identifier
  for a line, and no order form has ever carried it. If a question ever needs "which product", the
  answer is a `PRODUCT` peripheral reached along an edge — slice 5's content — and **never**
  splitting this string back apart, which would be a reach into a key's internals from a layer
  that must not know it has any
* Bad, because re-keying an entity after it is loaded doubles its history, and the check that
  notices names the wrong cause. That is recorded here and left alone: the right repair is to drop
  the schemas and rebuild, which the build already supports, and a check that explained it
  properly would have to know what a re-key looks like

## Confirmation

`tests/test_mapping_rules.py` asserts that a composed key expression conforms to M2 — one entry,
producing a VARCHAR — and that two entries are still refused before the engine sees them.

A generated data check, one per contract with a composite key, counts the distinct composed keys
in `das__staged.<table>__current` against the distinct source key tuples and fails on any
difference. It is written against the shape that would break it — a separator-less concat over
parts whose lengths vary — and that case is constructed in `tests/` so the check is known to be
capable of failing, rather than known to pass.

What is **not** confirmed, and is recorded rather than claimed: nothing detects that a key
expression has *changed* between builds. The signature is a doubling of the description table,
which an existing check reports under a name that describes a different defect. Making that
check name the right cause would mean teaching it what a re-key looks like, and the repair — drop
and rebuild — is the same either way.
